Uniform Title: Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī Author: Brahmānandagiri Editor: Pañcānana Śāstrī
Description: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha.
Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: September 22, 2008.
Publisher: Unknown (pre-1900) Bengali Script;
Country of Publication: India; Title: Śāktānandatarangiṇī.
First Chapter: The Auspicious Invocation. Having prostrated before the eternal Prakṛti, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self;
The Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī is composed for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.
The meaning of the word *prakṛti*: Now, what is *prakṛti*? It is as follows: *Prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium of the three *guṇas*. Thus it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas). Their state of equilibrium is known as the Unmanifest (avyakta) or Primordial Nature (prakṛti).
That indeed is the Root-Nature (mūlaprakṛti), as well as Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Elsewhere also:
"O Dear One, there is a triad of qualities consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
when that Supreme Śakti acts as the presiding ground of these qualities."
She would be Prakṛti, and Puruṣa would be Sadāśiva.
Regarding the meaning of the word "eternal" (*nitya*), the *Śaktiyāmala* states:
"She in whom the birth of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others occurs by her own will."
That into which it dissolves again is proclaimed as the eternal one.
The meaning of the term *paramātman* is as follows: that which is both supreme (*parama*) and the self (*ātman*) is the *paramātman*; the sense is "the most excellent self.
And its excellence consists in its being the creator of the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others by its own will.

Alternatively, even though devoid of those respective sense organs, it is the substratum of the perceptions produced by those respective sense organs. And thus says the Śruti (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19):
"Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears."
"He knows the universe, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the primordial, great Puruṣa.
Thus, the Supreme Self (paramātman) is the substratum of eternal knowledge and activity, and by the principle of parsimony (lāghava), he is one alone.
And the individual self (jīvātman) is the substratum of produced knowledge and material nature (prakṛti), and it is infinite.

One might argue that, due to the distinctions among humans, animals, birds, and so forth, and likewise due to the differences in the bodies of Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, and others, the Supreme Self must indeed be manifold; however, this is not so, for it would be like the illusion of multiplicity in space caused by the differences of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as jars and the like.
Due to the delusion that the self is distinct because of the differences in bodies such as those of humans, animals, and birds;

because the oneness of the self is perceived when the body is destroyed during deep sleep, cosmic dissolution, and so forth; and likewise because of the multiplicity of deities such as Śiva who have assumed bodies for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees—
In this regard, [the objection is raised] due to the delusion of diversity; for a real entity is not established by means of delusion.
Now, he states the subject to be explained, which is the determination of the scope of the *ullāsa*:
"In the first *ullāsa*, I shall describe the body as it arises from karma."
I shall explain initiation in the second [chapter], and the determination of yoga in the third.
The morning rites are in the fourth [chapter], while the seat is likewise in the fifth;
the procedure for the internal sacrifice is in the sixth, and the daily worship in the seventh.
In the ninth [chapter], the arrangement of the garland, the characteristics of recitation,
the Mahāsetu, the Setu, and likewise the Kullukā are described in the tenth.
The purification of the face is performed in the Rudra [chapter], the preliminary rite (puraskriyā) in the twelfth,
the consecration of the King of Yantras (yantrarāja), and the offering of the oblation (balidāna) in the thirteenth.
The fruit arising from offerings such as ritual services is indeed in the fourteenth [chapter],
and likewise, the fruit of recollecting the name, performing worship, and so forth, is in the fifteenth.
In the Kali age, expiation for defects arising from association and the like is prescribed in the sixteenth [chapter];
likewise, the sacrificial pit in the seventeenth, and the fire-oblation thereafter in the eighteenth.
Then, the meaning of the names beginning with "Sarvamaṅgalā" was determined,
and the majesty of Goddess Durgā was specifically demonstrated;
having meditated upon the dust of the Guru's feet, this *Ullāsa-nirṇaya* was composed.
Regarding the sequence of the arising of the body,
in the *Jñānabhāṣya*, the Goddess said: "O Lord, what is the nature of the body, and by what action is liberation attained?"
Now I wish to hear; speak to me, O Moon-crested One.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that the body arises from karma;
when a woman is in her menses, she becomes pure on the fifth day.
Afflicted by the arrows of desire, she then seeks a man;
through the union of the female organ and the male organ, sexual intercourse occurs between the two.
O Goddess, from mutual touch great pleasure arises,
and likewise semen, which is dependent upon the prāṇa, apāna, and other vital breaths, flows forth.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
the reality of all these becomes manifest within the seed of blood situated in the body.
Then, O Goddess, it revolves within the navel cavity by means of the vital airs,
just as a potter fashions jars and other vessels upon his wheel.
In that manner, the vital wind (samīraṇa) enters the body of living beings within the womb;
it forms the embryo (kalala) in one night, and a bubble (budbuda) on the fifth day.
In ten nights it becomes blood; in fourteen days, a mass of flesh;
and when one month is fully completed, the mass of flesh begins to sprout.
In the beginning, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) arises as a mass, like a similar sprout;
in its center stands Mount Sumeru, which has the form of a backbone.
It is the abode of all beings, both moving and stationary, including especially the gods and others; it is also within Mount Meru.
The individual soul, shaped like the flame of a lamp, always resides within the heart;
just as a hawk tied by a string is drawn back again even though it has flown away.
In the same way, the individual soul (jīva) is bound to the vital breath and is drawn along by the prāṇa and apāna.
O Supreme Goddess, hear now of the retinue of the individual soul.
The eyes, the nostrils, the ears, and the tongue, O lotus-faced one;
the hands, the feet, and the secret organ and genitals, O Maheśānī, in due order, O beloved!
O Supreme Goddess! O Sovereign Lady! The navel, the mind, and those known as the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are all situated within the body.
And of all the senses, O Maheśānī, the mind is the charioteer; it is bound by its own sins and merits, O Beloved.
Indeed, through association, the individual soul performs all actions, both good and evil;
however, the soul that is pure and characterized by sattva is free from good and evil deeds.
Through the union with the vital breath (jīva), the mind always performs its proper function;
when two months are fully completed, fat (medas) is produced therein.
The marrow and bones [are formed] in three months; the hair and skin in the fourth;
and the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, throat, and belly in the fifth.
From blood semen is produced; from semen the arising of the drop (bindu) occurs.
From prāṇa wind is produced; from apāna there arises the fire of time (kālāgni).
From semen the channels arise; from semen fire is produced;
from flesh the excretions arise, and from that marrow is also formed.
Through the wind (vāyu) the vital breath (prāṇa) is produced; from the downward breath (apāna) fire arises. The tongue and the nose of all embodied beings are generated by the semen (śukra).
From *rakta* arise the left and right eyes;
from *prāṇa* arises the void (*śūnya*) as well as the two apertures of the vital breath.
In the sixth month, the face and likewise the feet [are formed], and in the seventh, all the limbs;
thereafter, in the eighth month, the joints reach full completion.
The skeletal support of the egg (the body), beginning from the base of the anus,
consists of thirty-two knots that are always to be known through wisdom;
in its center, all the channels are perpetually situated.
The Determination of the Channels Residing in the Body:
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third;
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī.
Alambuṣā, Kuhu, and likewise Śaṅkhinī as the tenth;
there are also seventy-two thousand other minor channels (nāḍikās).
The *iḍā* is on the left side, and likewise the *piṅgalā* on the right;
the *suṣumnā* is at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and the *gāndhārī* is in the left eye.
On the right is Hastijihvā, and Pūṣan is on the right ear;
Yaśasvinī is on the left, and likewise Ālambuṣā is in the mouth.
Kuhu is at the base of the *liṅga*, and Śaṅkhinī is above the head;
thus, these ten channels remain, closing off the gateway.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these five have attained stability both externally and internally; these are the qualities of the elements.
Bone, skin, as well as sinews, hair, and likewise flesh—
these are declared to be the five qualities established in the earth.
Excrement, urine, semen, phlegm, and blood—these are declared to be the five qualities; therein the water element is established.
Hunger, thirst, as well as sleep, delusion, and patience—these are declared to be the five qualities; within them, the fiery element (tejas) is established.
Opposing, drawing back, contracting, supporting, and likewise nourishing—
these five qualities are said to reside in the wind (vāyu).
Passion, hatred, delusion, fear, and likewise shame—
these are declared to be the five qualities established in space (ākāśa).
The determination of the winds residing in the body:
the vital breaths are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
and [the secondary winds] are nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
These ten qualities are said to be all identical in nature to the vital breath (prāṇa).
Prāṇa always dwells in the heart, while apāna resides in the region of the anus.
The *samāna* wind is located at the region of the navel, and the *udāna* at the region of the throat;
the *vyāna* pervades the entire body—these are the five principal winds.
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—
these exist within the thousands of channels in the form of the vital breaths (jīva).
Description of the Sheath of the Body:
Whatever qualities exist in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) reside within the physical body—
the netherworld (pātāla), the mountains, the worlds, and the nine planets beginning with the Sun.
The seven heavens beginning with Bhūḥ, as well as the names of all embodied beings, are all situated within the *piṇḍa*; I shall tell you their location.
Regarding the description of the seven netherworlds (pātālas) within the body:
one should know that below the feet is Atala, and above that is Vitala;
Sūtala is at the knees, and Tala is at the joints and apertures.
A wise person should perceive Talātala in the middle of the anus (or ankle), Rasātala at the root of the penis,
and Pātāla at the joint of the hips, starting from the feet.
The description of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ within the body:
Bhūrloka is in the region of the navel, while Bhuvarloka is likewise in the heart;
Svarloka is in the region of the throat, and Maharloka is in the eyes.
Above that is Janaloka, and Tapoloka is on the forehead;
Satyaloka is in the great yoni—thus are the fourteen worlds.
A description of the seven mountains and forests within the body:
Meru is situated in the triangle, Mandara in the upper world,
Kailāsa in the right corner, and Himālaya in the left corner.
Vindhya and Viṣṇu are above that; these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas).
O Maheśānī! Within the body, the description of the seven continents is as follows: Jambūdvīpa is situated in the place of the bones;
Kuśadvīpa is in the flesh, and Krauñcadvīpa is in the veins.
Śākadvīpa is situated in the blood that is in all the joints of living beings;
above that is Śālmalidvīpa, and Plakṣadvīpa is in the collection of body hair;
Puṣkaradvīpa is in the navel, and the ocean follows immediately after that.
A description of the seven oceans situated within the body: the salt-water ocean is in the urine; the milk-ocean is in the semen;
the curd-ocean is in the marrow; and above that is the ghee-ocean.
In another manuscript, the reading is "rasodake rasaḥ proktaḥ" (in the water of taste, taste is proclaimed).
Fat-water is proclaimed as the ocean; sugarcane juice would be the ocean of the waist-blood.
Among the bloods, the wine-ocean is mentioned; thus the seven oceans are described.
O Pārvatī! Listen, for I shall describe the mandala of the planets situated within the body and the mandala of the planets themselves:
the sun is located in the *nāda-cakra*, and the moon is in the *bindu-cakra*.
Maṅgala is said to be in the eyes, and likewise Soma’s son (Budha) in the heart;
Guru is in the belly, and Śukra is likewise in the semen.
Saturn is situated at the navel-cakra, Rāhu is always situated in the mouth, and Ketu is in the feet and the navel; thus the circle of planets resides within the body.

The recollection of previous births by the living being residing in the womb: "In the ninth month, the embodied being dwelling in the city of nine gates remembers everything— the mind and all the temporal modifications that cause transformation."
Having made pleasure and pain equal within their hearts,
men experience the fruits of both good and evil deeds performed in a previous birth.
Knowing all that to be fruitful, she entered the womb with her feet upward and her face downward, while those two of terrible appearance remained motionless.
If the mother enjoys food, drink, and so forth with pleasure, then he,
having placed his mouth at the region of the mother's navel, drinks from it.
Therefore, he lives within the womb; otherwise, death would occur.
I practice the auspicious knowledge that carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
"I shall indeed perform the worship of the gods, the twice-born, and my gurus with devotion, according to my fortune; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt."
"Having become a long-term practitioner of yoga, I shall be liberated and go to that state. Thus, while situated in the womb and afflicted by the torments of the womb, the living being—
who has attained the characteristic of consciousness— constantly contemplates this within the mind.
In the meantime, O Goddess, amidst the peril of the embryos of all beings, [he spoke].
In the ninth or tenth month, by powerful winds of childbirth,
the creature is expelled through the opening like an arrow, suffering with fever;
even when fallen, he does not know, for he remains unconscious as he drops from that place.
Due to the force of the winds of birth and the pressure upon the vaginal opening,
all the knowledge previously contemplated in the heart while in the womb is forgotten.
Just as when the elements have become like a womb, through the pressure [of birth], one constantly remembers one's mother; so too does hunger, a firm pain, [cause one to remember].
The cause for the distinction between female, male, and so forth is as follows:
if there is an excess of blood (rajas), one becomes a woman; if there is an excess of semen (śukra), one becomes a man;
and if there is an equality of the blood and the seed, a neuter (napuṃsaka) is born from that.
These five are also created for the embodied being while still in the womb:
lifespan, action, wealth, knowledge, and death itself.
Description of the stages of life:
an infant (*bāla*), a child (*śiśu*), a young boy (*pogaṇḍa*), and likewise a youth (*kiśoraka*); beyond that is the adolescent (*yuvaka*), and after that, the mature adult (*prauḍha*).
The very mature, the old, and beyond that the very aged,
as well as gray hair and death— these are proclaimed to be the stages of life.
At that very moment, one assumes a subtle body (ātivāhika-śarīra);
this occurs only for human beings, and never for any other living creatures.
It is declared that [the soul] becomes a preta-body in due course; of this there is no doubt. Then, when the sapindikarana rite has been performed by the kinsmen and men, [it attains liberation].
When a full year has passed, it attains another body;
thereafter, it goes to hell or to heaven according to its own karma.
"At that moment" means at the moment of death.
The manner in which living beings experience the fruits of their karma is as follows:
divinity, then humanity, the state of a beast, and likewise the state of a bird.
A living being attains the state of a worm or the state of an immobile thing through its own actions.
Immovable beings, those beginning with the mobile, birds, animals, and humans—
these are born or die within this cycle of existence, an ocean of suffering.
A living being is born through karma and perishes through karma alone;
when the body has perished, that very karma causes one to obtain a body once again.
Just as a calf finds its mother among thousands of cows,
so does one's good and evil karma follow after the doer.
Who else can alter powerful past karma?
O Goddess, it is said that the body is composed of karma; thus, each respective state is firmly established.
The Creator should ordain manifestation in accordance with the nature of karma;
O Goddess, O Beloved, all this world of the moving and the unmoving is essentially composed of karma.
The mother is action, the father is action; action alone is the supreme teacher.
Whether heaven or even hell, a person attains through action alone.
Constrained by his own merits and demerits consisting of pleasure and pain,
he [experiences] a body endowed with various births and enjoyment born of his own karma.
Regarding the description of the excellence of human birth: O Pārvatī, even after thousands upon thousands of births,
a living being may perhaps attain human status through the accumulation of merit.
Sleep, sexual union, and food are common to all living beings;
yet, O beloved, a human being is said to be possessed of knowledge, while one devoid of knowledge is a beast.
Prosperity is like a dream, youth is comparable to a flower, and even the highest lifespan is like a flash of lightning; yet for the man of wisdom, there is steadfastness.
Among the eighty-four hundred thousand types of bodies assumed by embodied beings,
true knowledge of reality cannot be attained anywhere except in a human body.
The classes of deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as all elemental beings, inevitably pursue destruction; therefore, one should practice that which leads to the highest good.
All living beings, under the influence of delusion, are devoted to their own bodies, wealth, wives, and so forth;
they are born and they die— alas, wretched, being deluded by ignorance!
O beloved, one should abandon saṃsāra, which is the source of all suffering, the locus of all calamities,
and the abode of all evils.
This body, wasting away moment by moment, is not perceived;
like an unbaked clay pot in water, its disintegration is not even noticed.
"Offspring are mine, my wife is mine, wealth is mine, and my kinsmen are mine"—
as the mortal speaks thus, the wolf of Time devours him by force.
By which the earth is burned and even Mount Meru is split asunder;
by which the waters of the ocean are dried up—what need is there to speak of physical bodies?
On the statement that delusion is the cause of saṃsāra:
Even a man bound by fetters made of iron cords may be released;
but one who is attached to women, wealth, and the like is never released.
O Goddess, those who lack knowledge repeatedly experience the bodily actions of pleasure and pain; in the next world, they go and come again and again.
Attachment is a bond without a rope; evil association is a most potent poison.
Righteous association and discernment are the two stainless eyes. How could that man who lacks these not be blind? How could he not stray from the path?
There are two words that are the cause of liberation: "mine" and "not mine," which lead respectively to bondage and liberation.
By thinking "it is mine," a living being is bound; by thinking "it is not mine," one is liberated.
Bondage arises from the superimposition of "mine," while liberation comes from being free of "mine";
just as a fish greedy for meat does not see the iron hook.
Likewise, the embodied being, greedy for pleasure, does not perceive the affliction of Yama,
having committed deeds pierced by sin and drenched with the clarified butter of sense-objects.
Mortality devours the human being ripened by the fires of passion and hatred;
O Kuleśvarī, this living soul departs, abandoning even its own body.
By what cause does the connection with women, mother, wealth, sons, and so forth arise?
A description of the nature of suffering in saṃsāra:
a hundred-year lifespan is exceedingly short, and sleep takes away half of it.
Half of that [life] is afflicted by the sufferings of childhood, disease, and old age, and even that [remaining half] is fruitless.
For saṃsāra has suffering as its root; he who possesses it is miserable.
O beloved, he by whom that [saṃsāra] has been abandoned is happy, and no other.
Human beings are constantly afflicted: by excrement and urine at dawn, by hunger and thirst at midday, and by passion and sleep at night.
People do not resort to divine medicine that destroys great diseases;
instead, they repeatedly engage in many unwholesome practices that increase those very ailments.
He who abandons the fruit of good deeds and performs evil deeds is like one who,
having stepped upon the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), seeks the milk of a sunflower.
Bodies are impermanent, and worldly prosperity is never eternal;
death is ever-present, so one must accumulate merit through the practice of Dharma.
That mortal whose mind is deluded is one who does not acquire the eternal Dharma by means of this unstable body that perishes at every moment.
For neither father nor mother goes there for the sake of companionship, nor does a son, nor kin; only dharma remains.
Bound by the snares consisting of son and wife, a man is not released—
whether he be wise or foolish, strong or weak.
Death is equal toward all everywhere— toward the lord and the poor alike—
from kings, from water, from fire, from thieves, and even from one's own kin.
Those who possess wealth are constantly in fear, like those who bear sin are in fear of death;
one should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's task in the forenoon.
Death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or not;
therefore, he who is always devoted to action through deed, mind, and speech is truly diligent.
He whose mind is free from the desire for fruits attains liberation;
"free from the desire for fruits" means devoid of the longing that produces one's own enjoyments.
Oh, the power of delusion and of that which is produced by its illusion!
O Goddess of the gods, could it delude even others, including the immortals?
Thus, from the words of the *Yāmala*: in the *Mārkaṇḍeya*, it is said—
“This Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) of Hari deludes this world with her.”
By that Mahāmāyā, the world of saṃsāra is deluded; not only is the world deluded, but even the minds of the gods. Indeed, that Blessed Goddess deludes even the minds of the wise.
"Having forcibly drawn them away, Mahāmāyā delivers them to delusion"—this refers to the praise of the wise; the meaning is "those who possess eternal knowledge."
The meaning of the term *mahāmāyā* is as follows:

she is called *mahāmāyā* because she is both great (*mahatī*) and illusion (*māyā*). She is *mahāmāyā* because she produces delusion for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*:
That very Māyā is Prakṛti, who deludes Śaṅkara,
as well as Hari, Virañci, and likewise other immortals.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa (6.61–63): "She who continuously causes that which was endowed with knowledge within the womb and impelled by the winds of birth to be born devoid of knowledge..."
And having applied himself to the delusion regarding his increasingly prior formative impressions,
he then [encounters] delusion, the sense of "mine," and doubt concerning knowledge regarding food and other such things.
Having repeatedly cast [the mind] again and again into anger, obstruction, and so forth,
one should thereafter swiftly engage it with desire, joined with contemplation day and night.
The differentiation of Mahāmāyā:
that Mahāmāyā is twofold—vidyā (knowledge) and avidyā (ignorance).
That Mahāmāyā which is the cause of liberation is vidyā; that Mahāmāyā which is the cause of bondage to saṃsāra is avidyā.
That is ignorance. In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"She is that eternal supreme knowledge which is the cause of ultimate liberation;
she alone, the Sovereign of all sovereigns, is also the cause of bondage to saṃsāra."
Elsewhere also it is said:
"Whether it be knowledge or ignorance, these two are both enveloped by Māyā;
that action which leads to bondage is proclaimed as ignorance."
That action which does not lead to bondage is proclaimed as knowledge.
Knowledge should always be cultivated, and ignorance never under any circumstances;
ignorance constitutes the bondage of karma, and through it, wisdom is destroyed.
From the destruction of knowledge comes loss; from loss, again, comes wandering in saṃsāra. From that terrible saṃsāra, moreover, comes even more terrible hell itself.
Therefore, ignorance should never be cultivated anywhere at any time.
Regarding the praise of knowledge:
that which is knowledge is Mahāmāyā, and she should always be served by the wise;
for the Śruti says, "Those who worship ignorance enter into blind darkness" (Īśa Upaniṣad 9).
Elsewhere also it is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) consists solely in being fixed within *saṃsāra*. In the *Rudrayāmala*:
"She who bestows happiness, she who bestows liberation, the eternal one, residing within all beings—when Māyā is pleased, then one attains perfection."
Māyā, the daughter of the mountain, is always to be saluted, praised, and worshipped at all times; she is to be heard and her glory is to be proclaimed eternally.
A wise person should not spend time in vain on activities such as gambling;
rather, he should spend it in the worship of the deity, japa, sacrifice, hymns of praise, and the like.
What is the use of other worthless talk when life is being spent away?
Therefore, O Goddess, by learning all the mantras and so forth from the mouth of the venerable Guru, one is easily liberated from the terrible bondage of saṃsāra.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Body," in the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī* composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme sage (*paramahaṃsa*), the holy one (*tīrtha*), and the renunciant (*avadhūta*).
The Second Chapter.
The Lord said: The Greatness of Initiation (Dīkṣā).
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me:
in the teaching of Śiva, there can be no liberation for living beings without initiation.
The machine does not exist without yoga, nor indeed does that [yoga] exist without mantra;
the practice of both together brings about the perfect realization of Brahman.
Just as a jar in a house enveloped by darkness becomes visible through a lamp,
so too the Self, though veiled by illusion, is brought within the range of perception by means of the mantra.
When the sixteenth year has arrived, one should perform initiation with a concentrated mind;
just as iron, through chemical juices and mantras according to the prescribed method, attains the state of gold.
"For the self thus pierced by initiation certainly attains the state of Śiva"—thus from the *Kulārṇava*. And in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"The rite of recitation (*japa*) and the worship of the deity must be performed by men who have received initiation."
There is no sin for those self-controlled ones, nor even the impurity of childbirth (*sūtaka*).
In the *Rudrayāmala*:
"In the Kali age, the wise man should worship the gods according to the procedures prescribed in the *Āgamas*."
For in the Kali age, the gods do not become pleased by any other ritual procedure.
Regarding the definition and etymology of the word *āgama*, the Rudrayāmala states:
"It has come from the mouths of Śiva and gone into the mouth of the Daughter of the Mountain."
Therefore, it is called the Āgama of the venerable Vāsudeva.
The plural number in "from the mouths" (*vaktrebhyaḥ*) is for the purpose of attaining the five traditions (*pañcāmnāya*). Thus it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"From my five mouths, the five traditions have emerged:
from the east and the west, and likewise from the south and the north."
It leads upward that which is situated below; thus it is called the Ūrdhvāmnāya (the Upper Tradition).
As many as are the grains of dust upon the earth, so many were proclaimed the mantras born of each individual Vedic tradition, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

The meaning is that, based on such statements as "the deity of all mantras is the bestower of their fruit," Vāsudeva is considered and accepted [as the deity]. Therefore, because he is not contradicted by the Vedas and because there is benefit [in following him], there is no exclusion of Āgama; for the word *āgama* refers exclusively to the true tradition (*sadāgama*).

Because of its primacy. For this very reason, Śiva speaks of the censure of false scriptures in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*: "O Goddess of gods! In the Kali age, people are for the most part of passionate (rājasa) and ignorant (tāmasa) nature."
Practicing forbidden acts, they delude many others;
O Goddess of the Gods, we two [consume] flesh, blood, and wine.
Those who bestow [gifts] without considering the dharma appropriate for their caste and stage of life become Brahma-rākṣasas, [as well as] bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
According to this statement, it is also said in the *Śrīkrama*:
"A Brahmin should never, under any circumstances, offer liquor to Mahādevī;
even if he desires the Left-hand path (*vāmamārga*), a Brahmin must not consume meat or liquor."
One should present those respective substances on the western side of the Goddess, at the side of the wheel;
however, these belong to the Śūdra alone and never to others.
A Vaiśya should offer pure honey; a Kṣatriya, however, honey mixed with ghee;
and a Brāhmaṇa should pour milk from cows into a copper vessel.
Coconut water in a bronze vessel is the purifier of all substances. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also:
"A Brāhmaṇa should offer cow's milk; a Kṣatriya, cow's clarified butter (gavyājya);
by Vaiśyas, honey should be given; and a Śūdra should perform [the offering] with flour-cake (paiṣṭī) and the like."

Regarding the reading *paiṣṭyādikam* (made from flour, etc. in this context, the reading *pauṣṇādikam* (related to the deity Pūṣan, etc. is also observed; if that were the case, it would constitute a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) even for a Śūdra. And so it was stated previously:
"Coconut water in a bronze vessel is a purifier of all substances for everyone."
One should present those various substances on the western side of the Goddess, at the side of the wheel;
however, these belong to the Śūdra alone, and never to others.

Because of this statement, and likewise because in many other Tantric passages the giving of primary substances and so forth to a Śūdra is prescribed, when there is mutual contradiction, one must resort to an option (*vikalpa*);
therefore, of those...
The giving of *surā* to Śūdras has thus become optional.

It is not merely that an alternative (*anukalpa*) is prescribed for a Śūdra in the absence of the [proper] substance; rather, even when the substance and other requirements are present, a Śūdra may perform worship by means of an alternative according to his own will. Thus, everything is beyond reproach.

Likewise, the practitioner who has been initiated by a Guru and relies upon the yoga of the mantra taught by Śiva and Śakti certainly becomes one who has accomplished his purpose. Thus it is said in the Āgamasāra:
"By Śiva and by the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti), through these two, everything is uplifted;
by means of these two, in the relationship of the signified and the signifier, Brahman is revealed.
Such is the meaning of the word *dīkṣā*.
The meaning of the word *dīkṣā* is stated in the *Yāmala*: "That which bestows radiant knowledge and likewise effects the destruction of sins—
for that reason it is celebrated as *dīkṣā* in this world by those who have mastered the Tantras."
Regarding the censure of worship by the uninitiated:
even if worshipped with thousands of ritual offerings accompanied by devotion,
the gods never accept the worship of one who is uninitiated.
All his actions are in vain; therefore, one who has not received initiation is a bound soul (paśu).
Regarding the rule for receiving the mantra, it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*:
But he who, having seen a mantra in a ritual manual (kalpa), should recite it without relying on a guru, [is a transgressor].
His lineage will perish and no fruit whatsoever shall be found for him.
In the *Yāmala*:
"One should receive the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*), which destroys all sins, from the mouth of the Guru."
Therefore, having made diligent effort, one should perform the practice of mantra-siddhi with a guru.
Regarding the meaning of the word *guru*, the *Yāmala* states:
"The syllable *gu* is said to bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*), and the letter *r* is the burner of sin."
The syllable *U* is said to be Śambhu; the Guru is remembered as being the essence of these three.
The characteristics of a guru are stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"One whose mother and father are pure, who has conquered his senses..."
One who knows all the scriptures, is distressed by the suffering of others,
speaks truthfully, is a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), is tranquil, and is of noble birth— such a twice-born man is declared to be a guru.
Regarding the procedure for honoring Brahmins:
because of the mention of the "twice-born" (dvija), the reception of mantras is from Brahmins. As stated in the Tantra:
"The twice-born who possesses virtuous conduct is indeed the guru of all the social classes."
Elsewhere it is also said:
"Having become devoted to one's own duty and having [received the instruction] from the mouth of a twice-born preceptor,
one attains all success and quickly achieves divinity."
A Śūdra who, having heard knowledge or even a mantra from the mouth of a Śūdra,
accepts it, goes to hell and certainly encounters suffering.
Regarding the fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*),
it is stated in the *Navaratneśvara*:
"The fruit of all initiations whatsoever is liberation."
This occurs because there is no distinction; however, these experiences are merely incidental.
In the *Yāmala*:
"An initiated Brāhmaṇa goes to the stainless world of Brahmā;
a Kṣatriya to the world of Indra, and likewise a Vaiśya to that of Prajāpati."
A Śūdra goes to the city of the Gandharvas by the power of initiation.
Consideration of the Initiation of Śūdras:

Regarding the eligibility for the initiation of Śūdras here, the scriptural statement "one should not give the *mantra* to a Śūdra" refers specifically to Vedic mantras, specific deities, and specific [Vedic] mantras. (As stated) in the Vārāhī-tantra:

The mantra of Gopāla should be given at the feet of Maheśa, as well as that of his consort, the Sun, and likewise the mantra of Gaṇeśa. He shall be entitled to initiation; otherwise, he would become a partaker of sin.
From this statement, it follows that there is no eligibility for Śūdras in mantras dedicated to other deities.
In the Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya Upaniṣad, the Śruti states: "They do not permit the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, the Yajus-lakṣmī, or [the worship of] Lakṣmī to women and Śūdras."

Thus it is said: "If a woman or a Śūdra should know the Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, the Yajus, or the Praṇava, he goes to the lower regions when dead" (1.3). Some also identify *Lakṣmī* as the *Śrī-bīja* or the *Lakṣmī-mantra*. There is also the ten-syllabled mantra of Gopāla and the twenty-two-syllabled mantra of Śyāmā.
Even a mantra containing the word *svāhā* may be given to a Śūdra, because it is stated in the *Kramadīpikā*: "It may likewise be given to all castes and stages of life" (1.4).
In this case, there is no requirement for spiritual attainment (*siddhi*), nor is there any defect such as hostility toward enemies.
And there is no consideration of eligibility here regarding the grasping of the Kālī and Manu mantras.
And because of the statement in the *Kālīkulasarvasva*: "Therefore,
a Śūdra has the right to undertake the ten-syllable mantra of Gopāla or the twenty-two-syllable mantra of Śyāmā."
Indeed, if a twice-born man gives a mantra joined with the word *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra,
the Śūdra shall go to hell and the Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state.
Thus, from the statement in the *Devīyāmala*,

it is understood that a Śūdra has no entitlement to mantras accompanied by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and *svāhā*; therefore, [the mantra] consists of twenty-two syllables containing *svāhā* within the *Gopāla* mantra accompanied by the *praṇava*.
If it is asked how a Śūdra has the right to the Śyāmā mantra, [the answer is]:
"O Goddess, O beautiful one, a Śūdra should constantly recite the Praṇava as taught in the Tantras and the Vahnijāyā (Svāhā); there is no need for deliberation on this point."

Thus, because the statement on the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) establishes that the *praṇava* and the *vahnijāyā* (the word *svāhā*) prescribed in the Tantras are to be uttered by a Śūdra, and because, through syntactic unity with that [statement], his entitlement is determined only for those mantras prescribed in the Tantras that are joined with both *svāhā* and the *praṇava*. This being so, where...

Wherever an injunction regarding the eligibility of a Śūdra is seen in a mantra that contains "svāhā" and is "licked by the Praṇava," it does not apply to the mantra in its original form; rather, it applies when syllables such as the Māyā-bīja are inserted in place of the "vahnijāyā" (svāhā) and so forth.
And thus it has been said:
Śūdras have the right to perform ten million recitations of the mantra of Śrī Viṣṇu and ten million recitations of the mantra of Śiva,
provided they are devoid of the word "svāhā" and the syllable "oṃ."
If a Śūdra recites [the mantra] after inserting Māyā (Hrīṃ) in place of the wife of Vahni (Svāhā),
he becomes a master of supernatural powers through that recitation and attains the Supreme Brahman.

Therefore, it is entirely clear that Śūdras have the right to practice only those mantras, such as those of Gopāla and others, which are accompanied by the Praṇava and other elements as prescribed in the Tantras.
Regarding the fruit of receiving initiation from a female guru:
initiation from a woman is declared auspicious and is remembered as being eightfold more meritorious than that from one's mother;
and in the case of initiation obtained in a dream, there is no deliberation required.
The term "women" does not refer to all women. A widow does not possess the status of a guru. As it is stated in the *Tattvasāra*:
"A woman who is virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to her guru, and has conquered her senses [is a guru]."
She who knows the essence of the meaning of all tantras, who is chaste, devoted to worship, and worthy of the Guru—she indeed shall be [the consort]; one should avoid a widow.
As for that which was stated:

"A widow has no authority [to perform rites] except by the command of her son and others; a maiden has no authority except by the command of her father; and a wife has no authority except by the command of her husband."
Thus, the statement indicating the gravity of the injunction is without foundation;

even if it were well-founded, it refers specifically to the subject of accomplished mantras, as established by its syntactic consistency with the statement: "A man whose mantra is perfected may render everything unfit for use fit."
Regarding the extraction of mantras,
it is stated in the *Gurudīkṣātantra*:
"A mantra of knowledge (vidyā) especially follows even one who has died."
The mind alone proclaims a person's prior actions.
O Great Goddess, if this [nature] were not present, how could there be human status? And O Pārvatī, how could his mind be directed toward initiation?
Therefore, O Goddess, one should diligently extract the preceding vidyā.
Regarding the rule for writing the mantra,
it is stated in the *Gurudīkṣātantra*:
Listen, O beloved! Bakula, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa are the jewels among leaves;
O Maheśānī, O beloved, one should write the Śakti-mantra upon a Vaṭa leaf.
O Goddess of gods, O Maheśvarī, one should recite the mantra of Viṣṇu at an Aśvattha tree and the mantra of Śiva at a Bakula tree,
using red sandalwood paste or saffron.
O Goddess, one should write the Śakti-mantra with sandalwood paste; O Supreme Sovereign, one should write the Viṣṇu-mantra and the Śiva-mantra with ashes.
"One should inscribe" means that one should write the mantra of each respective deity upon seven leaves for each.
"The wise person should diligently perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) with that mantra" means that one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* of each respective deity.
Having worshipped according to one's capacity with offerings, O Supreme Goddess.
Then, O Maheśvarī, the disciple, holding the arghya vessel in his hand,
should offer it to the Sun with this mantra while reciting it as a practitioner of mantras.
Regarding the materials for the *arghya* offering, he says: "Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, clarified butter, curd, and likewise honey."
Red karavīra flowers as well as red sandalwood.
This eightfold offering is indeed proclaimed for the Sun;
O Maheśvarī, one should not offer the arghya to Bhāskara with water from a conch shell during the Gāndharva [lagna].
The mantra for offering the *arghya*:
Oṃ! O God, protector of the earth, endowed with all powers, please accept this *arghya* from me and reveal the primordial wisdom (*pūrvavidyā*).
Having offered the *arghya* and paid obeisance with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*), one should then recite:
"Oṃ! Sūrya, Soma, Yama, Kāla, and the five great elements—these nine are the witnesses here in this world of both auspicious and inauspicious actions."
All the gods residing within my body are witnesses to my mantra;
grant me the knowledge acquired in my previous births into my hands.
O Maheśānī, having recited this Śāktikī initiation mantra, one should quickly extract a leaf;
having extracted a single leaf, one should cause it to be placed in the hand of the Guru.
O Parameśvarī, having studied the series of syllables and established the bridge, O Maheśānī, the Guru should recite those mantras one hundred and eight times.
Placing his hand upon the head of the disciple, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. (According to another source: the Guru, facing east, while the disciple stands facing west.
He should repeat it three times in the right ear and once in the left ear.
Regarding women and Śūdras, one should apply this reflection in the opposite manner.
And this refers to Viṣṇu and others. Regarding Śakti, it is said:
"Having sipped water, become self-restrained, and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, accompanied by the ṛṣi and other [limbs]."
O Goddess of the Gods, one should recite the mantra eight times into the left ear.
This initiation is proclaimed as the Śākta initiation in all tantras;
having received the Great Vidyā from the Guru, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru; one must not practice stinginess regarding one's wealth.
One may cause it to be given to the guru, to the guru’s son, or to the guru’s wife.
In the Kulārṇava:
"When the venerable Guru is pleased, one attains the pleasure of the deity;
and when the deity is pleased, the accomplishment of the mantra becomes certain."
In the Kali age, one should perform initiation by the gift of a jewel-leaf;
thereafter, the practitioner of mantra becomes perfected—of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, that man who performs initiation without this knowledge—
his initiation is indeed fruitless, and at its conclusion he shall go to hell.
Then, O Maheśānī, the disciple should prostrate himself like a staff upon the ground, saying:
"O Lord, by Your grace I am fulfilled in every way;
I am liberated from the great bond of illusion and death, and I am Śiva."
Having spoken thus, O Goddess of the Gods, the disciple, with his mind fixed on that [Guru], should prostrate at the feet of the venerable Guru and remain upon the ground, restrained in speech.
O beloved! As long as one has not obtained permission from the venerable Guru to rise, the Guru should cause the disciple to rise while reciting this mantra:
Arise, my child! You are liberated; be possessed of perfect conduct. May fame, prosperity, beauty, intelligence, longevity, strength, and health ever be yours.
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"Having imparted the mantra, the Guru must certainly not observe a fast;
otherwise, he becomes a worm in the hell of great darkness."
When a mantra-practitioner, having received initiation, performs a fast,
the deity always becomes enraged and, having uttered a curse, returns to his own city.
Regarding the initiation of instruction (*upadeśadīkṣā*) in the *Tattvasāra*:
"During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), in a field of the perfected ones (*siddhakṣetra*), or in a temple of Śiva..."
The mere proclamation of the mantra is called "instruction" (upadeśa).
In the Rudrayāmala: "In the case of Śyāmā, Bhairavī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, and Bhairava,
as well as Majjughoṣa and Raudra, the five-limbed [rite] is not accepted by the wise."
In that regard, concerning Guhyakālī, there is indeed the initiation of the five abodes (pañcāyatanī-dīkṣā). As it is said in the Viśvasāra:
"The wise one should worship, in due order, within the four corners of the outer enclosure (bhūpura)."
O Maheśānī, one should worship Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, and Śakti in their proper order, placing the principal deity in the center.
The lack of necessity for deliberation on the wheels (*cakras*) and so forth during initiation (*dīkṣā*).
That base beast among men who performs the counting of the *cakras* during initiation is fallen and most sinful; he is born as a worm in excrement.
What is the use of debts, or wealth, or even the analysis of signs and so forth?
One should completely avoid the consideration of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* [planetary states].
"O Great Goddess, there is no truth in the consideration of lunar mansions and the like;
O Śaṅkarī, there is no calculation of zodiac signs and so forth—thus it was spoken by Śaṅkara."
In the Āgamakalpadruma:
"During the transit of the sun and likewise during a solar eclipse,
no consideration whatsoever of the ascendant or other such factors should be made."
In the *Yāmala*: "During the autumn season, on the Yugādi day, during lunar or solar eclipses,
and at the awakening of Durgā, one need not examine whether the time is auspicious or inauspicious."
Regarding the rule for receiving specific mantras at specific times,
the *Matsyasūkta* states:
"At a great sacred ford (*mahātīrtha*) during the time of an eclipse (*grahaṇa*), there is no restriction concerning the time."
One should not recite the mantra of Viṣṇu during a lunar eclipse, nor should one recite the Śakti mantra during a solar eclipse.
In the *Yāmala*: "One who desires to live should not impart the *śakti-mantra* during a solar eclipse;
likewise, one should not receive it either, if one wishes for one's own welfare."
Regarding that, there is a specific rule:

here, the word *śakti* is intended in the sense of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), according to Udayākara, because of the context. For this very reason [it is said]: "The mantra which consists of the seed-syllables of Śrī Kāmakalī and the mantra of Lopa-mudrā..."
When obtained during a solar eclipse, it bestows swift results upon men.

Thus, even the statement of the *Yāmala* is consistent. The reading in the *Kulamūlāvatāra* is "the *parā*, the *śrī*, and the *kāma*-bījas. However, the commentators on the *Śivadīkṣā* maintain that in the preceding statement, the term "mantra-word of Śakti" refers to mantras other than those beginning with the *śrī*-bīja. In the *Yāmala*:
Whether at the rising of the ascendant or not, on whatever lunar day it may be,
initiation should especially be performed in accordance with the command of the Guru.
Neither the lunar day, nor religious observances, nor worship, nor ritual bathing,
nor the practice of recitation serves as a cause for initiation when a true Guru has been found by one's own will.
All days, all planets, all lunar mansions, and all zodiac signs—
on whatever day the Guru is pleased, all these bring auspiciousness. Initiation should take place whenever there is a desire, in accordance with the command of the Guru.
Regarding the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of mantras, [the text] then states the ten purificatory rites in the *Śāradā-tilaka* (2.112):
"Birth (*janana*), life (*jīvana*), and thereafter striking (*tāḍana*), as well as awakening (*bodhana*)."
Then there is consecration, as well as purification and nourishment.
Satisfying (tarpaṇa), kindling (dīpana), and concealment (gupti)—these ten are the purificatory rites for mantras.
The extraction of mantras from within the Mātṛkā is known as "birth" (janana).

The letters of the *mātṛkā* are those beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *kṣ*. This is because of the statement in the *Tantra-gandharva*: "The letters of the *mātṛkā*, beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣ*, are proclaimed as the *mātṛkā*-syllables. He now describes the drawing of the *mātṛkā*-yantra:
On the ground smeared with cow-dung, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus with sandalwood paste or a stylus, one should place the third [syllable] located in the pericarp.
The vowels are to be placed twice each upon the filaments, and the consonant groups (vargas) upon the eight petals.
In the third [layer], the Mātṛkās— the five groups of letters from *ka* to *ma*, along with *ha* and *sauḥ*— are to be recited in their proper order.
Then, one should write the letters from ya to anta and from śa to ha according to their characteristics.
Thus ends the Mātṛkāyantra. From that [yantra], one should extract the mantra from birch bark and so forth using fragrant paste.
Having placed the syllables of the mantra between *praṇavas* (oṃ), the wise person should recite it.
Those proficient in mantra and tantra call this "living."
The recitation may be performed tenfold or hundredfold. As it is stated in the *Viśvasāra*:
"The wise practitioner should recite each of the syllables of the mantra either separately a hundred times or ten times;
having written down the syllables of the mantra, he should strike them with sandalwood water."
The practitioner of mantra should strike each [syllable] with the wind [vowel *i*]; that is declared to be "striking" (*tāḍana*).
In another tantra it is said:
"One should strike all the syllables with sandalwood water."
Then, having written the mantra, the practitioner of that mantra should awaken it by reciting the mantra either a hundred times or ten times;
he should strike it with oleander flowers (*karavīra*) equal in number to the syllables of that mantra, ending with the word "yānta" (the letter *ya*). This is the awakening.
The mantra-practitioner,

while reciting the seed-syllable *ram*, should perform the consecration with the mantra using *aśvattha* leaves according to the number of its syllables, following the procedure taught in the *Svatantra*, for the sake of purification.
In another tantra: "I consecrate such-and-such a letter of the mantra, joined with the heart [mantra].
One should perform the consecration eightfold, or perform the consecration for each [letter] individually.

"Consecration with water from *kuśa* grass or with milk has been prescribed. Having thus reflected upon the mantra mentally, the practitioner of mantra should burn away the three impurities within the mantra using the *jyotis-mantra*; this is indeed the purification (*vimalīkaraṇa*).
The mantra consisting of *tāram*, followed by *vyoma*, *agni*, and *manu*, is considered the *daṇḍī-jyoti-mantra*.

The *manu* is the fourteen-syllable mantra ending with the staff (*daṇḍī*) and the nasalization (*anusvāra*). Thus, it is "oṃ hrauṃ. Sprinkling each syllable of the *manu* with water consecrated by *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra is considered the ritual restoration (*āpyāpana*) performed according to rule.
Otherwise, one should satisfy [the deity] with water, saying "I satisfy such-and-such mantra, namaḥ";
with honey in the case of a Śakti mantra; and with water mixed with moon-juice (milk) in the case of a Vaiṣṇava mantra.

In the Śaiva tradition, libation (tarpaṇa) with ghee and milk is prescribed; one should perform the libation ten times. The conjunction of the Tāra (Om), Māyā (Hrīm), and Ramā (Śrīm) is called the "illumination" (dīpana) of the mantra.
"The best of practitioners should kindle it one hundred and eight times. Thus it is said. In another tantra, it is stated that there is a sevenfold kindling.
As for the concealment of the mantra being recited, it means its non-disclosure.
Thus are the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for mantras.
Regarding the statement that one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) is to be worshipped daily, it is said in the *Viśvasāra*:
And having received the Great Vidyā, O Dear One, one should recite it until the end of life;
there is no alternative regarding its worship, even in the event of the death of a great guru or other such occasions.
Whether out of delusion or by fate, if the practitioner does not worship [it], his total destruction will occur; Sadāśiva shall slay him.
Whether in an impure place or a pure one, in any location and at any time, one should worship with supreme devotion; no deliberation is required in this matter.
In the Rudrayāmala:
"One may perform worship even during death or birth, or even when afflicted by disease;
this procedure is declared for all occasions and bestows the fruit of all desires."
The Ritual for Worship by One Under Impurity:
Now I shall describe the worship for one under impurity (sūtakin) as enjoined by the Āgamas;
having bathed and performed the daily rites through mental action alone.
One should worship by means of the yoga of meditation according to the very sequence of external worship.
External worship should be performed regarding the Goddess because of the specific injunction; and so it is said in the Vārāhītantra:
"O lady of excellent vows, [this applies] to Tārā, Kālī, and Tripurā."
During both birth-impurity and death-impurity, one should not abandon the recitation of mantras and ritual worship.
In the *Yāmala*:
"Whether impure or pure, whether walking, standing, or even sleeping,
there is no fault in mental recitation (*mānasa-jāpya*) at any place and at all times."
In the Viśvasāra:
"Whether waking, lying down, rising, walking, or even eating, there shall be no fault for one whose mantra is perfected; he may always recite it even during a state of ritual impurity."
There is no conceptualization by day, nor at night, nor at the conclusion of the twilight.
Now, on the greatness of the Guru:
The Guru is the sovereign lord of all the gods; the Guru is the witness of what has been done and what has not been done.
Having fully honored him, one should always perform every action by his command.
Having received the permission of the Guru, one should perform going, worship, recitation, eating, and likewise reflection; for him, success comes even without [further] recitation.
In the Tantra: "One should meditate on the venerable Guru three times a day, worship the Guru three times a day,
and constantly contemplate the Guru as the supreme cause three times a day."
O Goddess, one should indeed worship no other guru except one's own;
whether he is present before one's eyes or absent, one should bow to the guru every day.
If one resides in the same village, one should always prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day;
if one resides within the distance of a *krośa*, one should bow to the guru every day with devotion.
A disciple should prostrate from half a yojana away on the five festival days;
starting from one yojana, up to a limit of twelve yojanas.
O beloved, O lady of beautiful limbs, one should prostrate before the venerable Guru for as many months as have passed;
however, if the venerable Guru is far away, O daughter of the mountain,
one should worship the Guru twice within the course of a year.
"Twice" means once during the northern course [of the sun] and once during the southern course; such is the meaning.
O Goddess! he who does not practice in this way shall become a Brahma-rākṣasa. He who sleeps or sits in one place together with his Guru [is likewise cursed].
He goes to a terrible hell for as long as fourteen Indras [reign]. In the Tantra:
"The disciple, seeing the Guru, should rise and leave his seat."
Even one who is distinguished by birth, learning, or wealth, upon seeing his teacher from afar,
should joyfully prostrate himself like a staff on the ground and then perform circumambulation.
One should go before him as he approaches, follow after him as he departs, and stay at his side after bowing; one should then proceed only with his permission.
One should serve while looking at his face and carry out his commands and so forth with respect;
one should not speak untruth before him, nor should one engage in excessive chatter.
Having become a disciple, one should never, under any circumstances, engage in lending or borrowing money, nor in the buying or selling of goods, together with one's teacher.
"The guru is mother, father, master, kinsman, and friend—the guru is all. Holding this constantly in mind, one who is the soul of all should worship the guru.
One should avoid performing separate worship and displaying arrogance in the presence of the guru;
one should relinquish the authority to give initiation, explain the scriptures, and exercise lordship before the guru.
One should worship whatever is seen— a seat, a bed, a garment, an ornament, a sandal, a shadow, a wife, or anything else— just as one would worship the deity itself.
As [one's devotion] is toward the deity, so it is toward the mantra; as toward the mantra, so toward the guru;
and as toward the guru, so toward one's own self—thus is the sequence of devotion traditionally taught.
One should never step over the bed or seat of the guru, nor his vehicle, sandals, or shoes; likewise, one should never step over his bath-water or his shadow.
Elsewhere it is also said:
"One should not step over the shadow of the deity, the shadow of the guru, or the shadow of the Śakti.
O Goddess, even if one does so out of negligence, one should perform worship before the guru."
He goes to a terrible hell, and that worship becomes fruitless;
one should not approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands.
One should offer fruits and flowers according to one's ability;
whatever is performed with devotion and in accordance with one's capacity, it is dedicated to the Guru.
Whether small or great, the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor;
yet, O Goddess, a miser who fails to give for the sake of his guru shall go to the Raurava hell.
He who, intending to defeat his guru, renders the guru’s word false and establishes his own word instead,
is cooked in the ocean of hell.
One should never utter the name of the guru at any time except during the time of recitation,
O daughter of the mountain— whether one be a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra.
The wise eat with devotion the excellent remnants of their teacher;
O lady of beautiful limbs, should the teacher come to the disciple's house, [he should be honored].
O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion, the disciple’s abode is equal to ten million suns and planets;
for that day is indeed the time of a lunar eclipse.
By the mere sight of the Guru, one is liberated from all sins—
whether it be the Guru, the Guru’s son, or the Guru’s wife, O lady of excellent complexion.
O lady of lovely limbs, if the most excellent of practitioners should proceed by transgressing [the rules],
then at that very moment, O lady of tremulous glances, he goes to hell after hell in succession.
In the *Uttarakalpa*:
"Whether in the presence or in the absence of the Guru, one should carry out his command.
(O Śaṅkarī, hear now the procedure for when he is absent and how to obtain his authorization)."
And at the time of worship, O lady of beautiful limbs, the Guru, or his son, or even his wife, Maheśvarī, should come to the disciple’s residence.
Then, O Dear One, setting aside the [external] worship, one should worship one's own guru;
for even if one takes a small amount of the guru's property that has not been given, [it is a grave offense].
One may enter the womb of animals and be constantly devoured by carnivorous creatures;
however, by meditating upon and worshipping the thousand-petaled lotus feet of the Guru, one is liberated.
Having offered praise and joined my palms, with my mind intent on meditation, I say:
"O Lord! You have already ordained what was to be done; please show me Your grace."
"May there be no contradiction here through the grace of Your Reality"—
having thus prayed with this mantra, one should perform what has been instructed.
In the Mahiṣamardinītantra,
the Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Supreme Lord, out of compassion [speak], O Parameśvara."
O Śaṅkara, tell me in detail the procedure for the worship of the Guru!
Īśvara said:
O lady of beautiful limbs, O beloved, the divine and heroic [path] has been described by me many times before;
O Goddess, I shall now declare to you in brief the sequence for human beings.
O Parameśānī, the Guru, the Supreme Guru, the Guru of the higher and lower,
and likewise one's own Guru, are without doubt directly Brahman itself.
That Guru shall always be the Supreme Guru, Viṣṇu himself on earth;
his Guru is the Guru of both the supreme and the non-supreme, Maheśvara in person.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is the divine Maheśvara.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, the Guru is directly composed of Brahman.
I bow again and again to the Lord, whose form is an unbroken circle, who pervades all, the Master of all, the God who grants everything.

Salutations to you in front, on both sides, and behind—salutations again and again! One should perform the meditation upon the venerable Guru at the three junctions of the day, and the worship of the Guru at the three junctions of the day.
One should constantly meditate at the three junctions of the day upon the Guru, the supreme cause;
O lady of excellent hips! without the Guru, there is never any accomplishment whatsoever.
O Maheśānī, O beloved, having remembered the Guru day after day,
one should worship him with mental perfumes, incenses, and likewise with the most excellent lamps.
With various kinds of foods to chew, foods to eat, and drinks, as well as curd and milk,
O beloved, and with jackfruits, coconuts, and plantains;
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should worship one’s own guru with various kinds of food;
for, O Goddess, one should not worship any other guru apart from one’s own guru.
O Maheśānī, O beloved, one should worship with devotion using fish and meat;
O lady of beautiful limbs, one should always worship with devotion using perfumes and garlands.
With gold and silk garments, as well as those made of cotton—
both plain and variegated, exceedingly fine and captivating.
O Goddess, one should always worship one’s own guru with various kinds of seats covered with red woolen cloths, as well as with diverse ritual substances.
O Goddess of beautiful limbs, one should always worship one's own guru with various ornaments made of gold and silver.
O Maheśānī, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should recite the mantra of the Guru;
O Maheśānī, one should worship the wife of the Guru according to this rite.
O beloved, one should perform daily worship toward the sons of the guru and their children as one would toward the guru himself, according to this procedure.
O lady of beautiful limbs, in the absence of the guru, one should worship the wife of the guru;
in his absence, O fair-hipped one, one should worship the daughter of the guru.
In their absence, O Maheśānī, one should worship the preceptor’s daughter-in-law;
in the absence of these, O lady of beautiful limbs, one should worship a member of the preceptor’s lineage.
O beautiful woman, in the absence of one's own lineage, one should likewise worship the maternal grandfather of the preceptor,
or the maternal uncle, or the maternal aunt, according to this rite.
O Goddess, O beloved, if he does not worship according to this rite,
that practitioner shall instantly become one who requires expiation, O Goddess.
If the practitioner does not go to the temple of the Guru-deity within the course of a year, it is always equal to the city of Kāśī.
O Maheśānī, he who beholds the Guru’s abode as equal to Kāśī,
O Goddess, that practitioner shall instantly become equal to Śiva.
Having reached the house of the Guru, one should consume his leftovers;
at that very moment, O Dear One, the practitioner shall suddenly attain success.

O lady of excellent complexion, O Supreme Goddess, O daughter of the Mountain, one should not practice the Vidyā or the Mantra without first having partaken of the remains of the food of one's Guru and deity.
O beloved with tremulous eyes, one should never, at any time or in any place, look upon his face; for it is like a pit of excrement.
O Goddess, O beloved daughter of the mountain, by consuming the remnants [of the offering], the purification of the mouth is achieved for Brāhmaṇas,
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike.
With devotion, they eat the various kinds of excellent food left over by the guru;
for the food remaining from the guru, O beloved, is always composed of bliss.
O lady of excellent complexion, O fair-limbed one, if the best of practitioners should proceed by transgressing his guru, or his guru’s son, or his wife;
At that very moment, O lady of tremulous glances, one goes from hell to ever higher hells;
yet, O Pārvatī, daughter of the mountain, whether it be the temple of the Guru-deity or a mere hut,
it becomes like Mount Kailāsa itself.
O lady of pure smiles, whatever is most dear to the practitioner in this world,
all that he should give to the guru with devotion and with the utmost effort.
At that very moment, O Goddess, the perfection of the mantra arises suddenly,
if one receives the command of the Guru and recites it incessantly.
At that very moment, he shall suddenly attain perfection and become a lord of the eight siddhis;
and at the time of worship, O lady of beautiful limbs, she shall come to the disciple's dwelling.
O lady of excellent complexion, O beloved, if the guru, the guru’s son, or the guru’s wife [be present],
one should then set aside that worship and worship one's own guru.
O beloved daughter of the mountain, for the purpose of worshipping the deity, one should give all the perfumes, flowers, and other offerings to the guru and then perform the worship;
at that very moment, O Goddess, the deity will suddenly attain satisfaction.
In the Rudrayāmala:
"Whether it be the guru, the guru’s wife, or even the son who has arrived..."
Even if the eldest disciple is in the midst of performing worship, he should abandon all other acts of worship;
by the elder's command, the disciple should perform the worship—this is the definitive conclusion of the scripture.
One should worship one's own guru or his son with devotion, using various perfumes, flowers, incenses, and even food offerings.
The Guru is Lord Hara himself, his wife is the beloved of Hara;
the son of the Guru is Gaṇeśa—one should perform the worship while contemplating them thus.
The wife of the guru, O Maheśānī, is the very embodiment of the Goddess herself;
one should contemplate the son of the guru as being like Gaṇeśa, O Goddess.
O Goddess, for the disciple, that day is equal to ten million solar eclipses;
O lady of excellent complexion, that day is superior even to the time of a lunar eclipse.
By the mere sight of the Guru, one is liberated from all sins;
therefore, O lady of tremulous glances, a wise person should bestow gifts at that very moment.
With the aim of pleasing the guru, a wise person should make gifts of gold, sesame seeds, garments, and especially silver.
When the venerable Guru is pleased, one attains the grace of the deity;
when the deity is pleased, the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly occur.
O lady of beautiful limbs, one should never utter a falsehood in the presence of the Guru;
for the body of the Guru, O Great Goddess, is the supreme form of the deity.
O Maheśānī, the grace of the Guru is the root of worship and the great state;
the word of the Guru is the root of mantra, for the Guru himself is the Supreme Brahman.
By this method, O Goddess, one should meditate upon the Guru every day;
then, O lotus-faced one, accomplishment arises suddenly.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Initiation," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme renunciant (*paramahaṃsa*), the holy Avadhūta.
The Third Chapter: Determination of Yoga.
Without worship, the Goddess does not bestow fruit upon men.
In the Tantra:
"Whether meditated upon, remembered, worshipped, praised, or even saluted—
whether knowingly or unknowingly— he grants liberation to his worshippers."
From such passages as these, it is understood that the fruit of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) is not possible without worship and other such rites.
Regarding the cause for the manifestation of the form (*vigraha*),
one must consider in what manner worship and other rites should be performed toward the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*).
Because [the Absolute] is devoid of a body, in what manner could it possibly grant liberation and other such boons?

For this very reason, for the benefit of practitioners, the Śrī Rāmatāpanīya Upaniṣad and the Kulārṇava state that Brahman is twofold, distinguished as *saguṇa* (with attributes) and *nirguṇa* (without attributes): [The text continues with the verses from the Rāmatāpanīya and Kulārṇava.]
The conceptualization of forms for Brahman— which is composed of consciousness, non-dual, fruitless, and bodiless— is for the sake of the purposeful practice of its worshippers.
The meaning of this is as follows: "of the one consisting of consciousness" means of that which consists of knowledge. In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* it is said:
"She who, in the form of consciousness (*citirūpeṇa*), stands pervading this entire world.
"Of the non-dual, the one. And so it has been stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
For the one supreme Brahman is described through manifoldness;
she who is the very nature of the supreme Brahman appears through the distinction between the gross and the subtle.
The Gopālatāpanīya-śruti also states:
"The one supreme Brahman indeed appears as a fourfold [manifestation] through Māyā."
Therefore, Brahman alone, through Māyā, becomes manifold in the form of male and female like an actor;
it appears as having many forms by means of its multiform Māyā.
Thus says the Śruti. "Niṣkala" means devoid of parts; that is, free from Māyā. In the Āgneya Purāṇa it is said:

"The supreme Hari, the omniscient, is to be known as both *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts). He who resides within the body is to be known as *sakala*, while he who is devoid of a body is *niṣkala*."
The term "Hari" is an illustration [of a broader category]. In the *Yāmala*:

"Mahāmāyā is considered to be twofold: with attributes (*saguṇā*) and without attributes (*nirguṇā*). That which is joined with *māyā* is with attributes; that which is devoid of it is without attributes."
"Of the bodiless" means devoid of a body demarcated by limbs such as the mouth, hands, and feet.
As stated in the *Bhūtaśuddhi*:
"The supreme Brahman is without fruit; whence could there be attachment, and whence could there be pleasure?"
O beautiful lady, for Brahman there are no forms, no activities, and it is devoid of the senses; indeed, all births and actions belong to Brahman, yet for [the individual soul] they do not exist.

There is also the reading "bhāvinī" [in the phrase] "santi bhāvinī" regarding *prakṛti*. This means [the state] of those practitioners (*upāsaka*) who possess both devotion and the yoga of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-yoga*). In the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "For all mortals, the divine age of the Lord is auspicious."
Everything suitable for meditation is fruitless even for yogins.

The meaning is: "for the yogins," that is, for those possessing the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), and the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*). In the *Āgneya Purāṇa* it is said:
"He who is affectionate toward His devotees [is the refuge] of the virtuous and the vigilant devotees."
Though formless, he becomes manifest in their forms as a benefactor;
for the sake of the practitioners' goals, he bestows the fruits of the fourfold aims of life.
And so it has been said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"She alone, when propitiated, bestows upon men enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
And in the Bṛhannāradīya:
The conceptualization of your form is for the sake of granting liberation to your devotees.

The characteristic of propitiation (*ārādhanā*) consists of meditation (*dhyāna*) and worship (*pūjā*). These two, when preceded by the knowledge of difference (*bhedajñāna*), bestow enjoyment (*bhoga*) and heaven (*svarga*); however, when preceded by the knowledge of non-difference (*abhedajñāna*), they bestow liberation (*mukti*). And for that purpose—

The meaning is that this involves the conceptualization of the form of the creator, Brahmā. Meditation (*dhyāna*), however, is the knowledge directed toward a body delimited by specific parts such as the face, hands, and feet, which have arisen from the respective phonemes constituting the mantra of each particular deity.
This is the essential meaning.
Thus it is also stated in the *Garuḍa*:
"If it is formless, it would not be stable; therefore, one should contemplate a form."
The twofold nature of meditation is also stated in the *Yāmala*: "Meditation, moreover, is of two kinds, distinguished as gross (*sthūla*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*)."
Subtle is the knowledge of the mantra-body; gross is the contemplation of the formal body.
That which has hands, feet, a belly, a mouth, and so forth is the gross form;
the subtle form is that of primordial nature (prakṛti), while the supreme is remembered as consisting of pure knowledge.
O Maheśānī, subtle meditation never arises;
O Maheśānī, by performing gross meditation, one attains liberation.
In the *Yāmala*: "The body of the deity certainly arises from the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
By reciting the mantra whose essence is that particular seed-syllable, one becomes identical with Brahman."
O Goddess, one should meditate upon her as instructed, through the yoga of meditation as described;
she is that Goddess whose form is the support of the universe, manifesting in the form of the phonemes.
Regarding the seed-syllable (*bīja*), he states the definition of the seed in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having extracted the single syllable as the primary seed, the subsequent one is the power (*śakti*). The first is *ka*; the subsequent is *ī*. The letter *ra* is the *kīlaka*. In the *Gāndharva*:
The eternal, single-syllabled Brahman is the imperishable, supreme state.
By reciting this syllable-mantra even once, one becomes fit for union with Brahman;
having recited it, one accomplishes everything—what is the fruit of many recitations?
The gross and the subtle are indeed one. Thus it has been said in the *Yāmala*:
"Clarified butter has two forms: solidity and transparency;
whether in its solid state or its transparent state, it is undoubtedly clarified butter alone."
Also in the *Pādma*: "Just as a lamp arises from a lamp, so shall it be.

Thus says the statement. Alternatively, the conceptualization of the two Brahmans (the worshiped and the worshiper) is for the purpose of knowing their non-difference. And so it is said in the *Kaurma*:
But those who consider themselves distinct from the Supreme Lord do not behold that God; their exertion is in vain.

The term "Īśvara" is an illustrative designation. Thus it is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "O Goddess, one should contemplate oneself as the Supreme Goddess, who consists of all deities, who consists of all mantras, and whose nature is supreme bliss."
Now, following this context, the description of the Yoginīs and the knowledge of Yoga is being written.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another [teaching], the samādhi that destroys worldly existence.
This means it is the destroyer of worldly existence and the destroyer of rebirth.
One should meditate upon the charming lion in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus;
above the lion is a red lotus, and above that is Śiva.
Upon him, the Great Goddess, who can assume any form at will, sports;
the Great God is a white preta, and the Lotus-born One is a red preta.

Alternatively, the reading is "Brahmā on a red lotus. Hari and Hara are likewise to be known; O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon these vehicles of great power according to the yoga of meditation as it has been described.
With a restrained mind, one should meditate upon one's own self as being of the nature of the Goddess;
whatever else is similar to her, one should likewise conceive of that as one's own.
One should always honor one's own guru, deity, and self as being identical.
As it is said in the Śrīkrama: "O Goddess, one should contemplate oneself as the primordial Śakti."
One should contemplate [the deity] through mind, speech, and indeed through body.
Furthermore, elsewhere it is said:
"By contemplating [the deity] as non-different from oneself, a person attains identity with that."
By constantly contemplating "I am He," one becomes identical with Him;
one should cultivate the realization: "I am the Goddess, I am none other, I am liberated."
Through the contemplation of Rudra one becomes Rudra; through the contemplation of Viṣṇu one becomes Viṣṇu;
and through the contemplation of Durgā one indeed becomes Durgā—it cannot be otherwise.
Practicing in this manner day after day, O Pārvatī,
one is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence and from the sufferings of old age, death, and the like.
Praise of the Yoga of Meditation:
For one who is devoted to the yoga of meditation, there is no need for worship whatsoever.
