Without ritual deposits, without worship, and without the preliminary practice of recitation, accomplishment arises from the yoga of meditation; indeed, it is not otherwise, O Pārvatī.
This great knowledge of Brahman has been told to you, O Goddess;
having learned it from a guru, O Goddess, one may cross the ocean of worldly existence.
"I am Brahman"—through such realization, ignorance shall dissolve.
O beloved, having reflected thus, "I am He," one should always conduct oneself accordingly.
Just as foam, waves, and the like, O Sage,
arise from the ocean and dissolve back into the ocean, so too does the world dissolve into the Self.
Thus ends the yoga taught in the Gandharva-tantra.
Therefore, for the benefit of practitioners, Brahman assumes the forms of both female and male.
In the Viṣṇuyāmala, Viṣṇu’s words to the Goddess are as follows:
"O Mother, no one knows that supreme form of yours."
The gods worship that form which is gross, consisting of Kāla and the rest.
O beloved, one may meditate on the Goddess in female form, or one may meditate on her in male form;
or one may meditate on Brahman as partless, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.

The characteristics of the manifestation in female form (*strīrūpāvatāra-lakṣaṇa*): manifestations in female form are those whose bodies are demarcated by such limbs as breasts and hips. For example: Kālī, Nīlā, Mahādurgā, Tvaritā, and Chinnamastakā.
Vāgvādinī, Annapūrṇā, and likewise Pratyaṅgirā again;
Kāmākhyāvāsinī, Bālā, Mātaṅgī, Śailavāsinī,
and all such Vidyās bestow their full fruit in the Kali age.
Elsewhere it is also said:
"Some call her Umā, others Lakṣmī;
others call her Bhāratī, and others Ambikā, the Daughter of the Mountain."
Some call her Durgeti, Bhadrakālī, Caṇḍī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī,
Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and others Indrī.
The supreme seers declare that she is Brāhmī, as well as Vidyā, Avidyā, and Māyā; they likewise call her Prakṛti and the Supreme.
The characteristic of the descent as a person (*puruṣāvatāra-lakṣaṇa*):
descents delimited by a body that is itself delimited by limbs such as the penis are those in male form, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others. Likewise—
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, as well as Rāma,
Rāma, and Rāma, Buddha, and Kalki— these are the ten.

And so forth. A neuter deity is certainly not to be worshipped by householders, because it does not produce fruit. Furthermore, from the statement, "For householders, all [deities] should be [worshipped]; for celibate students, indeed Brahman;
and for householders, all should be," it follows that Śiva, Durgā, Viṣṇu...
Worship should be performed by placing [the deity] at the forefront. And so, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, as cited in the Vimalānanda-bhāṣya:
"For human beings, the goddess Umā, as well as Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva [are to be worshipped]."
Whichever deity is favored by a person, that alone is his personal deity;
however, when worshipped without distinction of purpose, she grants the desired objects to men.
Worship should be performed toward men without making distinctions. Regarding the Goddess in the Śaiva tradition, there is this statement of Īśvara: "He who praises one indeed praises all."
He who censures even one among them censures all of them indeed.
Regarding the fruit of censuring the Lord:

for the Lord, there is neither happiness in praise nor suffering in censure, because He is free from both pleasure and pain. However, for the censurer, there is only hell. Thus it has been said in the Bhāṣya:
One should contemplate the oneness of the Goddess, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
one who creates division goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.
"Until the dissolution of the world" (āhūtasaṃplavam) means until the time of the final cosmic destruction (pralayakāla). In the Vārāha Purāṇa it is said:
"As is Durgā, so is Viṣṇu; as is Viṣṇu, so is Śiva. A wise person should not perceive these three as distinct, for they are one and the same."
That person of deluded intellect who, being a sinful man, contemplates these [sects] otherwise through partiality, goes to the terrible and fierce Raurava hell.
In the *Yāmala*:
"They perceive that which is to be reached through meditation as being of various kinds according to differences in inclination.
In the *Tantra*:
The great illusion of cold is but one, having resorted to various names for the purpose of deluding the world; therefore, one should remain even-minded.
One who is attached to the path of worldly activity (pravṛtti-mārga) should perform worship according to the various types of initiation (dīkṣā);
however, one seeking the path of cessation (nivṛtti-mārga) should abandon the doctrine of duality.
Praise of the Worship of Śakti:
One should perform the worship of the Goddess, setting aside the worship of Śiva and Viṣṇu, because of her gentle nature and because she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Śiva—
Through the worship of Viṣṇu, there is merely liberation attained by means of physical austerity. Thus, in the Śāradā-tantra, these are the words of Śiva addressed to Bhuvaneśvarī:
"Even now, you remain in the prime of youth for all the worlds."

O daughter of the King of Mountains, you are exceedingly tender; according to the *Samaya-tantra*, it is sometimes said that for some there may be enjoyment (*bhukti*), for others liberation (*mukti*) alone,
but for this practitioner, both enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of his hand.
In the Rudrayāmala:
Where there is worldly enjoyment, there is no liberation;
where there is liberation, there is no worldly enjoyment.
For those who worship the pair of Śiva’s lotus feet,
where indeed do worldly enjoyment and liberation reside?
He who desires both enjoyment and liberation from other philosophical systems [is truly blessed].
Can a man truly become wealthy by means of wealth obtained only in a dream?
O Pārvatī, just as the delusion of silver arises with respect to mother-of-pearl,
so too [does it arise] for one who desires enjoyment and liberation from other philosophical systems.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of Non-dual Yoga," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme renunciant (*paramahaṃsa*), and the holy Avadhūta. 3.
The Fourth Chapter: Now, the morning rites, as stated in the *Yāmala*:
If one worships the Goddess with devotion without having performed the morning rites,
that worship is as fruitless as a ritual devoid of purity.

Having arisen during the *brāhma* hour, one should contemplate the Guru and the Deity within the supreme point (*parabindu*) called Śiva, located in the thousand-petalled lotus upon the crown of one's own head.
The *brāhyamuhūrta*, however, is the final muhūrta of the night. Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"They know the *brāhyamuhūrta* to consist of two *daṇḍas* remaining at the end of the night."
The meditation on the venerable Guru (Śrīgurudhyāna) is as follows:
[He is] resembling the full moon, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Clad in white garments, adorned with white garlands and white unguents.
One should meditate with the intellect upon the supreme abode, the imperishable one called the God, joined with the red Śakti on the left thigh, having elevated it into union with Śiva.
Having meditated thus, one should perform worship before oneself with offerings consisting of the five elements.
The mental worship of the venerable Guru consists of the principle of fragrance (gandhatattva), which is the earthly element, performed by means of the little finger.
One should offer the great flower consisting of sound by means of the first finger;
one should employ the great incense in the form of wind with the two index fingers.
Through the yoga of the central channel, one attains the great lamp whose form is radiant energy;
likewise, through the yoga of the nectar-finger, one obtains the food of immortality.
It is taught that betel, accompanied by a salutation or joined with palms pressed together (*añjali*), originates from speech (*vāgbhava*).
One should join everything with its respective seed-syllable and with a salutation;
one should diligently recite the mantra of the Guru without any deceit.
The Guru-mantra: as for the Guru-mantra—
O Sovereign of the Gods, Vāṇī, Bhuvaneśānī, and Ramā indeed [constitute it].
O Goddess, these three syllables are established within the mantra of the Guru.
Then, at the end of one's own guru’s name, one should write "Ānandanātha";
and at the end of the word "raktaśakti," one should then write the word "ambā."
Having uttered "Śrīpādukām," one should recite "I worship" (pūjayāmi) while muttering [the mantra];
then, having offered [the deity] in the form of light, one should satisfy the Guru with a hymn of praise.
In the *Śyāmārahasya*:
"Having worshipped with mental offerings such as perfumes and flowers, one should recite the *vāgbhava* mantra;
then, one should perform the hymn of praise as declared in the *Kubjikātantra*."
Praise of the Guru:
Oṃ, salutations to you, the giver of the great mantra, whose form is Śiva;
to the illuminator of the knowledge of Brahman, the deliverer from the suffering of saṃsāra.
Salutations to you, the exceedingly gentle, the divine, the hero, the destroyer of ignorance;
salutations to you, the Lord of the Kula, the bestower of the Kulakaula upon others.
Salutations to you, O Guru, who awakens one to the reality of Śiva, who illuminates the reality of Brahman, and who grants fearlessness to spiritual practitioners.

Salutation to the Guru, whose form is liberated from both existence and non-existence, who exists for the sake of awakening to the state of conduct within non-conduct, and who is the cause of all being.
Or this may be read as: "To the one who is empowered (Śākta) and liberated from existence and non-existence.
Salutations be to You, Śambhu, who illumines the divine state;
salutations again and again to the All-pervasive One (Vibhava), whose very nature is the bliss of knowledge.
Salutation to Śiva, the Lord of Power (Śaktinātha), whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
who takes form at will, who is desire itself, and whose essence is the art of amorous play.
To the one who instructs in the worship of the family, whose very nature is the conduct of the family,
and who is the manifestation of his own radiant power on the left side.
Salutations be unto Maheśa, the Lord of Knowledge, to pure Consciousness;
salutations be unto You, whose very nature is all knowledge—salutations again and again.
O Goddess of gods, the practitioner, having risen in the morning, should daily recite this hymn while facing the direction of the Guru; thereby, the vidyā becomes propitious.
If one does not recite this at the beginning of the worship of the Kula lineage,
that worship shall be fruitless and will lead to malevolent magic.
Thus ends the Śrīgurustotra as declared in the Kubjikā Tantra. Next, one should recite the Kavaca (armor). Then, one should prostrate.
The mantra for prostrating before the Śrī Guru is as follows:
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed— the state which is of the nature of an unbroken circle and by which all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge.
An Exposition of the Six Wheels:
Now, as a digression, the arrangement of the six wheels is written down.
It is held that there are thirty-five million channels (nāḍīs) in the body, along with half of that number.
Among them, ten are declared to be the principal ones; of those, three are considered the most excellent.
The principal channel within the spinal column, which has the form of the moon, sun,
and fire, is that channel whose nature is Śakti and which is the very embodiment of nectar.
And she who is named Piṅgalā on the right, having a male form and the nature of the Sun,
resides in the center of Meru and extends from the root to the aperture of Brahmā.
That Suṣumnā, consisting of all splendor, is of the nature of fire;
it resembles the pomegranate flower and is considered another form known as Śivā.
Within the Suṣumnā is the Citrā, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons;
she consists of all the deities and reaches the hearts of yogins. In her center is the Brahma-nāḍī, having the form of a lotus fiber.
The description of the Mūlādhāra-cakra:
The six lotuses situated at the knots of the Suṣumnā in their proper order;
the first is the Mūla-cakra, known as Ādhāra, which is intensely red and has four petals.
Joined with the syllables VĀ, DI, SĀ, NTĀ, and RṆA, it is red in color and captivating to the mind.
The womb situated in the pericarp is the Supreme Goddess known as Kāmā;
that womb, O Supreme Mistress, consists of will, knowledge, and action.
For Kandarpa, known as Aparā, resides within that triangular base;
in its center is the self-manifested liṅga (svayambhūliṅga), which possesses a cavity and faces westward.
And one should meditate, O Supreme Goddess, upon Śiva, beautiful and dark-hued;
for by that path, Kuṇḍalinī indeed performs her coming and going.
Piercing through the city again and again, Kuṇḍalī always goes and returns;
there, in the form of a flash of lightning, is the supreme deity Kuṇḍalī.
Having the form of a slumbering serpent, it is endowed with three and a half coils and is wound like a poisonous thread in a counter-clockwise direction.
O Maheśānī, she always remains surrounding Śiva;
having covered with her mouth that door through which one must go to the supreme, stainless Brahman, the Supreme Goddess lies in deep sleep.
The Explanation of the Svādhiṣṭhāna and Maṇipūra Wheels:
At the base of the linga is the great lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which has six petals and is joined with the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *la*. At the navel, however, is the Maṇipūra.
It is endowed with ten red petals, inscribed with the letters beginning with 'ḍa' and ending with 'pha'.
The opening of the unstruck lotus in the heart: O Goddess, the twelve-petaled unstruck lotus has petals corresponding to the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*, and it resembles molten gold.
In its center is the Bāṇaliṅga, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns;
there, the unstruck (anāhata) mantra, consisting of the Śabdabrahman, is perceived.
For that reason, that lotus is celebrated by yogis as being called "unstruck" (āhata).
The description of the Viśuddha-cakra: In the region of the throat is the cakra named Viśuddha, smoke-colored and beautiful,
endowed with sixteen petals associated with the vowels beginning with 'A'.
Since purity is extended for the individual soul through the vision of the *haṃsa*,
it is called the pure lotus, known as space, and most wonderful.
The explanation of the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*): the one called "command" is between the eyebrows;
it is the supreme two-petaled wheel, joined with the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa*, stainless and most beautiful.
In the center of that is the great liṅga called Itara, possessing the luster of gold;
there is the transmission of the command (ājñā-saṃkramaṇa), renowned as the "Command of the Guru.
Above that is the one called Kailāsa, and above that is Bodhinī.
The opening of the thousand-spoked wheel is the thousand-spoked great lotus, endowed with *nāda* and *bindu*. Śiva is manifest as the form of emptiness; the circle is the supreme *kuṇḍalinī*.
Having the form of three and a half coils, she possesses a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
In the *Yāmala*:
"The coiled energy (*kuṇḍalinī-śakti*), endowed with the three qualities (*guṇa*), is the sphere of emptiness; O Great Goddess, Maheśvara is the very form of Śiva."
Taking the form of a serpent, she always remains there, encircling Śiva.
The Bindu, whose essence is the union of Śiva and Śakti, bestows the fruits of both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
That eternal Goddess exists in the form of Sound (Nāda) and in the form of the Yoni.
In the *Bhūtaśuddhi*:
"O lady of pure smiles, the source of the *bindu* consists of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā;
O Great Goddess, it stands above all, for the *bindu* is the very nature of Brahman."
In the *Gandharvamālikā*:
"Bhava is known as the Bindu, and Bhavana is the Triangle.
Because of its connection with Bhava, Bhavana gives rise to the three worlds."
O Goddess of the gods, O Sovereign Lady, one should contemplate the five elements and the mind as the sixth,
situated respectively within the six cakras in due order.
The delightful city of Śiva, together with its essence, is free from suffering and adorned on all sides with divine trees that bear flowers and fruits eternally.
The beautiful city of Sadāśiva is adorned with wish-fulfilling trees;
it consists of the five elements and is endowed with the three qualities (guṇas).
O Pārvatī, it possesses the four Vedas as its four branches and is always endowed with flowers and fruit;
its blossoms are yellow, black, white, and red.
Having thus meditated upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), which is green, variegated, adorned with various beautiful flowers, and beneath which is a jeweled altar (ratnavedikā);
There, above, was a beautiful couch adorned with various jewels,
strewn with mandārava flowers, and made fragrant by various perfumes.
There, O beautiful one, Mahādeva always resides;
one should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva, who resembles pure crystal.
O beloved, he is strewn with many jewels, long-armed, and captivating;
his eyes are serene with happiness, and his face is perpetually smiling.
His body was adorned with earrings on his ears, beautified by a necklace of jewels,
and graced by a garland of a thousand red lotuses.
Śiva has eight arms and three eyes, with lotus-petal-like eyes;
his feet possess beautiful anklets, and his body consists of the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
In this way, O lotus-eyed one, one should meditate upon his gross body—
the God who is established in the center of the lotus, free from desire, and whose form is sound.
In the form of sound, Mahādeva never has any activity;
likewise, in all the wheels (cakras), one should contemplate the form of Śakti.
Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Sadāśiva,
and Paraśiva— these six are proclaimed as the Śivas.
He speaks of the powers (śaktis): "O Goddess, Ḍākinī is in Viśuddhi, while Rākiṇī is in Anāhata;
Lākinī resides in Maṇipūra, and Kākinī is in the region of the Liṅga."
The goddess Śākinī resides in the Ādhāra, likewise Hākinī in the Ājñā;
Yākinī is situated in the Brahmarandhra, bestowing the fruit of all desires.
One should meditate upon the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, who resides within the self-manifested liṅga;
she is dark-hued, subtle, the embodiment of creation, and the essence of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
One should contemplate her as transcending the universe, consisting of the nature of knowledge, and possessing an upward-facing form.
"Red" should be understood as referring to Sundarī.
Kuṇḍalī, the supreme deity, is born from the syllable *huṃ*.
By means of the *haṃsa* mantra, Kuṇḍalī sustains the body and the self.
Through the Kuṇḍalinī Yoga, by means of the mind and vital breaths conjoined with the intensified fire,
one should lead the Kuṇḍalinī, together with the individual soul (jīvātman), upward to the Supreme.

Having pierced the fourteenth knot by way of the six chakras and the junctions, as well as through the path of the Suṣumnā, they go out through the aperture of Brahmā; then, by means of the mantra "Haṃsa," one should bring the Goddess to the thousand-spoked wheel.
O Supreme Goddess, O Great Goddess, having gone to that place where Sadāśiva Mahādeva resides, [one finds] Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity.
The goddess Rūpavatī sports with the arousal of desire;
by the fragrance of her lotus-face, the supreme Śiva is delighted.
Having awakened her there, O Supreme Goddess, one should dwell above that, O Beloved;
for Kuṇḍalinī, O Śivā, kisses the lotus-face of Śiva.
O Goddess of the gods, O Beloved, Sadāśiva may sport for even a moment;
O Supreme Goddess, at that very instant, nectar is produced, O Devi.
O Goddess, the nectar arising from that is as reddish as lac-dye;
with that nectar, O Mistress of the Gods, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity.
Having satiated the deities of the six chakras there with a stream of nectar,
the wise one should then bring [the consciousness] back to the mūlādhāra by that same path.
One should effect the dissolution of the mind there by means of the very process of going and returning;
practicing thus day after day, O Pārvatī.
"One is liberated from the bonds of existence through old age, poverty, suffering, and the like;
thus has been described the supreme yoga, which consists of the binding of the *yonimudrā*."
In the *Yāmala*: "The woman of the *kula*, having left the *kula*, enters the *kula* once again;
she, remaining unmanifest (*avyaktā*) and truly alone, takes her delight therein."
In the *Saṃketapaddhati*:
"The aggregate (*piṇḍa*) is proclaimed to be the power Kuṇḍalinī; the word (*pada*) is celebrated as the Haṃsa;
the form (*rūpa*) is to be known as the Bindu; and that which transcends form (*rūpātīta*) is the fruitless (*niṣphala*)."

By this sequence of piercing the six chakras, having led Kuṇḍalinī to the thousand-petaled lotus and united her there with Sadāśiva, one should bathe the Supreme Deity and the Śivas, Śaktis, and others residing in the six chakras with the nectar arising from that union; then, by means of the mantra "So 'ham" (I am He), once again—
"But the meaning of the sentence is that one should bring [the deity] to its own place.
For it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "The wise one should bring [the deity] to its own place with the mantra 'So 'ham'."
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction!
Upon [his] head is a thousand-spoked lotus, red in color and facing downward.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon the peaceful Guru together with his Śakti;
and at the Mūlādhāra, the Great Śakti who assumes the form of Kuṇḍalinī.
If the visualization in all the lotuses proceeds only with the faces turned downward,
then how can there be contemplation of the Guru and the Deity therein?
Furthermore, how could there be stability in that support at its lower part?
Or, even if it were situated with its opening facing downward, how could contemplation take place?
The illustrious Mahādeva said: "O Goddess, O you who are honored by heroes, what you have spoken is indeed appropriate;
yet, in this very matter, doubt arises—of this there is no uncertainty."
O Supreme Goddess, those lotuses situated within the Suṣumnā are now described by me as the cause for the destruction of doubt, O Mistress of the Gods.

O Goddess, that entire lotus is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman and consists of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman); it faces in every direction. Furthermore, both worldly engagement (pravṛtti) and renunciation (nivṛtti) are situated within the living being as two states of existence.
The path of worldly engagement is saṃsāra; [it leads] to the Supreme Self, which is the cessation [of that engagement].
When contemplating the path of engagement, one should visualize the downward-facing [lotuses].
And in the paths of the yoga of cessation, they are always directed upwards;
in this very way, through the distinction of states, non-doubt arises.
The Practice of Yoga for Householders:
Now I shall further explain the practice for householders.
[One should meditate upon] the Goddess Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity, who resides in the *mūlādhāra*.
O Maheśānī, at the time of enjoyment, having visualized [the deities] as far as the tip of the tongue,
the wise one should place the purified fish, meat, and other offerings into her mouth.
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer oblation into the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī at every morsel;
O Great Goddess, the wise practitioner should act in this manner.
There may arise a desire for food; yet that which is designated as the *jīva* remains unstained. In this very manner, the upper lotus is produced.
And when the posture of the Guru is correctly assumed with beautiful limbs,
the knot of the heart is pierced and all doubt is severed.
O Goddess, through the cultivation of devotion toward the guru and others, success then arises;
yet the foolish-minded man, having abandoned the milk-rice in his own home, wanders for alms.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, the state of being a madman arises;
thus has this essence been told, as perceived by my own knowledge.
Now, the description of another method of Kuṇḍalinī Yoga: I shall now proclaim the Yoga by which one becomes identical with the Divine;
O Dear One, as long as Kuṇḍalinī remains asleep in the root-lotus.
During that time, nothing whatsoever—be it mantra, yantra, or ritual worship—is accomplished;
the period of sleep is the flow of the left [channel], while awakening is the flow of the right.
Recitation during the time of sleep for ministers, however, yields fruitless results;
one should know the time of awakening for both, O Pārvatī.
If that Goddess is awakened by means of many accumulations of merit,
then mantra, yantra, worship, and the like attain grace.
From the union of yoga and mantra, liberation arises and the perfection of the mantra remains unbroken;
once the mantra is perfected, the supreme state is attained—such is the definitive conclusion of the scripture.
One who is liberated while living shall attain supreme nirvāṇa at the end of the body;
liberation, which is the crossing over of saṃsāra, is expressed by the word "yoga."

Having abandoned sleep through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), recitations (japa), and sacrifices, she becomes identical with the universe. The foundational center (ādhāra) has four petals, while the self-abiding center (svādhiṣṭhāna) has six petals;
there is a ten-petaled lotus at the navel, and one with as many petals as the sun (twelve) in the heart.
There should be a sixteen-petaled [lotus] at the throat, and likewise a two-petaled one between the eyebrows;
the one known as the thousand-petaled [lotus] is said to be on the great path of the Brahma-aperture.
"The thousand-petalled lotus, joined with the letters of the alphabet, faces downward, is white in color, and adorned with red filaments. Thus it is said.
(Regarding Sundarī, however, the color red is to be understood; because this is stated in the Samayātantra, otherwise a contradiction would arise.)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva,
and Paraśiva— these six are proclaimed as the Śivas.
Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Śākinī, Lākinī,
as well as Kākinī and Śākinī— these are proclaimed to be the Śaktis.
In the foundation, in the region of the heart, and especially between the eyebrows,
there are those known as Svayambhū, Bāṇa, and likewise the one known as Itara.
O Maheśānī, one should contemplate the three genders as being predominant:
Earth resides in the Mūlādhāra, and Water in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, O beloved.
O Maheśānī, the fire-element resides in Maṇipūra, and likewise the wind-element in the heart;
but in Viśuddhi, O lotus-eyed one, is the space-element.
O Maheśānī, at the *ājñācakra* is the mind, which accomplishes all aims.
Above that, O Parameśānī, there is always a lotus facing upwards.
Above that, O Maheśānī, one should always meditate upon the Guru, who is Sadāśiva.

Regarding the phrase "facing upwards": the meaning is that one should meditate upon the venerable Guru, who is the very form of Śiva, atop a twelve-petaled lotus facing upwards, which is situated above a thousand-petaled lotus facing downwards. Thus it is stated in the Yāmala:
I worship the twelve-syllable lotus, eternally attached within the interior of the lotus of the *brahmarandhra*, pure and wonderful, adorned with the opening of the channel of Kuṇḍalinī.
I worship the twelve-syllabled lotus with twelve petals.
What kind of lotus? It is adorned by the stalk of the aperture in the *kuṇḍalī*, that is, from the *mūlādhāra* lotus.

The path of travel is the presence of Sadāśiva in the form of a drop (bindu) within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus; its "stalk" (kāṇḍa) is the stalk that serves as its support, meaning the channel called Citriṇī.
It is adorned by it; the meaning is that it is the head-ornament of the *citriṇī* channel, like a lotus stalk.

It is called an "ornament" because the twelve-syllable lotus is situated at its tip. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is eternally attached within the interior of the lotus of the *brahmarandhra*, the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*).

The meaning is that it remains attached in the region below the pericarp (*karṇikā*), in a state of constant inseparable connection. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "avadapta," meaning white. Again, of what nature is it?
It is "adbhuta," meaning enchanting. Therein, according to the previously mentioned sequence, [one should contemplate] the venerable Guru in the form of Śiva.
One should meditate.
O Supreme Goddess, there are six cakras; Sadāśivapura is equal [to them]. O Great Goddess, Śaktipura is above Sadāśivapura.
That very [reality], situated above the Kalā known as Nirvāṇa, is the city of the power of Nirvāṇa;
it is called the abode of Śiva by the Śaivas, the Supreme Person by the Vaiṣṇava groups, and generally the station of Hari and Hara by some others.
Even other lords of sages, who delight in the essence of bliss from the pair of the Goddess’s feet, [seek] that stainless abode of Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
The method for the downward return of Kuṇḍalinī:
O Maheśānī, having sported with Śambhu, one should bring Kuṇḍalī, the supreme deity, from the Sahasrāra down to the Mūlādhāra.
One should contemplate that supreme power as having become one with Śambhu;
there, one should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī in the form of one's chosen deity.
Always sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts,
endowed with fresh youth, and adorned with all ornaments.
Resembling the full moon, red in hue, with eyes that are ever-flickering,
endowed with various jewels, auspicious, and her feet adorned with anklets.
She likewise has a girdle of tinkling bells at her waist, adorned with jeweled bracelets;
she possesses the beauty of ten million Cupids and always wears a sweet smile.
Having meditated thus, O Śivā, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
having recited it with the *mātṛkā-mālā*, one should bring it to the *ājñā-cakra*.
There, one should join the supreme Kuṇḍalinī with the other [liṅga];
having meditated upon her there as consisting of Brahman, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Then, having led her into purification, one should unite her with Śiva;
meditating upon that chosen deity, O beloved, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having led her into the heart-lotus, one should unite her with the arrow;
meditating upon her in the form of the Goddess, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having led her to Maṇipūra, one should unite her with Śiva;
meditating on her in the form of the Goddess, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having led [the consciousness] to the Svādhiṣṭhāna, one should unite it with Śiva. Having united them, one should mutter the mantra while meditating on the Goddess and speak pleasant words.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should lead it to the crown of the head (mūrdhādhāra).
There, one should meditate upon the self-manifested (svayambhū) Liṅga, possessing a luster like that of a kunda flower.
White in color, with four arms, five faces, and three eyes;
adorned with various jewels, beautiful, and endowed with three and a half coils.
With a serene countenance and peaceful, adorned by his blue throat,
with matted locks and all ornaments shimmering, he possesses a radiance equal to the kunda flower.
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate within the six chakras upon Śivā, who consists of the universe—
the eternal, supreme Kuṇḍalinī, the Goddess in the form of a serpent.
O fair-faced one, [worship] the divine goddess who consists of the essence of the senses, who is manifest as nectar itself,
whose form is unmanifest, who is divine, and who is accessible through meditation.
O Goddess of the Gods, by meditating and reciting [the mantra], one becomes manifestly composed of Brahman.
O Goddess, he who performs this coming and going in this manner twelve times [becomes so].

He is liberated from all sins and attains perfection in mantra; it is not otherwise. Whether he dies there or there, whether in the Ganges or in the dwelling of a dog-cooker, one who knows Brahman is fit for becoming Brahman itself, O beloved; it is not otherwise.
Now, the prayer:
"O Goddess, I am not another; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow.
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss; eternally liberated and established in my own true nature."
Impelled by the Supreme Goddess residing in my heart, I act;
I have no task whatsoever anywhere in the three worlds.
I know what is dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is adharma, yet I have no aversion to it. O Great Goddess, dwelling within my heart, I do exactly as I am directed by you.
O Śrī Pārvatī, O Triśakti, whose essence is the consciousness of the three worlds, it is solely by the command of your feet that,
having risen at dawn, I shall follow the course of worldly existence for your pleasure.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he should go forth from his home self-restrained;
having sipped water and being purified, the practitioner of mantra should perform the cleansing of the teeth.
Regarding the procedure for cleaning the teeth,
the *Tantragandharva* states:
"He who worships the deity without having chewed a tooth-stick..."
O Goddess, that worship is fruitless, and upon death, one goes to hell.
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Having performed the necessary purification, rinsing the mouth, and cleaning the teeth,
and having completed the washing of the face and other such acts, one should perform the ritual bath."
Now, the mantra for washing the face, according to the *Dakṣiṇāmūrti*: *klīṃ kāmadevasarvajanapriyāya namaḥ* | One should then write: *klīmātmakaṃ kāmadeva-sarvajanam*.
This mantra, dear to the heart, consists of fourteen syllables for the purification of the teeth; one should wash the mouth with it for the sake of attaining perfection.
The procedure for bathing is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"All rites for human beings prescribed in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* have their root in bathing."
Therefore, one should practice bathing, which increases prosperity, nourishment, and health.
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "When the dawn has not yet risen, the practitioner of mantra, having performed the Vedic bath at a sacred ford or in pure water,
should perform the Tantric bath."
Regarding what must be done when digging another’s well, the Viśvasāra states:
"In the case of digging another’s well, one must always perform the removal of five lumps of earth."
The mantra for bathing is stated as follows:
"Arise, arise, O mud! Abandon the merit of another!"
May my sins go to dissolution; grant me peace always.
In the *Nīlatantra*:
"Having submerged again in the water, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*);
then, having made the resolve, the wise man stands in water reaching up to his navel."
For the pleasure of one's chosen deity, one should cause a bath to be performed everywhere;
for the sake of worshipping the chosen deity, a bath should be taken in a body of water.
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"Having brought the clay with the Astra-mantra, one should divide it into three parts there;
one part should be cast into water while reciting the mantra."
Thus, reciting the root mantra, one should smear [the body] from the crown of the head down to the navel;
the remainder, however, one should likewise smear from the feet up to the navel.
Having performed the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) upon the limbs, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one should invoke the sacred water (tīrtha) from the mandala using the heart-mantra and the kuśa-mudrā.
From the mandala means from the solar mandala.

The mantra for invoking the sacred waters (tīrthāvāhana): "O God, O Sun, by that truth through which all the sacred waters existing in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) have been touched by Your hands, grant me a sacred water."
Oṃ! O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in these waters!
Oṃ, O beautiful goddess, I invoke you here for the purpose of bathing;
come, O Gaṅgā, salutations to you who are endowed with all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having thus invoked [the deity] according to the rule, one should consecrate it with the root mantra;
having addressed it, one should join it with the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire within the water.
Having reflected thus, the practitioner should immerse himself in its midst while reciting the root mantra;
then, having emerged and performed ritual sipping (ācamana), he should subsequently perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
The *ācamana* mantra from the *Yāmala*: "The foremost of practitioners should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) with the principles (*tattva*) of Ātman, Vidya, and Śiva."
O Dear One, having placed the wife of Vahni (the letter *S*) at the end [of the mantra], the practitioner, having consecrated that water with pure water using the root-mantra,
should then wash away the impurity of the body with that water by means of the *kumbha-mudrā*.
One should sprinkle oneself ten times with the mudrā called *kalaśa*,
or else one should consecrate oneself seven times with water consecrated by the mantra.
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Pārvatī, when the left hand is made into a fist and placed over the right hand,
it becomes the auspicious mudrā called Kalaśa, which removes all sins."
In the Gautamīya: Having squeezed out the water from his garment, having washed it beautifully, and having sipped water while remaining silent,
he should put on two pure garments, an undergarment and an upper robe.
Seated upon a seat, one who desires liberation should sip water while wearing two uncut, white garments; one who desires worldly enjoyment should wear two red garments.
The procedure for the Śāktatilaka: O Dear One, one should apply a tilaka with red sandalwood paste or with sandalwood;
one should inscribe the weapon-mantra of the Goddess on the forehead, and then the seed-syllable of Tārā upon the heart.
The practitioner, the best among men, should cause the Śakti to enter the center.
The meaning is that one should draw the weapon-mantra of the particular goddess whom one worships.
O King, whatever Vedic rite one performs without the *tripuṇḍra*,
it shall be fruitless, even if performed by Brahmā himself.
Thus, from the statement in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*. And in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Whether one be a Vaiṣṇava, a Śaiva, a Śākta, or even a Saura, whoever performs worship without the *tripuṇḍra* goes to a downward state."
In the Śivadharmottara: "He who applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on his forehead with white ashes,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva."
The mention of "ashes" is illustrative; the *tripuṇḍra* should also be made with other substances. Thus it is said in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"One should always apply the *tripuṇḍra* everywhere using the ashes of a sacrifice."
If those are unavailable, one may do so with sandalwood paste, or with clay, or even with water.
Whatever action one performs without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) of ash,
all of it becomes utterly fruitless, just like sexual union with a barren woman.
If a twice-born man of beast-like intellect makes a mark with gaps,
a gap will arise for him in regard to dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the Vedic and Tantric twilight rites (saṃdhyā);
and one should ensure that the hand is not empty, using gold, silver, or kuśa grass.
In rites such as recitation (japa) and worship, gold and silver alone are used;
for the Śākta tradition, this is kuśa grass, not the darbha grass grown in the forest.
Silver should be worn on the index finger, and gold should be worn on the ring finger.
Now I shall explain the Tantric twilight ritual (*sandhyā*), which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Having sat down, the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) with water that is free from bubbles and impurities.

Then, having uttered the beloved of Agni (svāhā) in sequence for the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), for the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva), and for that which is beyond— the principle of Śiva (śivatattva)— he should offer oblations.
Facing either the east or the north, the wise person should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with these [mantras] ending with the *mūla-mantra*;
having then performed the sipping, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should recite the root mantra ten times over the water;
then, with *kuśa* grass, one should sprinkle that water on the ground three times and upon one's head seven times.
Having recited the root mantra, O Goddess of gods, one should then take water in the left hand;
having taken that water, O Goddess, one should recite the root mantra over it.
Furthermore, having consecrated it three times with the seed-syllables of Śiva, Vāyu, Water, Earth, and Fire,
and seven times with the root-mantra using the *tattva-mudrā*.

One should pour the dripping water over one's head, and having placed the remainder on the right [hand], one should draw it into the interior of the body through the *iḍā* [nāḍī]; thus, the accumulation of sins is washed away.
The practitioner of mantras should expel that black-colored water through the right channel;
having visualized it in the form of sin within his right hand,
he should cast it onto a diamond-stone (vajra-pāṣāṇa) in front of him while reciting the Astra mantra.
The procedure for libation (tarpaṇa): Having drawn the yantra in water, one should offer libations to the Supreme Deity;
having worshipped the Goddess there together with her retinue.
Having first gratified the lines of gurus, one should then gratify one's chosen deity;
facing north, one should gratify the Goddess alone.
"May the Mother of the worlds be satisfied, and likewise may Bhairava be satisfied;
having uttered the name at the end of the root-mantra, one should thereafter say, 'I satisfy [you].'"
At the end of the *svāhā* [mantra], one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) twenty-five times in this manner;
and one should perform the libation while uttering [the name] in the accusative case.
One should satisfy the retinue, numbering twenty-five, or ten, or even three,
with water from each individual handful.
Standing, one should offer three handfuls of water as an *arghya* oblation to the Sun with water,
while reciting the Sūrya mantra: "Oṃ Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ."

Having uttered "to Mārtaṇḍabhairava," joined with the power of illumination (prakāśaśakti), ending in the letter *ṅ*, and followed by "to him who is endowed with the planets and zodiac signs," one should utter the two *ṭha*s.
The mantra-practitioner should cast three handfuls of water for the sake of accomplishing the rites along with their ancillaries;
then, having cast another handful of water, [he should visualize the deity] situated within the solar mandala.
One should meditate upon the Goddess in the solar orb, having the very form of the Sun;
having recited the respective Gāyatrī mantra, one should offer the arghya water with this [mantra].
One should meditate upon the goddess Gāyatrī, who is seated upon the solar throne;
having performed meditation in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, the wise person should recite her mantra.
"Having performed meditation" means that one should recite [the mantra] after having meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī in the form of the three seed-syllables.
The meditation on Kuṇḍalinī:
O Goddess, Kuṇḍalinī is threefold, and likewise the three seed-syllables (bījas) are threefold;
one should contemplate the third Kuṇḍalinī at the crown of the head, whose nature is eternal bliss.
One should meditate on the Vāgbhava [syllable] at the root region, resembling molten gold,
and the eternal Vahnikuṇḍalinī, as red as the rising sun.
In the heart is the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
there is also Sūrya-kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is eternal bliss.
In the middle of the eyebrows is the seed-syllable of Śakti, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons;
there is Candrakuṇḍalinī, whose form consists of flowing nectar.
O Goddess, [I salute] Turyā-kuṇḍalinī, who consists of the three seeds within the Bindu, who is composed of the three Bindus, who is the solitary Turyā-kuṇḍalinī, whose form is pure knowledge.
At dawn, one should meditate upon Śivā in the Mūlādhāra, who has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, whose eyes are the sun, fire, and moon, and who holds a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow.
At midday, in the heart-lotus— one should contemplate the Goddess, resplendent in the bloom of fresh youth;
at evening, between the eyebrows.
In the evening, one should meditate upon the Goddess, who is the singular radiance of the three worlds.
One who is devoted to enjoyment should meditate at night upon that very same supreme digit, radiant and endowed with fresh youth, within the thousand-spoked [lotus] during the night.
The Procedure for the Recitation of Gāyatrī:
The wise one should recite the Gāyatrī twenty-eight times;
he should recite the mantra mentally, especially the Gāyatrī.
Regarding the Gāndharva [Veda]: because it causes one who sings to sing, it is called Gāyatrī;
even one burdened with great sins, if he should mutter it ten times, [is purified].
Truly, truly, O Great Goddess, one becomes liberated at that very moment if one recites the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
Being completely liberated from all sins, one becomes entitled to perform worship;
one should then recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.

Regarding what must be done with a wet cloth, the *Yāmala* states: "Standing in water reaching up to the navel while meditating on the Goddess situated in the sun, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; thus one obtains great prosperity."
Having dismissed the holy site with the *saṃhāramudrā*, remaining restrained in speech,
the pure-souled one, observing silence, should contemplate the supreme Vidyā within his heart.
Having become inward-minded, one should then enter the sacrificial ground.
This *śakti-sandhyā* has been proclaimed by me; it should be performed by the best of practitioners.
If the *sandhyā* is missed, however, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* ten times.
One should perform the *sandhyā* at the three periods of the day. Likewise, in the Śaiva Āgama: "The knower of mantras should perform the *sandhyā* in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.
Regarding the fault incurred by failing to perform the *sandhyā*, the Lakṣmīkulārṇava states:
But he who is devoid of the twilight devotions shall not obtain the fruit of initiation.

A Śūdra also has the right to perform the Tantric twilight devotions (sandhyā). As stated in the Viśuddheśvara: "A Brāhmaṇa should always perform the three twilight devotions according to the prescribed rules;
however, a Śūdra should perform the twilight devotion according to the procedure taught in the Tantra."

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of Morning Duties," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme renunciant (*paramahaṃsa*), the holy Avadhūta. 4.
The Fifth Chapter:
Determination of the Seat. Regarding the acceptability of the seat, the Gaurīyāmala states:
If one should perform the worship of the deities while standing in water,
or even while seated on a seat, one should not perform it in that manner without having stood up.
Having prepared a seat, one should worship it mentally in the water;
seated upon it, one should perform the recitation properly, with the mind fixed on the meaning of the mantra.
In the Sammohana Tantra:
"The practitioner, with a steady mind, should sit upon a red seat, situated in a house reddened by lac, or [sit] upon a red [seat] imagined by the mind."
The wise one should prepare a seat of kuśa grass, cotton, woolen blankets, or garments, or the skins of lions, tigers, or deer; this increases good fortune and wisdom.
Whether it be silk, or animal hide, or cotton cloth,
or even a leaf of the Śara reed, a palm leaf, a woolen blanket, or a seat made of Darbha grass.
Success in knowledge is attained on a black antelope skin, and liberation is achieved on a tiger skin;
however, householders have no entitlement whatsoever to the black antelope skin.
A householder who has not received initiation should never enter upon a black antelope skin;
however, an ascetic, a forest-dweller, a student, and a mendicant may do so.
On a cloth seat there is the destruction of disease; on a woolen blanket, the destruction of suffering.
He who uses a cloth seat causes a loss of his recitation, meditation, and austerity.
In this context, the prohibition of clothing refers specifically to sitting on a seat made of cloth alone; otherwise, a contradiction would arise.
Longevity is attained by sitting on a seat of *kuśa* grass, and liberation is attained on a tiger skin.
With a deer-skin one may have a daughter, while with a woolen blanket (kambala) there is supreme accomplishment;
for rites of pacification, a white blanket is prescribed, and for all purposes, a multicolored one.

For rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), however, silk is recommended; for the rite of liberation from suffering, a woolen blanket (kambala) is prescribed. For the worship of Tripurā, a red woolen blanket as a seat is auspicious.
In the collection of rites for worship, this [seat] should not be longer than two cubits, nor wider than one and a half cubits,
nor more than three finger-breadths in height;
then one should prepare a seat that is neither too low nor too high.
In the *Tantragandharvadhāraṇī*,
it is stated that suffering and misfortune arise from sitting on a wooden seat.
He sits upon a seat made of mango, neem, and kadamba wood, which destroys his lineage;
and he is deprived of prosperity on the bakula, kiṃśuka, and panasa trees.
A practitioner of mantra should avoid a seat made of bamboo, bricks, stone, earth, grass, or leaves, as it bestows poverty, disease, and suffering.
The *Gandharva Tantra* distinguishes the wooden seat: "A seat fashioned from *gāmbhārī* wood is praised; no other auspicious wooden seat is so.
O Śivā, one should make the wooden seat twenty-four finger-breadths in length."
For the worship of Mahāmāyā, a rug made of wool, skin, or cloth should be sixteen finger-breadths wide and four finger-breadths high.
An excellent seat is prescribed for Kāmākhyā, and likewise for Tripurā; for Rudra and Viṣṇu as well, a seat of kuśa grass is ordained.
On a seat of grass there is loss of fame; on a seat of sprouts, there is mental confusion.
One should adopt the prescribed posture, which bestows all accomplishments.
A practitioner should not assume an arbitrary posture during the rite of worship.
Otherwise,
a wise person should avoid a seat made of bamboo, stone, earth, wood, grass, or leaves, as it bestows the suffering of poverty and disease.
In the Tantra it is said: "If one sits on a wooden seat, one will become ill; on a bamboo seat, there will be the destruction of one's lineage;
on a stone seat, there will be an obstruction of speech; and on a leaf seat, there will be confusion of the intellect."
Elsewhere it is also said:
"On earth one is joined with sorrow; on wood, one's labor becomes fruitless."

The five postures are declared in sequence as follows: the lotus posture (padmāsana), the one called the auspicious (svastika), the fortunate (bhadra), the thunderbolt posture (vajrāsana), and likewise the hero’s posture (vīrāsana).
Regarding the characteristics of the lotus posture (padmāsana) and others: one who knows the ritual procedure should take the left foot and place it upon the right,
and likewise place the right foot upon the left.
Pressing the heels against the perineum with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose—
this is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is praised for the performance of recitation.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs, the practitioner of mantra should enter with an upright body; that they call the *svastika*.
Having placed the pair of ankles very firmly on both sides of the perineum,
one should bind the sides of the feet below the scrotum with both hands.
The Bhadrāsana has been described and prescribed by the sages:
having placed the feet successively upon the thighs, with the knees facing outward and the fingers turned inward.

One should place the hands as described; this is called the unsurpassed Vajrāsana. Having placed one foot below and likewise resting the other upon the thigh, with the body straight, the practitioner should enter [the posture]; this is declared to be Vīrāsana.
Regarding the description of the daily and occasional worship in the Rudrayāmala: "Worship is traditionally taught to be threefold: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya)."
In the Nīlatantra:
"The mantra-practitioner, devoted to daily service, should perform occasional worship."
One should perform the daily worship by day and the occasional worship at night; the performance of rites for specific desires belongs to both times—such is the settled conclusion of the scripture.
In the Rudrayāmala:
"One should always perform worship at night; success is attained at night, without a doubt.
Worship performed at night is fruitful, whereas worship during the day is fruitless."
Being pure, one should recite the Śakti-mantra at night even without performing worship;
indeed, recitation performed specifically at midnight yields exceedingly great fruit.
In the Bṛhattoḍala Tantra:
"He who worships Kālī, Tārā, and likewise Bhairavī at night shall in every way become the most excellent among the lords of the earth as far as the oceans."
Elsewhere also: "Mātaṅgī, as well as Bālā, Cāmuṇḍā, Chinnamastakā,
Bhadrakālī, Durgā, and likewise Jayadurgā."
If the recitation and worship of these [mantras] are always performed at night,
he will necessarily attain the state of Rudra after having enjoyed all pleasures without exception.
In the *Samayātantra*: "O Goddess with eyes like blue lotuses, worship performed during the day yields the fruit as described;
however, worship performed at night is multiplied by a hundred thousand."
Indeed, that period of exactly two muhūrtas following midnight is designated as the "Great Night" (Mahārātri); whatever is performed during that time becomes inexhaustible.
In the Tantra it is said:
"When the first watch has passed, one should perform the recitation until the end of the third watch of the night; however, one must not recite during the remainder of the night."
If the Śakti-mantra becomes manifest, there will be a progressive decline;
having come into the presence of the bound soul (paśu), one should abandon the daily worship.
If it is performed in the presence of an animal, it becomes fruitless due to negligence;
however, it must never be concealed among one's own practitioners.

O Supreme Goddess, it is declared that worship and recitation performed near a woman during the mantra of the *samaya* are a hundred times more effective and imperishable than those performed at Kāmarūpa.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of Postures," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme renunciant (*paramahaṃsa*), the holy Avadhūta. 5.
The Sixth Chapter: The Procedure for Internal Sacrifice.
Having abandoned the deity residing within oneself, one should contemplate the external deity.
Having abandoned the Kaustubha gem held in their own hands, they wander about out of a craving for glass.
Having visualized Śivā within one's heart as being present externally, one should worship her;
and for whichever deity it may be, according to their respective ornaments and vehicles.
O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate that very [mantra] during his worship;
now I shall describe the internal sacrifice (antaryajana) by which one becomes identical with the Divine.
Seated comfortably on an easy seat, facing either the east or the north.
Within one's own heart, one should meditate upon the supreme ocean of nectar,
and in its center, an island of jewels composed of golden sand.
It was adorned on all sides by divine celestial trees, such as the Mandāra and Pārijāta, which were beautifully in bloom and bore fruits and flowers perpetually.
The quarters of the sky were perfumed with the fragrance of various sweet-smelling flowers;
it was filled with the scent of blossoming blooms and swarms of joyful bees.
The quarters of the horizon were made resonant by flocks of warbling cuckoos;
it was adorned on all sides with divine, shimmering golden lotuses,
pearls, flowers, garlands, silken garments, and golden archways.
In the midst of that, O Goddess, one should meditate upon the enchanting Kalpa tree,
which has four branches representing the four Vedas and is endowed with the three qualities.
O beautiful one, there are yellow, black, white, and red flowers;
it is adorned with green and variegated blossoms, shining with many kinds of flowers.
O Goddess, it was adorned with cuckoos, bees, and many other birds;
having thus meditated upon the Kalpa-tree, one should then [meditate upon] the jeweled pedestal beneath it.
There, one should contemplate above a great, pervasive jeweled pavilion,
resembling the rising sun and adorned with jeweled stairways.
It was filled with rows of banners, provided with four gates,
enriched by the splendor of various jewels, and adorned with a wall of gems.
It was presided over by various world-protectors stationed in their respective places, as well as by Siddhas,
Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Mahoragas.
It was surrounded by kinnaras and apsarases sporting together,
and joined by throngs of celestial women devoted to dance and instrumental music.
It was adorned with banners bound with networks of tinkling bells,
and embellished with great rubies, lapis lazuli, precious gems, and yak-tail whisks.
It was adorned with canopies draped with large pearls and anointed with sandalwood,
agallochum, saffron, and musk.
In the center of that, O Goddess, one should visualize a great pedestal of rubies,
shining with the rays of the rising sun and moon and adorned with four corners;
there, one should meditate upon the lion-throne whose nature consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Maheśānī, one should place a cushion of flowers upon the lion throne.
Then one should perform the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā) according to the sequence prescribed in one's own ritual manual;
there, upon a lotus-seat of the deceased (pretapadmāsana), one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess.
The meaning is that one should perform meditation on one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
Having offered the two lotus-feet of Śrī and led her to the bathing chamber,
one should perform the application of unguents for her as she sits upon the lion-throne.
With camphor, agallochum, musk, and likewise with deer-musk,
along with the powders of saffron and gorocana, combined with various fragrances.
Having performed the rite of elevation for the goddesses, one should anoint them with fragrant oil;
[this is done] by hundreds of thousands of goddesses with thousands of golden jars.
Having brought her and bathed her with water, one should meditate upon the Supreme Deity;
then, having wiped her limbs with fine silk cloths, one should dress her in silk garments.
Having groomed the hair with *kaṅkatī* wood, one should perform the binding according to the prescribed rite;
a cluster of silk, adorned with various jewels, should be placed upon the mass of hair.
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead and vermilion at the parting of the hair;
one should offer a beautiful conch shell inlaid with the tusks of the king of elephants.
One should likewise give armlets for the hands, as well as bracelets and bangles,
and a golden ring adorned with various gems.
One should place anklets on the feet and an elephant-pearl on the tip of the nose;
one should offer flower garlands and ornaments according to one's capacity.
One should apply an ointment of fragrant sandalwood and sihla to all the limbs;
she is adorned with a golden, bejeweled bodice over her heart.
One should contemplate the Goddess in meditative absorption (samādhi) and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth;
having then executed the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsajāla), one should always worship her within that absorption.
One should worship Śivā, who resides in the heart, with the sixteen types of offerings;
one should offer a jeweled lion-throne and utter words of welcome and well-being.
O Goddess, one should offer water for the feet at the feet of Śiva and present the arghya offering;
one should then give the supreme nectar for rinsing the mouth into his lotus-like face.
One should offer the madhuparka into the mouth, and three times perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) into the mouth;
[and present] the divine, well-prepared supreme food contained within a golden vessel.
Food prepared with ghee from a tawny cow, accompanied by various side dishes;
(an ocean of nectar, a mountain of meat, a heap of fish, and fruits);
as well as food to be eaten, swallowed, licked, chewed, and sucked.
One should mentally offer betel leaf together with camphor.
Then one should indeed worship the covering of the Goddess with the mind alone;
having thus worshipped internally, one should mutter the mantra with the mind alone.
Having performed the recitation (japa) one thousand times or more, one should offer water to the Goddess.
[The deities are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These very [elements] are declared to be the couch of the Great Goddess.
One should prepare a bed resembling the foam of milk, adorned with various flowers;
there, one should place the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods, upon a bed of flowers.
The practitioner, a yogi, should contemplate her who delights in manifold pleasures;
he should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with dance, song, and musical instruments.
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for the sake of making the worship effective.
Now I shall explain the fire sacrifice (homa) by which one may attain the state of pure consciousness;
then, one should perform the oblation in the fire of consciousness within the sacrificial pit consisting of the substratum.
The Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self are proclaimed as the natures of consciousness;
one should meditate upon this form as the square fire-pit of consciousness (cit-kuṇḍa).

Beginning from the girdle of bliss (ānandamekhala) and marked by the three circles of the bindu, it takes the form of the womb of the half-measure (ardhamātrā); thus it becomes composed of the bliss of Brahman.
Having visualized the *iḍā* channel on the left side, the *piṅgalā* on the right,
and the *suṣumnā* in the middle, one should perform the purification (*dhauti*) according to the prescribed rule.
The master practitioner should conceive of both dharma and adharma as the sacrificial oblation;
having recited the root mantra, he should then mutter this verse:
In the fire of the nature of consciousness at the navel, eternally kindled by knowledge, I offer the functions of the senses as oblations with the ladle of the mind.
One should offer the first oblation with the mantra ending in the wife of Vahni (svāhā),
and after the root mantra, one should recite this other verse.
With the ladle of the mind, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses as oblations into the fire of the Self, which is kindled by the fuel of dharma and adharma, via the path of the *suṣumnā*.
One should prescribe the second oblation with the mantra ending in the wife of Vahni (svāhā);
then, having uttered the root mantra, one should recite this verse:
Supporting myself with the hands of light and space, and using the ladle of *unmanī*,
I perpetually offer the activities of the senses into the fire kindled by knowledge.
One should perform the third oblation with the mantra ending in the wife of Vahni (Svāhā);
then, having recited the root mantra, one should mutter this verse.
Into the fire of consciousness— which blazes within without external fuel, which stands as an obstacle to the darkness of delusion,
and which is the ground for the unfolding of some wondrous radiance— I offer the entire universe as an oblation.
Beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva.
Having offered oblations with that [mantra] ending in "svāhā," one should immediately perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
then, having recited the root mantra, one should utter this verse.
I offer this supreme nectar, filled within the vessel of the limited "I" (idantā),
as a full oblation into the fire consisting of the supreme "I" (parāhantā).
O Dear One, one should offer the five *pūrṇā* oblations with the mantra ending in the wife of Fire (*svāhā*).
Having thus performed the internal sacrifice, one becomes directly composed of Brahman.
In this very way, O beloved, householders worship the Supreme Goddess;
likewise, yogis and sages also worship her constantly.
A householder cannot achieve perfection through the mind alone;
rather, a householder achieves perfection through that very [practice] together with its external component.
In the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and in all external forms of worship, internal worship is prescribed;
therefore, without internal worship, one shall certainly not obtain the fruit of external worship.
O Maheśānī, internal worship yields ten million times the fruit of external worship;
what is the use of external worship, for all its exertion is entirely in vain?
In the absence of ritual offerings and the like, external worship is a mere torment;
that worship which is performed without ritual offerings becomes fruitless.
In another tantra:
"If there is external worship and even the availability of ritual materials, one should perform the internal sacrifice in this manner and then carry out the procedure for the external sacrifice."
In the *Yāmala*: "O Maheśānī, in the absence of an image, one should worship Śivā in the heart;
O beloved Goddess, the practitioner thereby obtains the fruit of all worship."
In the *Tantragandharva*:
"If food offerings (*naivedya*) are given to Mahādevī by means of the mind,
that man who is endowed with devotion shall become long-lived and wise."
One who mentally offers a garland of a thousand lotuses [to the Buddha] shall [enjoy the fruit] for thousands of koṭis of kalpas and hundreds of koṭis of kalpas.

Having resided in Devīpura, the glorious one shall become a sovereign ruler upon the earth. Furthermore, he who performs a circumambulation of Mahādevī even in his mind shall not behold the hells in the southern abode of Yama.
Even he who performs a prostration with devotion to the Great Goddess even in his mind,
having conquered the worlds, is glorified in the world of the Goddess.
"I worship the Great Goddess Mahāmāyā with devotion through various kinds of food offerings"— thus is he who is filled with such anxious thoughts.
He who repeatedly contemplates, "O brother, give me the food offering," shall conquer the worlds and be glorified in the world of the Goddess.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Internal Sacrifice," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (parivrājakācārya), the paramahaṃsa-tīrtha, and avadhūta. 6.
The Seventh Chapter: The Ritual of Worship as Taught in the Guptatantra.
Now I shall describe the worship consisting of bliss according to the secret Tantra.
By performing which, the best of practitioners attains union with Śiva.
O Maheśvarī, having entered the house of worship, the supreme practitioner should first bring water and perform the washing of his feet.
Facing north, one should perform the washing of the feet;
by day one should face east, and at night one should face north.
Facing north, one should always perform the worship of the Goddess and also that of Śiva;
having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), and then the word "Tat" (That).
A wise person, having first uttered "SAD," should perform his ritual action;
by remembering this at the beginning of actions, he becomes fit for union with Brahman.
At all times and in all undertakings, whether Tantric or Vedic,
one should perform every action enjoined by tradition while recollecting one's own vidyā.
Regarding the purification of the site, the *Gandharva Tantra* states:
"The gazing at the sacrificial ground is said to be performed with the seed-syllable of *varman*;
one should perform the sprinkling of the sacrificial ground with the *astra* mantra."
A place defiled by the unknown, as well as that which requires sweeping and so forth—
all such things perish, O Dear One, through the act of beholding it.
The earth, which attained its firmness through the bodies of Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
is eternally impure in all respects during the worship of the gods.
To liberate oneself from that fault, one should draw the seed-syllable of desire upon the ground,
using five-colored powders of various hues and endowed with diverse fragrances.
Strewn with heaps of flowers, adorned with bells and yak-tail fans,
it is as beautiful as the rising sun, delightful, and a source of satisfaction for the mind.
Thus, having taken refuge in the ground, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Having meditated upon the Goddess in the lotus of the heart, one should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with mantras.
O Goddess, one should sit upon the seat, having assumed the heroic posture (vīrāsana) or other such postures.
Having sat down for the preparation of the ritual substances, the practitioner should then place the substances before him;
the perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth on the right, and the lamps all around.
The food offering (naivedya) should be placed on the right, the left, or in front, but never behind.
A lamp of ghee should be on the right, while a lamp of oil should be on the left.
The incense should likewise be offered to the left or in front, but never to the right;
one should present the perfume, flowers, and ornaments before him.
One should place everything on one's right side and set the *arghya* offering on the left;
one should also place the *arghya*, the edible offerings (*cūṣyādi*), the food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth, in close proximity.
For the purpose of washing the hands, one should place the bowl on the back;
having prepared everything with effort according to one's own capacity.
Having sprinkled the articles of worship with the root mantra, the practitioner should display the *dhenumudrā*; this is declared to be the purification of the substances.
Whatever food, offerings, flowers, perfumes, and so forth there may be—
all of these must be covered until the Supreme One has been invoked.
For the Rākṣasas accept that which is without any covering.
Now, one should place the *śānti-kumbha* (peace-pitcher), fashioned from gold, copper, or other materials, in the northeast;
it should be twenty finger-breadths in height, with a neck measuring four finger-breadths.
The base is said to be eight finger-breadths wide, and the mouth is traditionally held to be eight finger-breadths;
it should be made firm and level—this is the measurement proclaimed for it.
Regarding the procedure for the pitcher (*kumbha*), it is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"The pitcher may be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, according to one's means;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for if [the rite] is performed so, it results in fruitlessness."
The water-pot (kumbha) should be thirty-six finger-breadths in both width and height;
it may also be sixteen or twelve, but one should not make it smaller than that.
Regarding the placement of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *Gāndharva-tantra* states:
"Having sprinkled the vessel with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, one should then place it to the south;
having honored it with pure water, the wise practitioner should mutter the root mantra."
One should sprinkle everything with that water from the vessel used for sprinkling.
Regarding the purification of the water contained in the support (ādhāra), the Gāndharva-tantra states: "Alternatively, having prepared a square mandala with water..."
Oṃ, with the Vaṣaṭkāra mantra, [place] the jar together with its base upon the maṇḍala.
One should establish there the mandalas of Fire, Sun, and Moon,
and worship Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī therein.
Whatever other defilement may occur in the vessel or the water through ignorance, all that goes to destruction; that water shall become fit for worship.

The procedure for placing the *arghya* water: having prepared the *arghya* at the door, that procedure is now described. Having washed the vessel with the *astra-mantra*, one should fill it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should consecrate it with the *praṇava* alone; this is known as the general *arghya*.

The meaning is that one should consecrate [the door] ten times with the *praṇava*. Having sprinkled the door with *phaṭ*, one should worship the deities with the seed-syllables; O Supreme Goddess, the seed-syllables *gāṃ*, *vāṃ*, *kṣāṃ*, and *yāṃ* have been declared.
The best of practitioners should worship Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and likewise Yoginī at each door in this sequence.
In the *Viśvasāra*:
"If one bypasses the worship of these [deities], there shall be no accomplishment in any age.
One should worship the door-keepers in the sequence beginning from the north."
One should worship Brahmā and Vāstudeva here in the center of the house.
Having prepared a mandala upon the seat and worshipped it, the wise one should cause [the disciple] to ascend;
having purified speech, body, and mind, he should thoroughly purify the ground.
"Oṃ, purify, vajra-ground, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"— with this mantra,
the supreme guide immediately thereafter gazes with his divine vision.

One should dispel divine obstacles with mantras and weapons, those moving in the intermediate space with [mantras], and terrestrial obstacles with three blows of the heel; thus one should ward off obstacles.
In the *Viśvasāra*:
"Vision with unblinking eyes is proclaimed as divine vision (*divyadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the purification of the hands, the *Yāmala* states:
Or, facing either the northeast or the east, one should cleanse the hand with flowers while reciting the root mantra; O Goddess of Gods, one should then discard that flower to the left.
The *Yāmala* states the mantra:
"The elemental [syllable] joined with the sixteen digits of the moon, followed by the fire [syllable] joined with its sixteen digits,
ending with the feminine suffix (Ṅi) and then accompanied by *phaṭ*— this is proclaimed as the mantra for purification."
The letter *ai* is elemental (*bhautika*). The digit of the moon is the *nāda-bindu*. Fire is the letter *ra*.
The sixteenth digit is the letter *aḥ*. Thus: *aiṃ raḥ astrāya phaṭ*. This means "for purification," that is, for the purification of the hands.
Also in the *Tantragandharva*:
"The most excellent practitioner, having taken a red flower together with its fragrance,
[places] that flower upon the palm of his hand by means of this very mantra."
Then, having wiped [the vessel] with the left hand,
one should sprinkle it with the Kāma-bīja and smell it with the Vāgbhava-bīja;
O Pārvatī, one should cast this [water] toward the northeast with the Śara-bīja.
In that very context:
"From rubbing [the hands] comes the purification of the hands; from wiping [the back], the purification of the backs;
the gods are pleased by the [water] from the nose, and it is the confluence of all sacred fords."
By casting it away, all obstacles are driven far off;
furthermore, whatever defilement of the hands caused by contact with foul odors or food remnants is thereby removed.
One should destroy all that which is of unknown form by means of this rite;
having performed the purification of the hands, one should then perform the triple clapping of the palms (tālatraya).
The preceptor [should perform] the weapon-ward off above with the weapon-mantra, and likewise the binding of the directions;
with the mantra "huṃ phaṭ svāhā," he should do so upward, downward, and in all directions.
The mantra-practitioner should perform three claps and then carry out the binding of the directions;
the wise one should effect the binding of the directions with ten snaps of the fingers.
Having dispelled all obstacles, one should then purify the flower;
then, with palms joined in reverence, one should bow to the three Gurus on the left.
In the Āhata-tantra, regarding the three gurus: "O Dear One, one should lead the Guru, the Para-guru, and likewise the Parāpara-guru on the right side, and Gaṇeśa and the Goddess upon the head."
In the Gandharva [tradition],
there is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the Ṛṣinyāsa, and likewise the Pīṭhanyāsa; furthermore,
the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) for the hands and the body, and the Mātṛkānyāsa.
O Maheśānī, through the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa), one becomes identical with the Divine;
this alone is the daily rite, while other [placements] are proclaimed as optional (kāmya).
Only when a god worships a god, and not a non-god, does he worship the god;
a non-god, while worshipping a god, shall not partake in the fruit of that worship.
In the Vāsiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa:
"One who is not Viṣṇu, yet worships Viṣṇu, shall partake in the fruit of that worship;
having become Viṣṇu, he worships Viṣṇu, thus remembering."
In Bhārata:
No one who is not Viṣṇu should praise Viṣṇu; no one who is not Viṣṇu should worship Viṣṇu; no one who is not Viṣṇu should remember Viṣṇu; and no one who is not Viṣṇu shall attain Viṣṇu.
In the future:
one who is not Rudra shall not remember Rudra; one who is not Rudra shall not worship Rudra;
one who is not Rudra shall not glorify Rudra; and one who is not Rudra shall not attain Rudra.
One who is not a goddess should not proclaim the Goddess, nor should one who is not a goddess worship her;
rather, having become identical with her through the ritual placement (nyāsa), and having become the Goddess herself, one should worship her.
In the Āgneya-purāṇa:
"Through the worship of Rudra, Rudra becomes Viṣṇu; through the worship of Viṣṇu, he becomes Sūrya; and through the worship of Śakti, he becomes Śāktya and the rest."
"From the worship of Śakti"—that is, from the worship of Śakti and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), Gaṇeśa and others are included.
"By this very [method], through mere ritual placement (nyāsa), a man becomes like a god.
Likewise, through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), meditations (dhyāna), and ritual placements, one's body becomes divine.
Due to the abundance of nyāsas, the fruits are likewise manifold.
