Regarding the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*),
the *Tantragandharva* states: "The body, which by its very nature is always impure and composed of the five elements..."
O Maheśvarī, it is always indeed joined with impurities and urine.

O Goddess of the Gods, for the sake of its purification alone, the preceptor [should act] with the syllables of air, fire, and water, with the seed-syllable of the moon, and with the seed-syllable of the earth.
Drying, burning, likewise scattering ashes, raining nectar, and flooding— these should be performed by means of pūraka, kumbhaka, and recaka [breathing techniques].
O Śivā, this purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) consists of the cleansing of the elements that have assumed the form of a body through contact with the unmanifest Brahman.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in this manner, one should perform the placement of the arghya and other offerings;
thereafter, one should perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās and the nyāsa of the mantra.
One should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and carry out the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages and other elements;
having performed the nyāsa on the hands and limbs, one should meditate upon oneself as the Goddess.
Thereafter, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
These three should be practiced both in the natural order and in reverse order.
The practitioner of mantras should present the *arghya* offering according to the rules and the prescribed ritual.
He should fashion a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square;
having worshipped them with flowers, the practitioner of mantras should place the support (*ādhāra*) therein.
Having worshipped with "Obeisance to me, the fire-mandala, the self of the ten kalās," the wise one should place the arghya vessel right there.
Having performed the cleansing with the syllable *phaṭ*, the best of practitioners should worship [the vessel] with the mantra: "Oṃ!
To the solar orb (*arkamaṇḍala*), the essence of the twelve [suns], at the end of the twelve [fingers]."
One should worship the solar orb with the mantra ending in "namaḥ";
O Goddess of Gods, having filled it with pure water using the root mantra.
One should worship the moon-maṇḍala with the mantra ending in "namaḥ," namely: "Oṃ, to the moon-maṇḍala, to the one at the end of the sixteen [digits], to the self of the kalās."
Having performed the worship, the best of practitioners should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*);
there, he should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, *dūrvā* grass, and so forth.
Having touched [the water], one should mutter the root mantra; one should then duly apply the limb mantras.
Having worshipped thoroughly with the heart mantra, one should cover the water with both hands.
"With both hands" means by means of the *matsyamudrā*.
Having protected [it] with the *astra-mantra* and veiled it with the *kavaca*,
one should form the *dhenumudrā* and seal it with one's own *mudrā*.
One should contemplate that water as nectar and perform the sprinkling of the ritual substances.
With perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass— this is declared to be the *arghya* for all the gods.
Regarding the subject of Śiva, for householders, [the offering] with dūrvā grass and its sheaths is as follows:
"He who should place a three-leaved [dūrvā] stalk, hollow within, upon my head,
would be poor in this life and go to hell at the end."
Whatever is offered to the deities without water from the arghya vessel— that is, whatever is given— it shall all be fruitless.
The water for washing the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be placed to the north of the water for honoring (arghya);
beside that, one should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka) mixed with honey.
This [mixture] of śyāmāka, dūrvā grass, lotus, and viṣṇukrāntā is prescribed;
it should be offered as water for the feet (pādya) in the foot-basin and as the respectful offering (arghya) in the arghya-basin.
One should provide nutmeg, cloves, and kaṅkola for the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Having first consecrated the ritual substances, one should subsequently place those prescribed in the Tantra.
Mātṛkā is said to be of two kinds: the higher (parā) and likewise the lower (aparā).
The supreme [power] is to be known within the Suṣumṇā, while the inferior one resides within the body.
Now, the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the *Mātṛkā* according to the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The *ka*-group is in the middle of *aṃ* and *āṃ*; the *ca*-group is in the middle of *iṃ* and *īṃ*."
Uṃ ūṃ are in the center the ṭa-group; eṃ aiṃ are in the center the ta-group.

Oṃ Auṃ! O Maheśānī, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the *pavarga* in the center and the *yavarga* in the center of *aṃ* and *aḥ*, beginning with the heart and extending to the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
One should meditate upon the Goddess, whose nature is consciousness, from the base of the body up to the aperture of Brahmā;
then, satiating her with streams of nectar flowing from the *bindu*, one should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters.
The Internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa:
Now, O lotus-faced one, listen to the internal mātṛkā-nyāsa.
One should place the sixteen vowels upon the throat-lotus, which has thirty-two petals.
One should place the twelve letters beginning with *ka* upon the twelve-petaled heart-lotus;
one should place the ten letters beginning with *ḍa* upon the ten-petaled lotus at the navel.
One should place the six [syllables] beginning with *va* at the base of the *liṅga* on the six-petalled lotus;
and one should place the four syllables beginning with *ba* on the four petals of the *ādhāra*.
O Dear One, one should place the two syllables *hakṣau* upon the two-petalled lotus situated between the eyebrows;
having mentally uttered each individual letter starting from the syllable *dhru* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, this is proclaimed as the internal placement (*antaryoga*).
"Beginning with Dhruva" means beginning with the Praṇava. In the Śāradā-tantra it is said:
"Listen attentively to me regarding the external nyāsa of the Mātṛkās."
On the forehead, the face, the circular eyes, the ears, the nostrils, and the two cheeks;
On the lips, teeth, head, the joints of the arms and feet,
the tips [of the fingers and toes], on both sides, on the back, at the navel, in the abdomen, and on the heart and shoulders.
One should place the letters of the Mātṛkā in sequence upon the shoulders, the heart, the pair of hands and feet, as well as the belly and the face.
Regarding the mudrā for the placement of the *mātṛkā*, the *Mānasollāsa* states:
"One may perform the placements mentally, or one may place them with flowers;
or, in all ritual acts, one may place them by joining the thumb and the ring finger."
In the Gautamīya: "The Mātṛkā is said to be fourfold: the simple, joined with the Bindu, with the Visarga, and with both; I shall tell you the secret."

O Dear One, one should place the final and penultimate vowels, devoid of the *bindu* and *visarga*. The Vidyā alone bestows knowledge; with both [the *bindu* and *visarga*], it bestows liberation. With the *visarga*, it grants sons; with the *bindu*, it bestows the *bindu*.

The meaning is that she is the bestower of the *bindu* (the point) and the bestower of liberation. He who performs the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*— which brings wealth, fame, long life, and destroys the impurities of the Kali age— is indeed the venerable Sadāśiva himself.
Now, regarding the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa), it is stated in the Navaratneśvara:
"Upon the head, the base, the heart, and likewise upon the three eyes."
O Goddess, [place them] on the pair of ears, on the face, and again on the two arms.
One should perform the placement of knowledge (vidyā-nyāsa) on the back, the two knees, and likewise on the navel;
for one who has thus performed the placement, he is directly Paśupati himself, though appearing as a bound soul (paśu).
In the *Phetkāriṇīyatantra*: "Having encapsulated [the mantra] with the syllable *oṃ*, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) using the root mantra;
one may perform it fivefold, ninefold, or even sevenfold."

Having recited the root mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) from the head down to the feet, from the feet up to the head, and from the heart up to the mouth; this is the meaning. Thus ends the placement of the Vidyā (*vidyā-nyāsa*).
In Viśuddheśvara—
one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) with the Vidyā immediately thereafter;
one should perform the inhalation (pūraka) through the left channel (nāḍī) with sixteen recitations.
Then, one should perform retention (*kumbhaka*) in the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) through sixty-four recitations,
and exhalation (*recaka*) in the *piṅgalā* channel with half that number of recitations.
Furthermore, the practitioner should perform the opposite [of the previous sequence] according to his capacity;
and if he is unable to do that, he should practice breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) in four ways.

"Caturddhā" (fourfold) means: inhalation (*pūraka*) by reciting the root-mantra four times, retention (*kumbhaka*) by reciting it sixteen times, and exhalation (*recaka*) by reciting it eight times. In case of inability even for that, [one should follow] the *samayāṅkamātṛkā*.
One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* channel once with the root-mantra;
then, O fair-faced one, one should retain it in the central channel for the number of Vedas [four times].
One should exhale through the path of Piṅgalā according to the sequence of the number of eyes (two),
again and again in that same order, so that it occurs three times.
The filling of air from the outside into the abdomen is *pūraka*;
the retention of air like a completely filled jar is *kumbhaka*;
and the expulsion of air from the abdomen is indeed *recaka*.
In the Jñānārṇava: "The retention of the nostrils by means of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—
excluding the index and middle fingers— is to be known as prāṇāyāma."
O Goddess, without breath control (prāṇāyāma), there is no fitness for worship.
In the *Yāmala*: "One should place the Seer (*ṛṣi*) on the region of the head, the Metre (*chandas*) in the lotus of the mouth,
the Deity (*devatā*) in the heart, and the Seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the secret region."
One should place the Śakti on the two feet and the Kīlaka on all the limbs.
"One should assign the sages" means that one should assign the respective sages, meters, deities, and so forth, as required by each particular context.
[This is stated because] when the sages, meters, and deities are not assigned...
The practitioner who merely mutters [the mantra] shall not obtain the fruit therein.
Regarding the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), the *Śāradā-tilaka* states:
"One should perform the placement on the fingers, beginning with the thumbs, using the [six] limbs together with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*).
By 'limbs' is meant the specific limb-mantras prescribed in the relevant ritual manual (*kalpa*); by 'together with their respective seed-syllables' is meant those beginning with *namaḥ*."
In the Jñānārṇava:
"The mantras ending in *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* are of the same genus [as their respective deities].
Likewise, there are the heart, head, crest, armor, the three eyes, and the weapon."
In the Śāradā-tilaka:
"Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the weapon-mantra on the two palms, one should perform the triple clapping and so forth;
with that very [mantra], being composed, one should bind the directions with snapping sounds."
Now follows the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
thereafter, the wise practitioner should place the limb-mantras upon the heart and other parts.
First, "Salutation to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), and for the head, "The Beloved of Fire" (*śirase vahnivallabhā*).
"Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock," thus it is said; "Hum to the armor" is uttered;
"Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes" should be used; and "Phaṭ to the weapon" follows in sequence.
One should apply these six limb-mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra), as thus described, to the six limbs.
In the Rudrayāmala:
The heart is said to be formed by the middle, ring, and index fingers;
the head by the middle and index fingers; and the tuft (śikhā) is said to be formed by the thumb.
"The armor is said to be [formed] with ten [fingers], the eye is declared [to be formed] with three;
the weapon (astra) shall be formed with two fingers as previously mentioned—this is considered the arrangement.
Regarding "with three," it means with the index, middle, and ring fingers.
The index, middle, and ring fingers are prescribed for the three eyes in sequence;
O Goddess, if there are only two eyes, then [the mudrā consists of] the index and middle fingers.
In the Bhairavatantra:
"The practitioner of mantra should place the six limbs [of the ritual] either three times, once, or as is appropriate. In the Tantra:
One should perform the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa* with the six long vowels. As stated in the *Sārāvalī*:
"The assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*) should be performed with that seed-syllable by which the vidyā begins."
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:

"With reference to the single syllable, the first is the seed (*bīja*) and the other is power (*śakti*). One should perform the conceptualization of the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth by means of the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels."
In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha* regarding the *Kālīvidyā*: "Omitting the vowel of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should apply the six long vowels;
thus one should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). This rule is prescribed for all cases."
Even if worship, recitation, adoration, and fire-oblations are performed with perfected mantras,
they will not yield their fruits if they are devoid of the ritual placement upon the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Thus ends the necessity of the assignment of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). Next, one should perform the sixfold assignment (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) as prescribed in the respective ritual manual (*kalpa*).
The fruit of the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa):
one who performs the sixfold placement within his body becomes Gaṅgādhara himself.
Therefore, he should certainly perform worship and recitation every single day.
Even when this is accomplished, the best of practitioners becomes equal to Mahādeva.
O Pārvatī, if one who has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) should bow to one who has not performed it,
at that very moment the one who has not performed the nyāsa will have his heart torn asunder.

O Great Goddess, he whom those whose forms are folded into six parts salute shall immediately become short-lived; the deity trembles with fear. O Goddess, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), preceded by the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Regarding the meditation on the self in the *Tantragaṇdharva*:
the practitioner should meditate upon himself as adorned by divine women.
Upon his head was a divine great parasol fashioned with a thousand petals.
Seated upon a jeweled throne, situated within a house crimson with lac,
his face reddened by betel and endowed with various fragrances.
Adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and red sandalwood,
and richly arrayed with all ornaments, he was the very embodiment of the Goddess’s own form.
Adorned with fragrant flowers, ornaments, jewels, and so forth,
success comes into his hands and never into those of anyone else.

Then, for the meditation on the Goddess, one should meditate upon the Goddess within the heart-lotus with a mind focused on her; O Queen of the Gods, having taken a flower, [one should offer it] with the *trikhaṇḍa* mudrā.
The wise person, having closed both eyes and keeping the body, head, and neck straight, should perform that [meditation] with a steady mind, seated near the heart.
In that very context, he states the necessity of performing meditation with its fruit:
"The practitioner of mantra should perform meditation, which destroys all sins;
then [he should worship] the Goddess residing in the heart-lotus with mental offerings."
The practitioner should worship her according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, sacrificial oblations, and songs.
Then the practitioner should perform mental recitation and the fire sacrifice;
having paid homage and likewise offered praise, he should carry out the external worship.
Then, having led the Supreme Goddess, who was throbbing within the petals of the heart,
along the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the location of the head, [one should contemplate] the Great Goddess.
There, having united her who consists of pure bliss with Ānanda,
one should then bring her back to the original location near the heart.
Having brought her to the station of command,

the knower of mantras should cause her to purge through the right nostril with the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*), O Goddess, by means of the *vahni* (fire) channel at the navel; he should then establish the Goddess upon the seat over the flower held in his hand.
The invocation of the Goddess: Come, come, O Blessed Mother, whose form is the grace bestowed upon devotees;
O Goddess, together with the Yoginīs, always protect me for my sake.
"O Goddess of gods! O you who are easily accessible through devotion! O Sovereign accompanied by your retinue!
Remain steadfast while I worship you.
Having meditated upon the Goddess and invoked her, one should display the respective mudrās.
The respective mudrās are the five mudrās beginning with Āvāhanī (the invocation).
He states the prohibition of invoking [the deity] in a Śālagrāma stone and so forth:
"In a Śālagrāma, in a gem, in water, in fire, in the mind, or in a flower."
And there is no invocation for these, for the gods are always present there.
Regarding the rule for the offering of substances,
the *Yāmala* states the manner of worship: "First, having uttered the root mantra, one should subsequently utter that which is to be offered."
The recipient [is indicated] at the end of that, followed by a word expressing the act of relinquishment;
thus, according to this very ritual sequence, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
One should not worship with only one hand; the appearance of the five fingernails is declared to be fruitless, for it is not auspicious anywhere.
O Maheśvarī, having scattered five handfuls of flowers upon the five locations— the feet, the base, the navel, the chest, and the crown— perform the worship of the six limbs and the other enclosures.
One should cast three handfuls of flowers upon the pair of the Goddess’s lotus feet.
Uttering this mantra, "I worship the Śrīpādukā," one should cast flowers three times with the right thumb and ring finger.
One should offer libation (tarpaṇa) into the mouth three times with the Tattvamudrā;
the joining of the thumb and ring finger is known to consist of the essence of Śiva and Śakti.
By the mere conjunction of these two, the substance becomes supreme nectar;
with that divine nectar, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity.
He has clearly stated:
"O Pārvatī, with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand,
one should satisfy the beautiful Goddess along with the mudrās and her vehicles."
Then, the practitioner should worship the six limbs there upon the body of the Goddess:
the heart-limb in the heart, and the head-limb in the head.
Having worshipped the crest-lock upon the crest-lock, the armor upon the entire body,
and the three eyes upon the three-eyed one, one should worship the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions.
The goddesses of the six limbs, eternally conjoined with the syllables *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*, reside within bodies.
In the Tantra: "One should worship the Heart in the southeast, and the Head in the northeast;
the Crest should be worshipped in the southwest, and one should worship the Armor in the northwest."
Having worshipped the Eye in front, one should likewise worship it in the directions;
one should then fully worship the six limbs, which have the forms of the primary body.
In the *Śāradāṭīkā*:
"One should worship the lineage of gurus from the northwest (Vāyavya) up to the northeast (Īśa).
Regarding the lack of knowledge concerning the lineage of gurus, it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, one should worship the Unrecognized Guru, the Guru, the Supreme Guru,
the Higher-Lower Guru, and likewise the Parameṣṭhi Guru,
in the four corners starting from the southeast.

Regarding the corners starting from the southeast (Āgneya), the *Tantragandharva* states: "The northeast (Īśāna) shall be the southeast (Agnikoṇa); likewise, the northeast shall be the northwest (Vāyukoṇa). The southwest (Rākṣasa) shall be the northwest, and the southeast shall be the southwest."
In the Gandharva Tantra:
"Alternatively, one should contemplate all rays as having the form of goddesses,
constantly emerging just as rays emerge from the orb of the sun."
Likewise, the goddesses are born from the body of the Great Goddess;
one should satisfy the multitude of rays with the nectar-water from the Śrīpātra.
Having identified the eastern direction, one should worship the deities of the limbs;
for when the gods abide in their own proper places, they bestow all desired fruits,
but when deprived of their own places, they yield the fruits of sorrow and suffering.
Regarding the determination of the directions such as the East, the *Navaratneśvara* states:
"The space situated between the object of worship and the worshipper is established as the eastern direction."
O Śivā, in all forms of worship, the Dakṣā [line] is to be known as being to the right of the one to be worshipped, the Uttarā likewise to the north, and the Paścimā to the west.
"In every respect" refers to the six-limbed worship (*ṣaḍaṅgapūjā*). One should always place the head of the deity, facing oneself and facing the deity, covered with flowers.
At the time of worship, one should not wave the hand over the deity.
Regarding the subject of Tripurā:
if a deity such as Indra were to worship Tripurā,
the back of the Goddess would be the east, and the front of Tripurā’s city would be the west.

With palms joined in reverence, having obtained permission by saying, "O illustrious Goddess Amukī, I worship your enclosure," one should worship the enclosure. Then, upon the lotus petals within the circle, starting from the front petal of the Goddess:
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship in sequence by moving counter-clockwise;
one should worship the deities of the limbs according to the very sequence prescribed in one's own ritual manual (kalpa).
In the Kulārṇava:
"One should worship three times, or even once, according to one's desire.
In the Yāmala:
One should worship the weapon of the Goddess in the cardinal directions, and then worship the Goddess again,
followed by her retinue together with their vehicles and their respective groups.
Likewise, having worshipped and gratified [the deities] with all ritual offerings,
one should recite the mantra "May they be pleased" and offer the worship to the Goddess.
One should present worship to the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth; one should satisfy the Supreme Goddess specifically with the water of the special arghya offering.
The method for the recitation of the mantra:
Having meditated upon the Kāmakalā within one's body, one should perform the recitation of the Vidyā;
preceded by the recollection of the meaning of the mantra, one should perform the recitation a thousand times or more.
In the *Bṛhacchrīkrama*:
"A practitioner should never recite [the mantra] with fewer than thirty [repetitions]. In the *Tantra*—
One should perform the recitation one thousand times, or even a hundred, or ten;
for these, it is remembered that the rule for recitation is to add eight more.
O Goddess, one should offer the recitation with perfumes, flowers, and water for the guest-offering (arghya);
one should present the recitation, which is composed of light, into the left hand of the Goddess.
The knower of mantras, with the mantra "You are the guardian of the secret, even more secret than the secret," should then perform the *nīrājana* rite ten times with lamps.
Praising [the deity] and circumambulating [them], one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
O Dear One, one should perform the surrender of the self with the mantra of self-surrender.
The surrender of the self is stated in the *Yāmala*: having recited "from this time forward," one should then utter "prāṇa-buddhi... and so forth.
With respect to the states of the body and its attributes, [these occur] in waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
In all circumstances, one should remember [the Lord] through mind, speech, and action— by means of both hands, the two feet, and likewise the belly.
O beloved of Agni, may whatever has been thought of as "the penis," as well as whatever has been spoken or done—
all that indeed be an offering unto Brahman.
One should also recollect my Praṇava, myself as the entire deity to be accomplished (sādhyadevatā) in the feminine dative case, the Tāra (Om), and likewise "Tatsat."

One should offer worship to the Goddess with water for the guest-offering (arghya), unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and roots, using the mantra "May she be worshipped. One should offer the worship to the Goddess while maintaining a disciplined mind, contemplating: "It has been accepted by the Goddess."
In the Viśvasāra:
"Whether due to lack of knowledge, negligence, or deficiency in the means of accomplishment—
whatever is deficient or excessive, you ought to forgive it all."
O Goddess, O treasure-house of compassion, please forgive all of that— whether it be lacking in material offerings, lacking in ritual action, or devoid of faith and devotion— out of Your grace.
Whatever action I perform, whether it be great or even very small, all of that must be forgiven by you, O Mother of the World; here I join my palms in supplication.
In the Kulārṇava:
"O Great Goddess, the wise man, with palms joined in reverence, should recite the protection mantra:
'Oṃ! Kālī shall provide protection for my son, and likewise Karālī shall provide protection for my body.'"
May Durgā bring about the destruction of my enemies with her boisterous laughter, and may Tārā establish me in sovereignty.
One should recite the hymn known as the *Sahasranāma*, the means for attaining liberation.

Having praised [the deity] with hymns, O Goddess, one should then recite the *kavaca*, which grants all desires. Indeed, O Goddess, without the *kavaca*, if a Śūdra were to perform the recitation (*japa*), [it would be fruitless].

Indeed, one should recite the armor-mantra (*kavaca*); that is to say, one should recite the armor-mantra conjoined with the *svāhā* and the *praṇava*. Having circumambulated the Goddess and paid obeisance, one should dismiss her.
Afterwards, having established one's own *vidyā* within the lotus of one's own heart.
Having smelled the flower through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, one should then remove it;
with the mantra "Forgive me," one should dismiss the Goddess into the heart.
In the Bhairavītantra:
"O Goddess, one should dismiss [the deity] with the Saṃhāra-mudrā, saying 'Forgive me.
O Bhairavī, one should give a hundredth part or a thousandth part of that *naivedya*."
Then, one should give [the remainder] to an outcaste woman (cāṇḍālī) with the mantra "Svāhā," according to Manu.
Alternatively—
O Goddess, one should worship the Goddess who dwells in the *nirmālya* with that very *nirmālya*;
the *nirmālya* should be worn upon the head and used as an ointment for all the limbs.
One should partake of the food offering after giving it to a devotee;
then, having consecrated a flower and sandalwood paste one hundred times with mantras, one should place them on the head and upon the forehead.
Having held [it], one will certainly bring even the three worlds under control by the mere sight [of it]:
"Whomever I tread upon with my foot, whomever I behold with my eye," [so it shall be].
Let him alone become a slave, even if he were equal to Śakra;
for by applying this tilaka, he could delude even the three worlds.
Whether fresh or even stale, the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) becomes defiled; therefore,
one should apply an ointment to the machine kept in a secret place,
or one should discard that *nirmālya* at the root of a tree or in water.
In the Rudrayāmala: "He who, having recognized this Supreme Deity through merits accumulated in previous births,
worships her with a spirit of devotion, immediately becomes the abode of prosperity and wealth."
"By the mere propitiation of which liberation while living (jīvanmukti) arises"—so says the scripture.

The worship of the Goddess is declared to be threefold: external, internal, and likewise [the third]. External worship consists of the worship consisting of mantras and the contemplation of the gross form.
O Dear One, worship with mental offerings is the internal [form of] worship.
O Goddess, without the yoga of action (karmayoga), the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga) is not perfected;
perfection occurs through either knowledge or action, and not otherwise.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of Morning Duties and the Determination of the Authority for Daily Worship," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme sage (*paramahaṃsa*), and the renunciant (*avadhūta*). || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter:
The Determination of the Rosary.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall explain the complete determination of the rosary.
One should always perform the daily recitation (japa) with the hand, but never the optional recitation (kāmya).
However, O beautiful one, if a rosary is unavailable, one may perform even the optional recitation with the hand.
Now, regarding the *karamālā* (finger rosary) in the *Yāmalatantra*: three joints of the ring finger, three joints of the little finger,
three joints of the middle finger, and the base joint of the index finger.
One should recite [the mantra] in a clockwise sequence across the ten joints;
this is known as the Śaktimālā, the illuminator of all mantras.
O Pārvatī, know that the two joints of the index finger are Meru;
if a person performs japa there, at the tip or in the middle of the index finger, four things of his perish: life-span, knowledge, fame, and strength.
In the Śrīvidyā: O Maheśvarī,
[one should touch] both the root and the tip of the ring finger and the middle finger,
and three joints of the little finger and the index finger.

O Goddess, the space between the ring finger and the middle finger is known as Meru; these two together constitute the site where one should recite the mantra of Tripurasundarī in a clockwise direction.
The method of recitation with a rosary of beads:
Having placed the hand at the heart and positioned the fingers obliquely,
one should always perform the recitation while covering both hands with a cloth using the right hand.
One should separate the fingers and slightly contract the palm;
for through the separation of the fingers, the recitation flows out through the gap.
Whatever one recites upon the tips of the fingers, whatever one recites while crossing over the *meru*,
and whatever one recites at all the joints— all that shall become fruitless.
In the *Yāmala*, it states the rule regarding beads: "A rosary fashioned from exactly one hundred and eight gems constantly bestows sovereignty and, at the end of the body, grants liberation."
With twenty-five beads it bestows liberation; with thirty, it grants the increase of wealth.
A rosary consisting of fourteen beads bestows liberation and increases enjoyments.
With twenty-seven beads all objectives are attained; with fifteen, it is used for malevolent rites (abhicāra).
(There is also a reading: "by twenty-five for malevolent rites")—by fifty, the accomplishment of one's purpose; likewise by fifty-four;
and by exactly one hundred and eight, all attainments are said to be achieved.
The eyes of Tripurā should be fashioned from rudrākṣas and red sandalwood.
In the *Vārāhītantra*, concerning the domain of Bhairavī:
"A rosary should be made of gold, jewels, crystal, or fashioned from conch-shell; it may also be made of coral, but one should avoid the *putrajīva*."
In the ritual of Dhūmāvatī, one should fashion a garland from *dhustūra* flowers found in a cremation ground;
one may also prepare a garland for Bālā using red sandalwood.
A rosary made from the teeth of Kālikā, from a "royal tooth" (rājadanta), or from Meru is recommended for the worship of Ugratārā; likewise, a rosary of Mahāśaṅkha is praised.
Likewise, the *unmukhī* and the *mālikā* should be known as bestowing success;
for those devoted to Śakti, the rosary should be made of crystal or red sandalwood.
A rosary made of rudrākṣa beads is known to bestow the fruits of the four aims of life;
one fashioned from silver and gems grants all desired objects when used for recitation.
A garland made of gold and jewels bestows all desires;
a garland fashioned from coral bestows abundant wealth.
A crystal rosary brings good fortune, one made of pearls likewise does so,
and one fashioned from conch gems produces fame that pervades the world.
A garland fashioned of gold always leads to the liberation of men;
it should be kept secret constantly, O Goddess, for the attainment of desired goals through the practice of japa.
In the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"If one should recite [mantras] with rudrākṣas, or with indrākṣas, or likewise with crystal beads,
one must not employ others in between, such as those made of putrajīva and so forth."
Whatever else one might employ in the rite of recitation with a rosary,
that [rosary] which makes things dear does not grant him either his desires or liberation.
In the *Yāmala*:
"O Dear One, if a practitioner of mantra recites the *śakti-mantra* with rudrākṣa beads, he falls into misfortune; that recitation of his is fruitless."
Regarding this, he states the counter-argument in that very same place:
"Kālikā, Chinnamastā, Tripurā, and likewise Tāriṇī—
all these are not defiled by the recitation [of mantras] using a rosary of rudrākṣa beads."
In the Rudrayāmala:
"One should never recite [mantras] with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads during the day, except for the preliminary practice (pūrvacaryā); otherwise, O fair-faced one, there is a fault herein."
If one performs any Tantric or Vedic rite, such as japa, homa, and so forth, without wearing rudrākṣa beads, all of it shall become fruitless.
Regarding the specific fruits of different types of rosaries, the *Mantradevaprakāśikā* states:
"On the joints (of other wood), it is eightfold; on *putrajīva*, it becomes tenfold;
on a conch rosary, it would be a hundredfold; and on coral, a thousandfold."
In the case of crystal, the merit is ten thousandfold; in the case of pearl, it becomes one hundred thousandfold;
in the case of lotus-seed (padmākṣa), it is one millionfold; and likewise, in the case of gold, it is ten millionfold.
In a knot of *kuśa* grass and in *rudrākṣa* beads, the merit becomes infinitely multiplied;
with a rosary of white lotus seeds, the fruit of recitation shall be immeasurable.
The procedure for the rosary is here described in brief; having diligently obtained beads according to their availability and their specific form, the method for the akṣamālās is told.
They should be equal in shape to one another, neither too thick nor too thin,
free from defects such as insects, and never worn out.
One should wash each of those separately with the five products of the cow;
[one should also use] a white thread made by a twice-born woman, free from knots.
Whether made of cotton or even of silk thread,
having tripled it and then folded it three times, one should tie it according to the rules of the craft treatises.
A silk band for all castes bestows everything desired;
a thread made of cotton grants dharma, kama, artha, and moksha.
Then, reciting the root-mantra and the weapon-mantra, one should wash the thread;
taking each individual gem, one should then join it to that thread.
Having joined mouth to mouth and tail to tail,
one should place a single-peaked mountain of the same kind in front as the *meru*.
Taking each individual bead, one should fashion the *brahmagranthi* knots;
thus one should string the rosary while recollecting the *tāra* mantra in the heart.
One should oneself recite the mantra, while another should utter the *praṇava*;
then, by turning it three and a half times, one should firmly form a knot.
Then one should apply either the *brahmagranthi* or the *nāgapāśa*;
one should make it resemble the tail of a cow or the tail of a serpent.
One should not make [the string] without knots; it is not defective on the back of Mount Meru.
Indeed, there is no defect here at all, for it is eternally without knots.
Of Kālī and Tvaritā, of the one called Vajra in the sixfold division,
and especially of Totalā, Vanavāsinī, and Vārāhī.
For no other [deity] than Caṇḍikā is a knotless [rosary] prescribed;
having thus fashioned the garland, the best of mantra-practitioners should purify it.
If a person recites the mantra with a rosary that is not fixed [to the body],
one should know that all of it is fruitless, and Caṇḍikā becomes angry.
The Ritual for the Consecration of the Garland:
Now, the consecration of the garland according to the method of the Tantra is described. Having first prostrated to the Guru, one should then consecrate the rosary for recitation.
On an auspicious lagna, on an auspicious day of the week, under an auspicious asterism, and on an auspicious lunar date,
the mantra-practitioner should perform the consecration ceremony either himself or through a preceptor.
Then, having performed the daily rites and prepared the general *arghya* offering,
one should place the rosary in the *pañcagavya* and consecrate it with the *śiva-mantra*.
The *Yāmala* states the *śiva-mantra*: "The letter Śa, joined with the vowel of the enemy (Ū), and adorned with *nāda* and *bindu*—
this is declared to be the *śiva-mantra* for the benefit of practitioners."
The letter *ha* is peaceful, and the vowel *u* is the sound of the enemy.
Immediately thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] with cool water;
one should wash [him] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and purify [him] with the *sadyojāta* mantra.
The Sadyojāta mantra, however, is as follows:
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta!
In every birth, do not lead me beyond [this state]; favor me, O source of existence! Salutations to Bhavodbhava!"
The wise one should wash [the image] with the Īśāna-sūkta, smear it with abundant perfumes using the Tatpuruṣa-mantra,
and fumigate it with incense using the Aghora-mantra.
The wise one should consecrate [the materials] with the Aghora Sūkta for at least one hundred times,
and should then harmonize them with the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should fashion a lotus shape using nine fresh leaves of the *aśvattha* tree;
in its center, one should place the rosary while reciting the root mantra of the *mātṛkā*.
Having thus consecrated the rosary, the wise practitioner should then unite its vital breaths (*prāṇas*) therein.
Having worshipped the Goddess there together with her retinue of attendants, one should consecrate those vital breaths— the vital breaths of the deity to be propitiated—
by means of the letters of the Mātṛkā in both direct and reverse order.
Having consulted with the preta, one should meditate upon Meru as being of the nature of the deity.

The meaning is: with the *preta* seed-syllable, namely the seed-syllable *haḥ auḥ*, having consecrated the fire according to the rule, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times. One should present the remainder of the oblation to the effigy with the thought that it is the deity.
If one is unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should perform double the recitation (japa):
"O Lord of the Tārā rosary, grant, grant me perfect accomplishment!"
O accomplisher of the meaning of all mantras, accomplish the pair;
then, bring about all siddhis for me, bring them about, svāhā!
Thus consecrated, this garland always grants the desired goal and likewise the fruit of all wishes during the rite of recitation.
Regarding the procedure for recitation with a rosary:
having worshipped the Guru, one should receive the akṣamālā from his hand;
at the beginning of the recitation, one should carefully worship the rosary after sprinkling it with water.
One should worship the rosary with the heart-mantra: *aiṃ hrīṃ akṣamālikāyai*.
Having worshipped it, one should then take the rosary in the right hand.
Having brought it near the heart, one should not touch it with the left hand;
being composed, one should place it in the middle part of the middle finger.
One should move the rosary, which is of medium size, with the tip of the thumb. One who is impure must not touch the rosary, nor should one allow it to fall from the hand.
One should not touch it with the index finger, nor should one show it even to one's guru.
For the sake of enjoyment, liberation, and nourishment, the wise person should perform recitation (japa) with the middle finger.
Even when reciting for each individual [mantra], the best of preceptors should rotate [the rosary] in this manner;
having completed the recitation, he should rotate the entire rosary, moving all the beads.
Having performed circumambulation once more, one should conclude it by beginning in this manner;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should thus recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times in this sequence.
One should recite the mantra up to the gross limit and offer it at the subtle level;
covering both hands with a cloth, one should always recite with the right hand.
Thus, the recitation from the subtle limit to the gross end is the withdrawal (saṃhāra).
One should not touch the rosary with one's own left hand;
having performed the recitation at the time of chanting, one should always place it in a clean location.
If the thread becomes worn out, one should string a new thread and recite the mantra a hundred times;
if it has been touched by an uninitiated twice-born person, one should perform a purification.
One should not hold the rosary in the hand, around the neck, or on the head; nor should it touch the thighs, feet, or lower lip, nor be moved by the left hand.
If it is unprotected or even moved, the rosary must undergo consecration once again.
O Goddess, I have described to you this rosary, which is difficult to find on earth;
it should always be guarded with effort if you are dear to me.
Now, the garland of letters is declared to be the fifty-fold garland; the thread consists of Śakti and Śiva.
Śakti, strung upon Kuṇḍalinī, has its single station at the end of the vowels (Alānta).
Variegated, with the luster of a lotus fiber, situated within the central channel of Brahmā,
and strung together by it— she should be meditated upon as the manifest embodiment of the waking state.
Resplendent with letters strung together like female serpents shining like coral within,
it consists of one hundred and eight syllables, arranged through ascending and descending sequences across the eight groups of consonants.
By means of the forward and reverse order, through the differentiation of the syllables of the mantra,
one should intersperse the syllables with the mantra and the mantra with the syllables.
One should fashion a rosary made of colored beads that reveals all mantras; the final syllable should take the form of Meru, and one must never allow it to be bypassed.
Having pronounced the phoneme together with its bindu, the wise one should thereafter recite the mantra;
[the sequence] from the letter 'a' to the letter 'la' is known as *anuloma* (direct order).
Again, one should recite the mantra beginning with the letter *la* and ending with *śrīkaṇṭha*; this is renowned as "in reverse order. One should then recite the letter *kṣa* alone.
The wise one should recite the mantra eight times for each of the eight groups of letters;
the wise one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times with full awareness.
The eight groups are as follows: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and śa.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Garland," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (parivrājakācārya), the supreme sage (paramahaṃsa), the holy Avadhūta. 8.
The Ninth Chapter: The Ritual of Japa.
O lotus-faced one, listen as I describe the ritual of japa.
For the purpose of recitation (japa) of all mantras, there is also the arrangement [of syllables] even without written script.
One should know that what has been performed [without this] is fruitless; therefore, O Dear One, one should first perform the placement (nyāsa).
And one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) at the beginning and at the end of the recitation (japa).
Regarding the different types of recitation (*japa*) such as the mental (*mānasa*), it is stated in the *Viśuddheśvara*:
"Recitation (*japa*) consists of the repetition of syllables; it is mental, whispered (*upāṃśu*), or vocal (*vācika*)."
That which is mental and within the range of one's own ears is known as *japa*.

The whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is declared to be within the range of one's own ears, while the audible recitation (nigada) is to be understood by others; thus, the threefold repetition (japa) is described.
Elsewhere also it is said:
"If one should clearly utter the mantra with syllables that are distinct sounds, articulated in high and low tones, that sacrifice of recitation is vocal."
One should utter the mantra slightly while moving the lips a little;
one should speak it with some sound—this is known as the whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa).
When, through the intellect, one contemplates syllable after syllable, letter after letter,
and word after word, that practice of reflecting upon the sounds is called mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*).
Whispered recitation is ten times superior to loud recitation;
mental recitation is even more distinguished than that, being a thousandfold superior.
The procedure for the recitation of mantras:
One should cause the deity to enter the mind and make the heart steady;
having brought the lips together in a closed position, one should remain with a steady mind and steady senses.
One should meditate on the syllables with the mind and not move the tongue or lips;
one should not shake the head or neck, nor should one show the teeth.
Following the sequence for extracting the mantra, the practitioner recites the mantra.
Then know that success has been attained; otherwise, success will not occur.

The meaning is: "by the very sequence of extracting the mantra," that is, by the sequence of knowing the vowels and consonants that constitute the mantra. The particle *eva* (only/very) serves for emphasis.
First there is meditation, then the mantra; at the conclusion of the meditation, one should recite the mantra (*manu*).
The practitioner, joined with meditative concentration and mantras, attains accomplishment swiftly.
In the Kulārṇava it is said:
"O Goddess, a hymn recited mentally or even spoken aloud, as well as the mental japa—
both are fruitless, like water poured into a broken vessel."
In the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi): "Whichever deity is prescribed for whichever mantra,
one should perform the recitation (japa) after mentally visualizing oneself in that form."
One should pronounce the phonemes gradually and indistinctly, neither too fast nor too slow,
in their proper sequence according to the order of beginning and end.
One that is too short is a cause of disease; one that is too long causes the loss of wealth.
One should recite [the mantra] joined with the syllables and the non-syllable, like a string of pearls.
In the Kulārṇava: "O Dear One,
being established in that, with one's life-breath absorbed in that, with a mind fixed on that, and having that as one's supreme goal,
one should mutter the mantra while contemplating the meaning of that state."
In the Rudrayāmala: "O Dear One, how can mantras be perfected for one who does not know the meaning of the mantras?
Being like a beast and devoid of [proper] disposition, he does not attain the fruit thereof."
For one who is ignorant of the meaning of the mantra does not enjoy the fruit of recitation.
The meaning of the mantra is the knowledge of the non-difference between the mantra and the deity. Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"O Supreme Goddess, the meaning of the mantra is the contemplation of the form of the deity;
the deity is of the nature of the mantra, and the deity is that which is expressed by the mantra."
The non-difference between the mantra and the deity exists solely through the relationship of the signifier and the signified;
for the deity is understood as residing within the mantra, while the mantra is traditionally held to be the signifier.
And when the signifier is fully realized, the signified itself becomes manifest.
He states another method in the *Bhūtaśuddhi*:
"O Supreme Goddess, listen attentively to the meaning of the mantra.
One should contemplate the Vidyā, resembling pure crystal, in the Ādhāra."
One should visualize [the goddess] as beautiful as the bandhūka flower on the *liṅga*, resembling crystal at the navel,
like emerald in the heart, and green in color at the *viśuddha*.
One should contemplate the Vidyā, which delights the four castes, within the Command;
O Supreme Goddess, the best of practitioners should meditate upon it within the six cakras.
The procedure for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the mantra is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"Having brought the mantra to the presence of the Guru, preceded by devotion to the Guru..."
Having diligently understood the ears, mouth, heart, eyes, and vital breaths of the mantra,
and having recognized the "stake" (kīlaka) of the mantras, one should perform the preparatory rites for the mantras.

It should not be understood that this statement refers exclusively to the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). For it is a prohibition against the mere recitation of mantras when there is an absence of knowledge regarding the ears and other senses. Thus it is said in the *Mantrakośa*:
"He who performs the recitation of mantras while there is an absence of knowledge regarding the ears and other senses..."
He shall indeed encounter poverty, misfortune, and even hell.
Elsewhere also:
"A mantra devoid of the heart and the eyes bestows poverty and affliction.
In another tantra:
Through knowledge of the anus, mouth, eyes, heart, and wisdom, one shall attain liberation;
there shall be immediate accomplishment and mastery of all sciences, for he is Śiva himself in person.
In the *Bhūtaḍāmara*:
"Through the purification of the senses and the mind, I shall describe the face and other features of the mind;
listen, O Goddess, for I shall proclaim the sequence of the body of the Kālī mantra."
O Priyavade, they know the sequence of the body for the Kālī-mantra and others as follows:
the nasal dot (bindu) is the ear, the sound (nāda) is the mouth,
the letter *ka* is the heart, fire (*ra*) is the eye, and the long vowel *ī* is the *kīlaka*.
Know, O Pārvatī, that the syllable *ta* is the heart of the Tāriṇī mantra;
know, O Sovereign of the Gods, that the syllable *ha* is the Śakti-mantra everywhere.
In the *Uttaratantro*:
"The science of breath (*prāṇavidyā*) is the great science; that science bestows liberation. Regarding the specific details of the twenty-two-syllable mantra of Śyāmā, the *Uttaratantro* states:
O Goddess, the syllable *krīṃ* is the head, and the syllable *krīṃ* is the forehead;
the three eyes are formed by the syllable *krīṃ*, and the nose by the syllable *hūṃ*.
The syllable *hūṃ* shall be the lotus-face, and the syllable *hrīṃ* the pair of ears;
by the syllable *hrīṃ* the neck is formed, and the letter *da* becomes the forehead.
By the syllable *kṣi* the tooth is formed; by *ṇe*, the pair of lips;
by *kā*, the two breasts; and the syllable *li* represents the region of the back.
By the syllable *kekāra* the arms are formed; by the syllable *krīṃkāra* the belly is formed;
the syllable *krīṃkāra* shall be the region of the navel, and the syllable *krīṃkāra* the hips.
The syllable *hūṃ* is the form of the womb; by the syllable *hūṃ*, the pair of thighs [is formed].
The syllable *hrīṃ* is the pair of knees; the syllable *hrīṃ* is the region of the ankles.
By the syllable *svā*, the pair of feet [is formed]; likewise, by the syllable *hā*, the nails [are formed].
In the *Yāmala* concerning the *Tārā-vidyā*:
"The aggregate of the Goddess of Speech (*vāgdevī*) is the form; the *praṇava* is the face;
the two dots situated upon the *māyā* and the *avadhu* are declared to be the eyes."
The syllable *ha* and the two long vowels (*ā*) are the ears; the two syllables *phaṭ* are the heart-form;
and the two breasts are formed by the opening of the womb and the belly.
The pair of *repha*s (the letter *r*) constitutes the two feet; the letter *ta* is the eye upon the garland;
and the nature of the four arms is declared to be the pair of *nāda*s.
The *kūrca* is the vital breaths, and the single braid (*ekajaṭā*) is held to be the entire body;
the *kūrca*, O Pārvatī, should be understood as the mouth in other mantras as well.
In other mantras, Ekajaṭā is [present] in those mantras devoid of the *praṇava* (oṃ); by means of the *kūrca* (hūṃ), which is the mouth,
there arise from the respective syllables constituting those various mantras the face, nose, lips, teeth, lower lip, hands, feet, breasts, vulva, and so forth.
The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] after having made the body delimited by the wind-element the object of knowledge.
Regarding the reality of the beloved (kāminītattva),
it is stated in the Kāmadhenu Tantra: "Now I shall further explain another marvelous reality, that of the beloved."
Listen, O Maheśānī, to the reality of the letter *ka*, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Listen to the supreme mystery and great wonder regarding the triangles:
the left line is Brahmā, and Viṣṇu is the right line.
The lower line is Rudra, and the vowel-measure (mātrā) is Sarasvatī herself;
Kuṇḍalinī is shaped like a hook, and the central void is Sadāśiva.
O lady of beautiful countenance, the left line resembles a flame of fire;
the ten lines are well-proportioned and resemble the autumnal moon.
The lower line is Rudra, possessing the luster of a great emerald;
the vowel *mātrā* is the direct manifestation of Sarasvatī, shining with the brilliance of a conch or milk.
That which is the goad and the earring, having the form of ten million streaks of lightning,
resembling ten million moons, and with a void at its center, is Sadāśiva.
O Supreme Goddess, within the voids, Sadāśiva is all-pervasive;
O Queen of the Gods, he who is the Lord consists of the fourfold division of kalās.

Brahmā is the power of will (icchā-śakti), Viṣṇu possesses the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and Rudra is the power of action (kriyā-śakti); he is all, possessing the form of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Sadāśiva is established by the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva;
Kālī, who bestows the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), resides within the voids.
Mardinī is established on his right side in embodied form;
Lakṣmī, the bestower of the four aims of life, is situated on his left side.
And that Sundarī, the Supreme Deity, remained within their wombs;
for this very reason, she who was born from the wombs of the three is indeed Tripurā.
O Pārvatī, because they are of the nature of the Supreme Self, they are established within the womb; and all other manifestations of Kālikā are likewise her various forms.
Abiding there, Brahmā creates; Viṣṇu is intent upon protection;
Rudra is the agent of dissolution; and Īśvara is Sadāśiva.
O Goddess of the gods, the Lord resides within that triangle;
this triangle is said to be the supreme Yoni-maṇḍala.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion, everything is born from the letter *ka*;
from the letter *ka* everything has arisen, including desire and absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
O Goddess, wealth also arises in that same way through the power of dharma;
moreover, the letter 'Ka' is the very root of all the deities.
The letter *ka* is the seat of the Goddess Tripurā, possessing five deities;
from the letter *ka* arises she who grants desires, who takes any form at will, and who is the throbbing, imperishable one.
She is the mother of all the gods, the bestower of the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya);
because she has attained absolute liberation, she is proclaimed as Kāminī.
One should meditate upon the supreme Kāminī, who resembles the hibiscus flower, liquid lac, and vermilion;
she has four arms, three eyes, and is resplendent with creeper-like arms.
Adorned with two breasts shaped like *kadamba* buds,
she was graced by conch-shell earrings, bracelets, armlets, and bangles.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Goddess, adorned with necklaces of jewels and garlands of flowers,
one should recite the syllable *ka* ten times while focusing on this beloved lady.
And having then recited [the mantra] while it is in full bloom, one shall partake in the fruit of the recitation.
Thus, O Goddess, has this wonderful reality of the letter *ka* been explained to you.
Now listen, O beautiful one, to this blossomed seed-syllable of Kālikā:
having taken the seed-syllable of the Earth (la), join it with the left eye (i).
O beloved, when joined with the half-moon (bindu), it becomes fully blossomed;
the letter *la* is the earth itself, the bestower of all jewels.
Her limbs are yellow, her garments are yellow, and she has the form of a yellow streak of lightning;
her face is serene with happiness, and she is adorned with jeweled earrings.
In this way, one should remember the seed-syllable; above that, O Beloved, one should place the supreme Kāminī joined with the letter *ka*, and contemplate it as being in full bloom.
O Maheśānī, she who is Mardinī is Vāmā, O Supreme Goddess;
she has the luster of molten gold and is endowed with ten arms.
The supreme devotee of Viṣṇu should meditate upon the Goddess, who possesses a graceful posture with the three bends (tribhaṅga), adorned with a mass of matted hair,
possessing three eyes and the crescent moon, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
seated upon a lion-throne.
The Goddess who consists of many forms, the letter *ka*, the supreme *Kāminī*,
white-colored and red-colored (or yellow-colored), smiling like a yellow *campaka* flower.
O Pārvatī, she is yellow-colored, black-colored, and possesses various wonderful forms;
she is the cause of the earth's origin and likewise that of the gods.
This seed-syllable is the great secret, the eternal birthplace of Viṣṇu;
above that is the principle of Nāda, the eternal form of the Yoni.
The Supreme Goddess, who has the luster of molten gold, is triangular in form, bears the moon upon her crest,
and is filled with an abundance of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
Above that, one should always contemplate the Bindu, which consists of Śiva and Śakti;
Śiva is directly of the nature of the Void, and the Bindu is the Supreme Kuṇḍalinī.
The void portion, joined with the digit (kalā), and the bindu are the imperishable bestower of liberation;
it has the form of three and a half circles and possesses a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
Having coiled around Śiva in the form of a serpent, she always remains stationed right there;
thus indeed one should meditate with devotion upon her who rests upon the seed-syllable and its power.
From the seed is born Brahmā, the Supreme Lord whose essence is knowledge;
having become composed of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahma), the Lord is both cause and effect.
O lady with tremulous eyes, that beloved woman is the supreme mother of Kṛṣṇa;
for when a sprout has emerged from a seed, the seed itself attains fruitlessness.
O lady of excellent limbs, this seed-syllable is always pervasive and consists of the essence;
joined with the letter *la*, it brings forth the imperishable Hari.
Having herself become Śakti and Hari, she is born; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having become conjoined with the letter *ka*, Śakti manifested herself.
O beautiful lady, all births and actions belong to *prakṛti*;
in recitation, meditation, and worship, *prakṛti* is firmly established.
O Dear One, the vital breath (prāṇa) wind is established in the upper corner of the letter Ka,
and the downward-moving breath (apāna) is always situated in the left corner.
In the southern corner, resembling pure crystal, is Udāna;
in the form of a branch is Vyāna, and likewise in the measure (mātrā).
Thus, O Goddess, this wondrous reality of the letter Ka has been told to you.
O lady of tremulous glances, for one who performs the recitation after knowing the nine principles within the letter *ka*, that recitation is indeed true recitation; of this there is no doubt.
O lady of excellent hips, if one recites this mantra ten million times without knowing its true reality, that recitation is not truly performed; it shall instead result only in constant repetition.
The exposition of the nine principles:
O beautiful one, the principle of the deity, the principle of breath, and the principle of the bindu;
likewise, the principle of knowledge, the principle of power, and the principle of the womb.
O beloved, this system of nine principles (navatattva) has been proclaimed according to the Kāmadhenu tradition;
for in this case, the deity, the vidyā, and the mantra are not obstructed in any way.
O Supreme Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion, O Yoginī, he is neither cursed nor pierced by any beings,
whether mobile or immobile.
The deity Mātṛkā is Māyā, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction;
yet, O fair-faced one, due to being devoid of the single syllable, she incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Beloved, one should meditate upon the Goddess as being under whose control she resides within the heart;
through the sequence of syllables of this meditation, one becomes manifest Brahman—of this there is no doubt.
O lotus-faced one, there is no fault in the syllable, nor in the cursing and so forth;
O beloved goddess, whatever fault has been committed, one should contemplate it as residing within the heart.
O Supreme Goddess, for the protection of the gods and for their own concealment,
men are indeed wretched and small-minded.
O Goddess, for the protection of the human and for the protection of the serpent,
I myself have indeed fashioned these two spells and mantras long ago.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, the asuras have met their destruction;
therefore, O fair-faced one, perform the recitation with every effort.
In the *Yāmala*, the determination of the meaning of the mantra states:
"The body of the deity certainly arises from the seed-syllable (*bīja*)."
In the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi): "O Supreme Goddess, O Pārvatī, know that very form which has been manifested through meditation to be the meaning of the mantra."
Regarding the locus of mantra, the Tantra states:
"Mantras that abide in their proper locus grant boons, and those that abide in meditation bestow fruits;
however, those devoid of the locus of meditation are enemies, even if they are well-perfected."
I shall proclaim the locus of mantra, the locus of mantra; listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance!
It is the Sakala, the Niṣphala, the Sūkṣma, and likewise the Sakalaniṣphala.
Śiva spoke of the sixfold mantra as distinct from the *kalās* and yet afraid of the *kalās*;
know that it is "with parts" (*sakala*) when situated in the *brahmarandhra*, and "without fruit" (*niṣphala*) below that.

The mental [state] is said to be subtle; residing in the heart, it is both with parts (sakala) and partless (niṣkala). Situated in the point (bindu), it is differentiated by its digits (kalā); beyond the digits, it is above that.
Kalā, Kuṇḍalinī, Nāda, Śakti, and that which is declared as Śiva—
these mantras, residing in the six locations, are proclaimed to be established in their respective places.
The meaning is that *dhyāna* (meditation) is precisely the contemplation of the phonemes constituting the mantra, according to the distinction between vowels and consonants.
As stated in the *Bhūtaśuddhi*:
He who recites a mantra devoid of consciousness is a doer of evil;
mantras endowed with consciousness are traditionally held to grant all accomplishments.
The Description of the Consciousness of Mantras and Other Matters:
"O lotus-faced one, listen to the consciousness of all mantras:
it is the thousand-spoked city of Śiva, a charming wish-fulfilling tree."
The four Vedas, with their four branches, are eternally endowed with flowers and fruits;
they are yellow, red, white, black, and likewise green.
O Goddess, having thus meditated upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), which is adorned with many flowers and frequented by bees and cuckoos, and beneath it a jeweled altar;
There above, O Maheśānī, he fashioned a beautiful couch for Hara,
adorned with a golden garland composed of various flowers.
There, having thus meditated upon Mahādeva joined with Mahākuṇḍalinī, O Great Goddess, one should recite the mantra which bestows the three aims of life.
O Goddess of the Gods, tears of joy, horripilation, bodily possession, and faltering speech arise suddenly; of this there is no doubt.
Even when a mantra endowed with consciousness is uttered but once,
the fruit thereof is obtained through a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million recitations.
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme consciousness of mantra has been declared—
whether in the Viṣṇu-mantra, the Śiva-mantra, or the Śakti-mantra, O Sovereign of the Gods. One should diligently cultivate the meaning of the mantra and the consciousness of the mantra.
Regarding the *yonimudrā*, the *Tantramuktāvalī* states:
"The practitioner of mantra, having sat upon a seat facing either east or north..."
O Goddess, one should contemplate the six chakras preceded by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The support (ādhāra) should have four petals, while the self-abiding (svādhiṣṭhāna) has six petals;
at the navel there is a lotus with ten petals, and at the heart, one with twelve petals.
There should be a sixteen-petaled [lotus] at the throat, and likewise a two-petaled one between the eyebrows;
that which is called the thousand-petaled [lotus] is said to be at the Brahma-aperture on the Great Path.

O Goddess of gods, in the foundation, situated in the center of the *kanda*, is a most beautiful triangle; in the middle of that triangle is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), endowed with auspicious characteristics.
Therein is the supreme self-manifested linga (svayambhūliṅga), born from the seed-syllable of desire;
above that, one should again meditate upon the digit of consciousness (citkalā) resting upon the swan (haṃsa).
One should meditate upon the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, who encircles the self-manifested liṅga;
she is the digit of consciousness, coiled, whose form is radiant energy, and who consists of the entire universe.
Having pierced the lotuses beginning with the *ādhāra*, the wise one should lead the Goddess, whose nature is radiant light, to the *brahmarandhra* by means of the *haṃsa* mantra.
O beloved, that goddess enjoyed with Sadāśiva for a mere moment;
O Supreme Goddess, at that very instant, nectar was produced, O Goddess.
O Goddess, the nectar arising from that is like the juice of lac;
with that nectar, O Mistress of the Gods, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity.
There, the wise one should satisfy the deities of the six cakras with a stream of nectar, and then lead it back again to the mūlādhāra by that same path.
Thereafter, O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate the rosary-beads (akṣamālā) as variegated,
with the luster of a lotus fiber, situated within the central channel of Brahmā.
Woven together by her in the center, she is manifest as the very nature of the Awakened One (Jāgrat),
through the differentiation of the syllables of the mantra in both direct and reverse order.
One should form a garland composed of syllables, in which the syllables are interspersed with the mantra and the mantra is interspersed with the syllables, which reveals all mantras.
One should not cause the final letter, which is in the form of Mount Meru, to be transgressed;
having pronounced that letter together with the bindu, the wise practitioner should thereafter recite the mantra.
The sequence beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *la* is known as *anuloma* (direct order).
Then, starting again from the letter *la* up to the end of *śrīkaṇṭha*, one should recite the mantra.
One should recite only the letter *kṣa*, renowned as *viloma*;
the wise person should recite it eight times with each of the eight letters.
The eight groups are: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and śa.
One should mentally recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
O Maheśānī, the Yonimudrā has been revealed out of affection for you.
He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the *yonimudrā*,
will find no accomplishment even through a hundred million recitations.
Thus ends the description of the Yonimudrā and the Mantra-śikhā;
regarding the Mantra-śikhā, it is stated in the Yāmala:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the most excellent of all supreme knowledges,
by the mere understanding of which the Vidyā quickly becomes propitious.
The goddess who resides within the root-tuber (mūlakanda) and has the form of a serpent—
her whirlpool-like circulation is called "prāṇa" by the wise.
Sounding indistinctly and sweetly like bees, ever-arisen,
they go through the aperture of Brahma and enter their own abode.
One should perform the mental recitation (*manotrāya*) there according to the very sequence of going and returning;
by that, the crest of mantras (*mantraśikhā*) is born, which illuminates all mantras.
Just as nothing at all appears in a house filled with darkness,
so too mantras devoid of their crest-syllables (śikhā) never attain accomplishment.
O Supreme Goddess, the instruction regarding the *śikhā* is concealed everywhere;
without it, there can be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of years.
Therefore, O Girijā, you too must guard it with great effort.
Regarding the interruption of impurity (*aśaucabhaṅga*), it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*: "First there is the birth-impurity (*jātasūtaka*), and at the end, the death-impurity (*mṛtasūtaka*)."
A mantra conjoined with two *sūtaka*s (impurities) does not bestow success.

The meaning is that there are two types of *sūtaka* (impurity): the *sūtaka* arising at the beginning of the recitation (*japa*), and the *sūtaka* occurring at the end of the recitation when death has taken place; thus, it is called "two-fold *sūtaka*.
As stated in the *Yāmala*:
O Supreme Goddess, having placed the seed-syllable of Brahmā at the beginning and end of the mantra,
one should recite the mantra seven times for the sake of liberation from the two types of birth-impurity.
The meaning is that for the sake of liberation from the two types of *sūtaka* (impurity), one should place the Brahma-bīja, the *praṇava*, at the beginning and end of the mantra;
then, one should recite that mantra seven times at the commencement of the recitation and seven times at its conclusion.
That mantra which is thus freed from the two types of *sūtaka* bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
O Goddess, the fourteenth vowel is meritorious and bestows accomplishment;
when joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, it is called the long *praṇava*.
For women and Śūdras, there is no breaking of the rules regarding the *praṇava*; that *praṇava* mentioned in the Tantras is also praised for women and Śūdras.
Therefore, that very one is proclaimed for women and Śūdras.
Regarding the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi):
"O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, a Śūdra should constantly recite the Praṇava as taught in the Tantras, ending with the Vahnijāyā (svāhā); there is no need for deliberation on this point."

Therefore, in the context of reciting a mantra encased by the *praṇava*, a woman or a *śūdra* should recite the mantra only after enclosing it with the syllable *oṃ*. Furthermore, the *vahnijāyā* (*svāhā*) mentioned in the Tantras is indeed the *hṛdaya* (*namaḥ*), used in place of *svāhā*.
It should be understood that one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), recitation (japa), and so forth, after having applied the word "namaḥ."
Regarding the method of counting,
the *Yāmala* states concerning the procedure for counting: "For if one performs recitation (*japa*) while transgressing the rules of counting, that recitation [is rendered fruitless]."
Therefore, the Rākṣasas seize them; for this reason, a wise man should always take account of this.
One should not mark the count of recitations with unbroken grains, nor with the joints of the hand, nor with grains of rice, nor with flowers,
nor with sandalwood, nor with clay.
Having mixed lac, kuśīda, vermilion, cow dung, and dried cow manure,
and having formed them into pills, one should perform the prescribed number of recitations.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of Japa, its Characteristics, and so forth," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (parivrājakācārya), the supreme renunciant (paramahaṃsa), the holy Avadhūta. 9.
The Tenth Chapter: An Exposition on the Great Setu (Mahāsetu).
Now, he states the purpose of the Great Setu and the other [practices]:
O Goddess, he who recites [the mantra] without the Mahāsetu incurs sin.
Having first recited the Mahāsetu, then the Setu, and then the Mantra—
in this sequence, O lady of excellent limbs— one should perform the recitation as desired.
In the Setumaṅgalatantra:
"O Supreme Goddess, he who recites the Great Mantra without the Setu shall suffer the loss of all his aims, and after death, he shall go to hell."
Regarding the Great Bridge (Mahāsetu), the *Yāmala* states:
"O Goddess, Mahāsetu is Sundarī and Bhuvaneśvarī."
The seed-syllable of Kālikā is that of Tārā, while the *kūrca* is said to belong to Tārā;
for the others, however, O fair-faced one, the seed-syllable of Vadhū is the Great Bridge (*mahāsetu*).
Regarding the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhūbīja*), the *Rudrayāmala* states: "O Goddess, the first of the vowels [Ā], the fourth of the consonants [Dha], joined with the letter *Ya*,
and combined with the *Lakṣmī-bindu*, is declared to be the seed-syllable of the bride."

The first of the vowels beginning with space (ākāśa) is the letter *sa*; the first of the fourth [group] is the letter *ta*; that which ends in *ya* is the letter *ra*. These three, joined together, form a compound. *Lakṣmī* is the vowel *ī*, along with the nasal dot (*bindu* or *anusvāra*);
joined with these two, it becomes *strīm*. Thus: "strīm."
O Goddess, one should never recite [the mantra] without the Great Bridge (mahāsetu);
even with a hundred million recitations, no accomplishment (siddhi) arises for him.
O Maheśānī, hear the description of the Setu, the mantra of the Setu, and the Kullukā of all;
O Maheśānī, the Setu-vidyā is the manifest embodiment of Brahman itself.
O Goddess of gods, one should recite that [mantra] at the beginning and at the end of the recitation of the mantra;
then, O Goddess, the mantra—and especially the vidyā—will become perfected.
Otherwise, O Goddess, my word would surely be in vain;
having established a boundary on both sides, one should perform the rite of recitation.
Just as water without a dam flows downward in an instant,
even so the mantra of sacrificers leaks away in an instant if it lacks a dam.
"At the beginning and at the end" means that one should recite the *setu-vidyā* before and after the recitation of the *mantra*.
He states the *sāmānya-setu* (the common bridge): [text follows].
The Praṇava is the bridge for Brahmins, and likewise for Kṣatriyas;
the syllable Phaṭ belongs to Vaiśyas, while Māyā is said to be for Śūdras.
Regarding the special bridge (*viśeṣasetu*), the *Yāmala* states:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme bridge of Sundarī."
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should then extract Saubhāgya as well.
Furthermore, O Supreme Goddess, having extracted Māyā again, this supreme three-syllabled Vidyā is declared to be the bridge regarding the subject of Sundarī.
*Sau* is the essential form (*svarūpa*). *Bhāgya* is the *visarga*. The mantra is as follows: *hrīṃ sauḥ hrīṃ*.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme *setu* (protective barrier) of Bhairavī;
having extracted *harapriyā*, followed by *surasā*.
Having joined it with the *audarya* (the letter *ra*), make it joined with half of the *bindu* (the nasal *m*).
O lady of excellent hips, this is the Vidyā of Bhairavī in the form of a bridge. The mantra is as follows: *hsa*.
Having first extracted the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), [place] the *hṛllekhā* (*hrīṃ*) immediately after that.
And this two-syllable vidyā of Tārā is called the bridge. As for the mantra: Oṃ Hrīṃ. For Śyāmā: [the mantra follows].
Having extracted the seed-syllable of sovereignty (*ai*), one should extract the *kūrca* seed-syllable (*hr*).
Again, having extracted sovereignty (*ai*), join it with the half-moon (*bindu*) and the crescent (*ardha*).
O Great Goddess, this is proclaimed as the *setu* (bridge) of Śyāmā. The mantra is as follows: *aiṃ hūṃ aiṃ*.
[The *setu*] of Bhuvaneśī is—
O Goddess, one should first utter the Praṇava, then the two Hṛllekhās;
thereafter, O Supreme Sovereign, one should extract the two Praṇavas.
O Maheśānī, this Vidyā of Bhuvaneśī is called the Setu (Bridge). The mantra is as follows: Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ oṃ.
[The mantra] of Annadā—
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme Annadāsetu.
First, having uttered Māyā (hrīṃ), one should extract Vahnijāyā (svāhā). The mantra is as follows:
hrīṃ svāhā.
Regarding Mahiṣamardinī:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme *setu* (protective mantra) of Mardinī;
having extracted the form of the letter Haṃsa, it is situated above Rañjinī.
Having joined it with the letter *ī*, make it conjoined with the half-moon (*bindu*);
then, O Supreme Goddess, one should extract the wife of Fire (*svāhā*).
This three-syllabled Setu-vidyā of Mardinī is proclaimed as follows:
the mantra is *hrīṃ svāhā*.
Of Viṣṇu—
O Supreme Goddess, having first extracted the Praṇava, one should then diligently join it with the syllable following Vāsava (the letter *i*) and Indirā (the letter *ī*).
Having uttered the syllable whose nature is *ṣṇ*, one should thereafter pronounce the seed-syllable of Bāli; having extracted it, make it joined with *edhitā*.
Again, having extracted the *praṇava*, O lady of pure smiles, it is the bridge of Viṣṇu; the mantra is as follows: *Oṃ viṣṇave oṃ* for Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, and immediately after that the Manmatha [seed-syllable],
and having again extracted the Praṇava, one obtains the beautiful Setu-mantra.
Regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the three-syllabled Setu mantra has been proclaimed. As for the mantra:
Oṃ Klīṃ Oṃ Rāmasya.
Listen, O lotus-petal-eyed one, to the beautiful bridge of Rāma:
