having first extracted the *praṇava* (Om), [place] the royal swan (*rājahaṃsa*) after that.
Having joined it with the *ācārya* (the letter *ya*), make it joined with half a *bindu*.
Again, having extracted the *praṇava* (*om*), this is the Vidyā in the form of a bridge.
This three-syllabled great vidyā is proclaimed as the Setu-vidyā. The mantra is as follows: *oṃ rāṃ oṃ*.
Having first extracted the [seed] of Śiva joined with *haṃsa*, which has the form of the ocean, then—
O Goddess Pārvatī, diligently join it with the half-moon;
this two-syllable Vidyā of Śiva is of the nature of a bridge.
As for the mantra, it is "Haṃsaḥ.
Among other gods and deities, the Praṇava is said to be the bridge;
for all those of the Śūdra caste, the syllable "Oṃ" is said to be the bridge.
Now, regarding the armor-dam (kavacasetu):
O lady of pure smiles, wherever the dam-mantra is prescribed,
O beloved, multiply that mantra threefold and make it the dam-mantra.
O Maheśānī, O beautiful one, there is a protective barrier (setu) for the armor;
O Maheśānī, that man who recites the armor without the barrier—
O Goddess of pure smiles, he is born as food for the Yoginīs,
whether among the Vaiṣṇavas, the Gāṇapatyas, the Śaivas, or the Śāktas, O lady of pure smiles;
having first and last offered the Great Bridge (mahāsetu), one should recite the armor (kavaca).
Now, regarding the purpose of the *kullukā*, it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*: [the purpose of the *kullukā*].
O Goddess, if one recites the great mantra without knowing the *kullukā*,
his four things— longevity, knowledge, fame, and strength (or wealth)— perish.
If a person recites the great mantra without knowing the *kullukā*,
he will meet his death or become insane.
O Dear One, that base person who mutters this Kullukā mantra without knowing it quickly meets his death and suffers the loss of spiritual accomplishment.
Likewise, all [practices] such as recitation will be fruitless; there is no doubt about this.
Therefore, with every effort, one should recite the Kullukā on the crown of the head.
In the Vārāhī Tantra:
"The mantra-practitioner should commence the recitation, beginning with the *kulluka*, according to the prescribed rule;
having completed the worship and the recitation, and having offered praise, he should recite the armor (*kavaca*)."
Regarding the determination of the *kullukā*,
it is stated in the *Viśuddheśvaratantra*:
"O Goddess, out of affection for you, that which is more secret than the secret is being told."
O Goddess, Mahānīlasarasvatī is the *kullukā* of Tārā. As for the mantra: *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ*.
This five-syllabled [mantra] is proclaimed as the *kullukā* of Kālikā.
O Parameśvarī, the mantra for Chinnamastā consists of Kālī, the *kūrca* (hūṃ), Vadhū (strīṃ), Māyā (hrīṃ), and ending with *phaṭ*:
namely, *krīṃ hūṃ strīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ*. O Maheśānī, the eight-syllabled *kullukā* of Chinnā is as follows.
And at the end of *vajravairocanīye*, one should proclaim the armor (*varma*): *mastraḥ*. Thus: *vajravairocanīye hūṃ*.
The seed-syllable of grace for Śambhu is *ma*; for Mañjughoṣa, it is the six-syllabled mantra.
One should likewise remember the word for the forehead (lalāṭa), which is the second vowel (e) joined with the moon (u).
The mantra of Śiva is *hauṃ*; that of Mañjughoṣa is *aravacanadhīṃ*;
and the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī is *hrīṃ*. The eight-syllabled mantra of Viṣṇu is "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya," beginning with the *praṇava*, and this is the *kullukā*.
The seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī is *hrīṃ*. For Viṣṇu, it is *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*.
The armor-seed (*varmabīja*) of Bhairavī is proclaimed as the *kullukā*;
the mantra is as follows: *hūṃ*.
The twelve-syllable *kullukā* of the illustrious Tripurasundarī consists of the *vāgbhava*,
the *kāma-bīja*, and *lajjā*, followed by "Tripure," then the word "Bhagavati," and finally one should extract the two *ṭha*s (svāhā) at the end.
The mantra, however, is: aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ tripure bhagavati svāhā.
Or alternatively:
One should extract the first seed-syllable, Vāgbhava; immediately after that, Kāmarāja; then Lajjābīja and Krodhabīja, ending with Phaṭ. The mantra is: Aiṃ Klīṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ.

Alternatively, the *kullukā* is proclaimed as being called the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*). The mantra is: *ka e ī la hrīṃ*. For Sarasvatī it is the *vāgbhava* (the seed-syllable of speech), and for Annadā it is the *anaṅga* (the seed-syllable of the bodiless one). For Sarasvatī: *aiṃ*.
For Annadā: *klīṃ*.
For Mātaṅgī, the first seed-syllable is *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) directed toward Dhūmāvatī. For Mātaṅgī: *oṃ*; for Dhūmāvatī: *hrīṃ*.

The *vadhūbīja* of Bagalā and the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī are as follows: *strīṃ* for Bagalā and *śrīṃ* for Lakṣmī. The *vadhūbīja* of Dhanadā is proclaimed to be the *kullukā*. The mantra is as follows: *strīṃ*.
O Supreme Goddess, for other goddesses their own mantra has been proclaimed, but for others, the seed-syllable of another and the *kullukā* are prescribed.
For Rāma:
having first extracted the Praṇava (Om), then the "royal swan" (Ha),
and having joined them with the Teacher (Ra), make it joined with half a Bindu (ṃ).
Again, having extracted the *praṇava*, this Vidyā takes the form of a bridge.
O lady of excellent hips, enclose this Vidyā with the *manmathas*;
then, O Goddess of gods, it becomes for Rāma as difficult to attain as heaven.
The five-syllabled great vidyā, concealed in all tantras, is as follows: *klīṃ oṃ vāṃ oṃ klīṃ*. Thus, O Goddess, have I briefly described the *kullukā* to you.
In the *Setumāṅgalatantra*:
"Having first extracted the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable] and immediately thereafter the *manmatha* [seed-syllable],
extract the seed-syllable of Bhṛgu and join it with the human emission (*manusarga*)."
O Maheśvarī, this Kullukā in relation to Sundarī should be understood; the mantra is as follows: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*.
Having first extracted Kāmadhenu, one should then [place] Lokabandhā after that.
O beautiful one, having again extracted the seed-syllable of Vāmanīyaka,
join it with the seed-syllable of Īti, and then append the half-moon (bindu).
This great vidyā of Bhairavī is thus proclaimed; the mantra is "kalarīṃ.
For Tārā, one should extract the seed-syllable of Māyā (hrīṃ), followed by two praṇavas (oṃ oṃ).
Furthermore, having extracted the Māyā, one should perform the recitation of the Kullukā.
By merely reciting the *kulluka* [mantra] one becomes a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). The mantra is as follows: *hrīṃ oṃ oṃ hrīṃ*.
[This is] for Kālikā.
The five-syllabled *kullukā* of Kālikā is proclaimed as follows: O Supreme Goddess, it consists of *Kālī*, *kūrca*, *vadhū*, *māyā*, ending with *phaṭ*. The mantra is thus:
*krīṃ hūṃ strīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ*.
O beautiful one, having extracted the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī that pacifies the *kālakūṭa* poison,
O beautiful one, join it with the seed-syllable of Vāmanī.
Having joined it with the Bindu and the Arddhacandra, O beautiful one, make it threefold.
O Maheśānī, this is the Kullukā-vidyā, worshipped by Viṣṇu. As for the mantra: Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ.
O Parameśānī, place the two Kūrca-bījas at the beginning and the end.
Then, O beloved, the *kullukā* of Mardinī becomes subject to one's will.
The meaning is that one should place the seed-syllable *hūṃ* at the beginning and end of the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā oṃ*. Thus: *hūṃ oṃ hrīṃ svāhā oṃ hūṃ*.
Mantras existing in the state of the bound soul (*paśubhāva*) consist solely of the form of phonemes.
When this is done, O Great Goddess, they attain mastery;
otherwise, O Goddess, one should never recite [the mantra] like a beast.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Setu, Mahāsetu, and Kullukā," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme renunciant (*paramahaṃsa*), and the *avadhūta*. 10.
The Eleventh Chapter:
Purification of the Mouth.
Regarding the purification of the mouth, it is said in the *Sārasvata-tantra*:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme purification of the mouth;
without performing which, O Varārohā, recitation and worship become fruitless.
O Goddess, he who recites with an impure tongue becomes a partaker of sin;
having recited ten times, one should indeed perform the purification of the mouth.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, wielder of the trident, bearer of the Pināka bow,
ocean of compassion, please tell me separately of each of the deities.
It is the purification of all branches of knowledge, as well as of the mouth and the teeth.
Śrī Mahādeva said: Listen to the purification of the mouth of the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī:
the Śrī-bīja, the Praṇava, Lakṣmī, the Tāra, and likewise Śrī and the Praṇava.
One should recite this six-syllabled mantra of Sundarī ten times. The mantra is:
*Śrīṃ Oṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ*. Listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the supreme and blissful purification of Bālā.
The Vāgbhava, the Bhuvaneśī, and the Vāgbhava again, O Goddess worshipped by the gods!
And this three-syllabled vidyā, O beloved, is eternally composed of nectar. The mantra is: *aiṃ hrīṃ aiṃ*.
Listen, O fair-limbed one, to the supreme purification of the mouth of Bhairavī:
the *praṇava* (oṃ), the seed-syllable *hasau*, and the *praṇava* again, O goddess worshipped by the gods.
One should first recite this three-syllable mantra ten times. The mantra is: *oṃ hasauḥ oṃ*.
Listen, O beautiful lady, to the supreme purification of the mouth of Śyāmā.
O Goddess, [place] one's own three seed-syllables, and then three *praṇavas*.
The three *kāmas*, the fire-bindu (*vahnibindu*), and adorned with the moon and its half;
this is the nine-syllabled mantra that effects the purification of the mouth.
The mantra, however, is: *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ*.
Listen, O fair-limbed one, to this unprecedented purification of the mouth belonging to Tārā.
Jīvanī is in the middle, and thereafter is Lajjā Bhuvaneśī.
This three-syllabled Great Vidyā, dripping nectar from the tip of the tongue, is as follows: *hrīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ*.
Listen now, O lady of beautiful limbs, to this unprecedented [mantra] which purifies the mouth of the world.
Having extracted the twelfth vowel and joined it with the *nāda* and *bindu*,
the wise practitioner should recite this triad ten times as Bhuvaneśī.
This three-syllabled mantra, which sports in various pleasures, has been fully described—the mantra being: *aiṃ aiṃ aiṃ*.
O lady of beautiful limbs, hear now the supreme purification of the mouth for Durgā.
Having extracted the twelfth vowel and joined it with the *bindu*, that triad is the mantra: *aiṃ aiṃ aiṃ*.
Now, O Goddess, I shall explain the purification of Bagalāmukhī;
the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbhava*) and the Mistress of the World (*bhuvaneśānī*), which is the seed-syllable of speech, O Goddess worshipped by the gods.
O Dear One, this three-syllabled vidyā is eternally composed of nectar. The mantra is: *aiṃ hrīṃ aiṃ*.
O Goddess, the purifier of Mātaṅgī is the goad and likewise the Vāgbhava;
this seed-syllable, consisting of the goad, should be known as being of the nature of three syllables.
This three-syllabled [mantra] is declared to be difficult to obtain for the purification of the mouth. The mantra is: *kroṃ aiṃ kroṃ*.
Listen to another, O Ṣauḍhe, regarding the purification of the mouth of Lakṣmī.
O Supreme Goddess, O Lotus-faced One, after the seed-mantra of Śrī,
one should again extract the seed-mantra of Śrī and perform the purification of the mouth.
This seven-syllabled lore (vidyā) is eternally composed of the four aims of human life (caturvarga). The mantra is: *Śrīṃ kamalānane Śrīṃ*.
Furthermore, I shall declare another [mantra] for the purification of the mouth of Durgā.
O Dear One, [the mantra] consists of Māyā (Hrīṃ) enclosed by the seed-syllable of Speech (Aiṃ), followed by "Durge Svāhā."
Bhuvaneśī and again the two seed-syllables of Vāc—
this ten-syllable vidyā always resides within my heart.
The mantra, however, is: *aiṃ hrīṃ aiṃ durge svāhā hrīṃ aiṃ aiṃ*.
I shall now declare another [mantra] for the purification of the mouth of Dhanada:
having extracted the Praṇava (oṃ) ending with the letter 'da' (da), it is adorned with the left ear (va).

The seed-syllable of Brahmā, conjoined with the *bindu*, should be known as consisting of three syllables. The mantra is: *oṃ dhūṃ oṃ*. O Maheśānī, this indeed is the purification for Dhūmāvatī. The mantra is: *oṃ dhūṃ oṃ*. For Bhuvanā, the purification is her own seed-syllable or the *praṇava*. The mantra is: [oṃ dhūṃ oṃ].
*Hrīṃ* or *Oṃ*.

O Goddess, the eighth letter from the letters of Rudra (the consonants), joined with *bhū*, *puṣṭi*, and *krūra*, is this one-syllabled mantra (*ekākṣarī-vidyā*) for the purification of the mouth and the granting of food. The mantra is: *klīṃ*.
O auspicious one, O lady of excellent complexion, listen now to the purification of the tongue for the goddess Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī and likewise for Bhadrakālī:
[it consists of] the sixth vowel joined with the nasal drop (bindu), followed by the seed-syllable of Lajjā (hrīṃ).
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, the first [mantra] is for the purification of the mouth of the Cāṇḍālī. The mantra is: *oṃ hrīṃ oṃ*.
It is enriched with the fourteenth vowel and adorned with the bindu and the half-moon.

O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of Śiva is the purifier for Bhadrakālī; the mantra is *hrauṃ*. For other deities, as well as for Viṣṇu and Śiva, and indeed for all other gods, the *praṇava* (oṃ) is the purifier of the mouth.
Or, O Supreme Goddess, having recited the Māyā mantra, one performs the purification of the mouth.
The word "should perform" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. As for the mantra of the other gods and goddesses: *Oṃ* or *hrīṃ*.
O fair-faced one, among all other gods and goddesses, one should perform the purification of the mouth ten times with the *praṇava* alone.
By the mere cleansing of the mouth, the tongue becomes nectar-like;
otherwise, the tongue is always filled with poison.
The tongue is defiled by eating; the tongue is defiled by false speech;
the tongue is afflicted by quarrels; the tongue is defiled by various faults.
How could that foolish world recite the mantra on the tongue?
A fool should never recite it without first performing the purification.
Whether one is a devotee of Śakti, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, or Sūrya;
or a devotee of Śiva, or even a devotee of another—let him perform the purification of the mouth.
If a deity should recite a mantra without having performed the purification of the mouth, [the mantra becomes ineffective].
All of that is in vain for him, O Goddess; the accomplishment of the mantra does not arise.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should diligently perform the purification of the tongue;
otherwise, if one recites the mantra without having performed the purification of the mouth, [the recitation is fruitless].
O Goddess of gods, he who recites that [mantra] undergoes a fall and becomes a partaker of sin;
therefore, O Goddess, one should diligently perform the purification of the tongue for him.
Thus ends the procedure for the purification of the mouth as taught in the Sārasvata Tantra. Then, having interrupted her sleep,
the Goddess said:
O Maheśāna, if at the time of worship the practitioner is overcome by sleep, how can the mantra be accomplished? What should be done then, O Lord?
O Lord, tell me by what rite one should recite [the mantra], or when one should not recite it;
O Lord of Gods, tell me also the characteristics of sleep.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me.
When the vital air has entered the *iḍā* [nāḍī], one should mutter the *śakti-mantra*, my dear.
By the mere recitation [of the mantra] at night alone, Caṇḍikā becomes the bestower of boons.
In the Rudrayāmala:
"O Dear One, when the vital air has entered Piṅgalā, then a person is overcome by sleep;
and when the vital air has entered Iḍā, then a person is overcome by sleep."
Thus, O Goddess, beloved, the characteristics of sleep have been told to you;
if one recites [the mantra] while asleep, what need is there for his recitation or worship?
"O Goddess, O lovely-limbed one, all that is as futile for him as weeping in the wilderness;
by this secret, the Eternal One has abandoned her sleep."
The mantra for breaking sleep:
one should first recite the seed-syllable of Kāmakalā and likewise recite it at the end of one's own mantra.
O Goddess, if one recites the mantra after performing this expiation, [the mantra becomes effective].
What does the southern wind matter to him? What is the use of sleep for one who is afflicted by disease?
Regarding the characteristics of mantra and vidyā, the Viśvasāra states:
"Mantras should be known as having male deities; vidyās are remembered as having female deities."
Mantras for males should end in *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*; those for females are considered to end in *svāhā*; and those for neuters should end in *namaḥ*. Thus, mantras are said to be of three kinds.
Regarding the characteristic of the illuminator (*dīpanī*), the Tantra states: "O Supreme Goddess, having placed the *yoni-mantra* at the beginning and end of the mantra..."
One should recite that seven times; it is proclaimed as the "kindler."
The *yoni-mantra* is the syllable *īṃ*. The meaning is that one should recite the root mantra, enclosed by those two [syllables], seven times. As stated in the Tantra:
"One should contemplate the entire body as being enveloped by the *yoni-mantra*."
Having meditated upon one's own self as Kāmakalā, the recitation of mantras, worship, and other rites should be performed.
Thus it has been said:
"Having meditated upon Kāmakalā within the body, one should perform the recitation of the Vidyā."
Having meditated upon it, one should always contemplate oneself as having the form of Kāmakalā.
In the Tantra: "One should contemplate the face as consisting of the upper bindu, the two breasts as the lower bindu, and the city of desire (Kāmapura) as the half-ha, which is one's own self."
This meditation on the Kāmakalā is great, more secret than the secret;
it must never be spoken to one who is not a disciple, nor ever to one who is not devoted.
O Goddess of the gods, if one were to reveal this anywhere— even among the hair—
it would lead to one's death before long through weapons, poison, and other such means.
Regarding the *yonimantra*,
the *Yāmala* states:
"The fourth vowel (*au*), joined with the *bindu* and adorned with the *nāda*."
The Kāmakalā is the great mantra proclaimed by Mahākāla;
therefore, one should meditate upon one's own self as having the very form of the Goddess.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Determination of the Purification of the Mouth, in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī composed by the wandering mendicant teacher, the Paramahaṃsa Tīrtha Avadhūta, the venerable Brahmanandagiri. 11.
The Twelfth Chapter:
The Characteristics of Puraścaraṇa.
Regarding the characteristics of *puraścaraṇa*, the *Haṃsamāheśvara* states:
Recitation, fire-oblation, libation, sprinkling, and feeding of Brahmins—
this fivefold worship is recognized in the world as *puraścaraṇa*.
In the *Yāmala*: "The worship of the five limbs, distinguished as Śākta and Vaiṣṇava in this world,
has been called *puraścaraṇa* by Śiva, the Supreme Self."
Regarding the purpose of *puraścaraṇa*, it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"Just as a living being deprived of life is incapable of performing any action,"
Even a mantra that is devoid of preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) is proclaimed to be effective in that way;
therefore, a wise person should either perform it himself or have a guru perform it.
In the Rudrayāmala: "A mantra that has been perfected through *puraścaraṇa* indeed bestows its fruit;
therefore, one who knows the mantra and desires success should perform the *puraskriyā*."
Of what use are fire-offerings, of what use are recitations, and of what use are the elaborate ritual placements of mantras,
if there is no preliminary service (*puraskriyā*) for the secret mantras?
For the preliminary service of mantras is said to be their primary life-force (*jīva*).
The preliminary rites for the day preceding the *puraścaraṇa*:
having performed the purification of the body, one should eat only sacrificial food (*haviṣya*);
then, having bathed in the morning, one should recite the *Sāvitrī* five thousand times.
Being pure, one should first recite the mantra one thousand and eight times, or three thousand times,
for the sake of destroying both known and unknown sins;
thereafter, one should satisfy the Brahmins with food, clothing, and seats.

In that regard, first the acquisition of the site (bhūmiparigraha) must be performed. As it is stated in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā: "At the outset, for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of this aforementioned mantra, I take possession of this ground so that my mantra may be perfected."
One should take possession of the ground according to its dimensions in every respect:
a site measuring one *krośa* in a village, or measured by one's own desire in the case of rivers and similar locations.

One should resort to ground extending one *krośa*, or even two *krośas*, from the city for the purpose of procuring food and other necessities; by resorting to such a location as a "lamp-stand," the performed ritual action yields its fruit.
The place where a man shines with a lamp is called a "lamp-place.
Having divided the ground into a square, one should draw a set of nine squares.
One should write the seven groups [of consonants] in order starting from the eastern cell;
the practitioner of mantra should write [the vowels] in the northeast—now listen to the sequence for the placement of the vowels.
Furthermore, the wise man should divide the central square into nine parts;
he should then write the vowels in the central and eastern squares and so forth, in pairs, following their sequential order.
One should know that its mouth is located where the first letters of the villages and so forth are situated in the eastern and other compartments, while its two hands are situated on both sides.
The two sides of the belly, the two feet, and the remainder are said to be the tail.
One who holds it in the mouth attains success; one who holds it in the hand has but a short life.
If [the planet] is situated in the belly, one remains indifferent; if it stands in the feet, one encounters suffering;
and if it stands in the tail, the practitioner is afflicted by imprisonment, eradication, and other such calamities.
This is declared to be the Kūrma-cakra, which bestows success upon practitioners;
having constructed it according to the rules, one should perform recitation there on an auspicious day.
One should commence the *puraścaraṇa* during the bright fortnight when the moon and stars are favorable and on an auspicious day; however, one should not perform it while Hari is asleep.

"When Hari is asleep" means during the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana). Therefore, that which was stated as forbidden regarding the southern transit applies specifically to the worship of Viṣṇu. For one who possesses the requisite capacity, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should be performed even during the southern transit. Thus it is said in the Yāmala:
In the autumn season, the great annual worship is performed;
during that fortnight, one should especially perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite.
Elsewhere also:
"Especially during the autumn season, having worshipped with devotion from the fourth to the ninth [day], one should recite eight thousand [times] at night."
Alone in a secluded place, one should perform the recitation in a dark chamber.

"Aṣṭasahasrakam" means that one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times every day. "In a dwelling of darkness" (timirālaye) means in a house like darkness, not one endowed with light; however, some say "in a dwelling of darkness" means at night. That is incorrect, because [the text] says "eight thousand at night," implying [the recitation] prior to night.
"Because it has already been established"—this is the general direction [of the argument].
Now, regarding the duties on the day of *puraścaraṇa*:
having honored one's own guru with many garments and ornaments,
one should thereafter commence the recitation (*japa*) following his permission.
O Great Goddess, having bathed in the morning and taken the ritual stakes (kīla),
the practitioner should approach the vicinity of the hut and perform the rites prescribed in the Tantra.
One should drive stakes made from milky trees, consecrated with weapon-mantras,
into the ten directions, and one should worship the Weapon-deity within them.
When the field is thus pinned, the mantra is not overcome by obstacles.
[The trees used are] the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Vaṭa, and milky-juiced trees.
Having worshipped the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) according to the prescribed rule;
having offered the oblation to the lords of the directions, one should then take refuge in the field.
The mantra for Kṣetrapāla is stated in the Tantra:
"The final letter of the alphabet (kṣa), joined with the nasal bindu (ṃ), followed by 'to Kṣetrapāla' and the heart-mantra (namaḥ);
preceded by the Tāra (oṃ), this eight-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as that of Kṣetrapāla."
The mantra is: *oṃ kṣauṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels.
[He is] like a mountain of blue collyrium, with tawny hair on his head, round and fierce eyes, and [attributes] held in hand.
I bow down to the god Kṣetreśa, who holds a mace and a skull-cup, who is clothed in space, adorned with serpents, and possesses fierce fangs.

Having meditated thus, one should invoke Kṣetrapāla and worship him upon the eight-petaled lotus. Then [one should worship] Analākṣa, Agnikeśa, Karāla, followed by Ghaṇṭākha, Mahākrodha, Kopa, and Piśitāśana.
One should worship Piṅgalākṣa with upright hair on the eastern petals;
one should then worship the world-protectors and their weapons in the same order as before.
Then one should offer an oblation of black-gram rice.
He states the mantra in the *Śāradā*:
"First, 'ehi' twice; then, 'vidviṣi' (or 'dviṣi') followed by two 'su's;
then 'bhañjaya' twice; and after that, 'tarjaya' twice."

Then, O beautiful one, [recite] the pair of obstacle-removing feet, followed by "Mahābhairava," and twice "Accept the offering of the Kṣetrapāla. This is declared to be the mantra for the offering, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
With palms joined in reverence: Oṃ! To you, Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra Mahākāla, who resemble the fire at the end of an aeon, to Bhairava, salutations; you should deign to grant me permission.

Having thus obtained permission and worshipped the guardians of the directions, Indra and the others, one should offer an oblation of rice mixed with black gram (*māṣa-bhakta*). As stated in the *Śāradā*: "Having approached the vicinity of the hut and having performed the general offering (*sāmānyārgha*)."
Having performed the worship of the door, one should then purify the place of recitation.
Beholding is performed with the root mantra, and sprinkling is considered to be done with the arrow mantra.
Regarding the *puraścaraṇa-saṃkalpa* in the *Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā*: "The syllable Om, *tat sat*, 'today' (*adya*), and also the month, fortnight, and lunar day..."
Having uttered the root [mantra] followed by that, I, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name...
One who desires success in this mantra should then perform a recitation of such-and-such a number;
then an oblation (havana) equal to one-tenth of that, and then a libation (tarpaṇa) equal to one-tenth of the oblations.
One-tenth of that is the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and one-tenth of that is the feeding of Brahmins;
thus shall I perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), facing either east or north.
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma);
then, having performed the assignment of the seers and other factors (ṛṣyādika), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as prescribed in the Kalpa.
Then, having performed the worship and other rites according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the recitation (japa) gradually,
neither indistinctly, nor too fast, nor too slow.
One should pronounce the syllables in sequence according to their initial and final order;
one should cause the deity to abide in the mind and make the heart steady.
Beginning at the time of dawn, one should recite until midday.
In the Kulārṇava:
"One should recite daily the same number with which the practice was commenced;
one must never make it less or more until the month is completed."
Actions that are deficient or excessive never bear fruit;
indeed, only those actions performed according to the prescribed rules yield results.
Bathing at the three sessions of the day is prescribed; however, if one is unable, it may be done twice or even once.
One who is practicing the mantra should worship the deity at the three junctions of the day.
One should not recite the mantra alone at two times or even once;
rather, one should worship the deity daily with ritual offerings according to one's ability.
One whose mind is not distracted by hunger, yawning, hiccups, and the like, attains the accomplishment of the mantra; therefore, one should be devoted to diligent effort.

If, by chance, yawning or similar occurrences happen, then one should perform *ācamana*, followed by *prāṇāyāma* and the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), and then recite the remainder of the mantra. Alternatively, one may recite after looking at the sun. And so it is said:
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"Upon seeing or speaking with outcastes who have fallen [from their caste],
upon sneezing, the passing of downward wind, or yawning, one should abandon the recitation."
Likewise, having sipped water (ācamana) upon reaching that place, and having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with its six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga),
one should properly recite the remainder [of the mantra], or else perform the visualization of the Sun and other deities.
The connection with the subsequent phrase is "having performed [these], one should recite. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), gods, Brahmins, and so forth are included.
One should sleep on a bed of *darbha* grass spread upon the ground after laying down one's own garment;
that garment must be washed daily, otherwise it brings obstacles and one may fall [from grace].
One should not sleep during the day, nor should one touch dogs and similar animals.
The best of practitioners should not indulge in women, meat, or honey;
for one who indulges in these, the preparatory rites do not succeed.
The rule regarding food and so forth is stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "Whether eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), vegetables, barley, milk, roots, fruits, or whatever else may be available there."
Or one who subsists on alms, or performs the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances,
[should consume] mango, Āmalaka, and the fruit produced from the Keśarin tree.
The fruit of the plantain, the tamarind, the lotus, and the orange—these fruits may be eaten; one should avoid all others.
An example of prescribed vegetables is as follows: peas, black pot-herbs, vāstuka, and hilamocikā.
The characteristics of *haviṣya* food are as follows:
winter rice, unboiled white rice, grains, mung beans, sesame seeds, and barley.
Kalāyaka, guṇīvāra, vāstuka, and hilamocikā.
Cane, black pot-herb, radish, and *kemuketa* grass; rock salt, sea salt, and the curd and clarified butter produced from cow's milk.
Milk from which the cream has not been removed, jackfruit, mango, harītakī,
long pepper, cumin, orange, and tamarind;
Sages declare that plantains, lavalī fruits, and emblic myrobalans, along with honey and molasses, when not fried in oil, constitute *haviṣyānna* (food fit for sacrificial offerings).
O Sage, one should avoid the roots of the *kemuka* and *kendu* trees as prescribed;
likewise, one should consume ghee, curd, or fruit, such as the coconut, as is appropriate.
The practitioner should likewise eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) and barley-based flour;
he should eat in such a way that there is no increase in the activity of the senses.
If, during the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) of generous householders or of twice-born ones who subsist on alms,
there should occur an impurity due to death (mṛtasūtaka), [the following applies].

Nevertheless, having made a firm resolve, one should never abandon the recitation; O fair-faced one, having performed the recitation according to the sequence prescribed in one's own ritual manual, one should not desist.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that [number], and the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that;
and with a tenth part of the libation, one should sprinkle the Goddess who is identical with the universe.

One should provide a meal for Brahmins with a tenth part of the initiation fee (abhiṣeka), and having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, one should feed many who are poor, blind, and miserable.
One should devoutly feed one's kinsmen, Brahmins, and others as desired;
having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), one shall accomplish one's own goal.

Regarding the rules for the fire sacrifice (*homa*) and other rites, it is stated in the *Gautamīya*: "At the end of the daily recitation (*japa*), the practitioner of mantra should perform a fire sacrifice with a tenth part of that amount;
O Sage, he should likewise perform libations (*tarpaṇa*) and ritual ablutions (*abhiṣeka*) with a tenth part of those respective amounts."
One should feed Brahmins every day to pacify any deficiency or excess;
or, when everything is complete, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites.
Alternatively, having fashioned a yantra on a gold leaf or similar material,
one should thereafter worship the Goddess there, together with her retinue.
The Ritual of Libation: One should satisfy that supreme Goddess; the procedure for this is stated here.
Having first satisfied the gurus, one should then satisfy the Root Goddess.
Having uttered the name at the end of the root mantra, and then [the word] "tarpayāmi" (I satiate),
the practitioner of mantra should perform the libation with "svāhā" at the end, according to the prescribed rule and in the proper sequence.
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "And one should perform the libation while uttering [the names] in the accusative case;
offering one handful of water for each, one should satisfy the multitude of rays."
Regarding the substances for libation (*tarpaṇa*), the *Viśuddheśvara* states:
"Libation is performed with water from the moon, and likewise with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."
Or one should satisfy [the deity] with honey according to the procedure taught by the guru.
In another tantra: "The best of practitioners should perform [the rite] everywhere with water from a sacred ford, milk, clarified butter, honey, or scented water."
By means of the liquid of black aloe-wood alone, one may bring the world and all else under control;
by means of water mixed with sandalwood, a person obtains good fortune.
With water mixed with saffron, one may paralyze the entire world;
with water mixed with white [pigment], one becomes equal to Bṛhaspati.
By means of water scented with camphor, a person may attract wine and food;
by means of water mixed with yellow pigment (rocanā), one is liberated from all obstacles.
Having meditated upon the Goddess within her mouth, one should perform the libation;
for it is declared in all the scriptures that this libation bestows auspiciousness.

Having performed this libation (tarpaṇa), the wise one, being absorbed in that [deity], should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with a tenth part of that [number]; then, regarding himself as the deity, he should worship [himself] while becoming one with that [divine essence].
Having fully uttered the root-vidyā, followed by the name of the deity ending with the word "am," and at the end of that [name],
one should perform the consecration with the words "I consecrate" (abhiṣiñcāmi) ending in "namaḥ."
Having thus meditated upon his own mantra at the crown of his head,
the practitioner should thereafter perform his own consecration according to his own count.
There, one should visualize the Goddess together with her limbs and the deities of her retinue;
one should then sprinkle water according to the respective number, sprinkling each of the attendants once.
Having thus completed the consecration, the best of practitioners should feed the Brahmins with the thought that they are deities, according to a tenth part of the number of consecrations.
In the *Yāmala*: "O Goddess, one should feed Brahmins as well as young maidens;
otherwise, the practitioner falls into the state of a bound beast (*paśu*) for failing to feed the maiden."
Then, one should feed the Brahmins accompanied by the mantras, regarding them with the thought that they are deities;
thereafter, one should worship the Guru with devotion using various kinds of offerings.
One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru according to the extent of one's wealth;
and having given it, the best of practitioners should perform a great worship (*mahāpūjā*).
The mantra-practitioner shall then become one whose mantra is perfected; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
In the Tantra:
"He who, despite possessing wealth, does not perform [the rites] according to the detailed prescriptions out of delusion, does not obtain this fruit; he is called a traitor to the deity."
The procedure for recitation when a limb [of the mantra] is missing is stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"If a limb should be missing, the recitation must be twice that number."
It should be performed with devotion by one who is unable [to do so fully], for the sake of accomplishing the practice along with its ancillaries.
In the Rudrayāmala:
"For Brahmins who are unable to perform the rite of fire-offering (homa), the recitation (japa) is said to be double;
for the other castes, it is declared to be threefold and so forth."
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"If one is unable to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*), the wise practitioner should perform recitation (*japa*) twice the number of oblations;
for women of the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, this specific count is prescribed."
Whatever caste a Śūdra may rely upon when performing an initiation as he desires,
the number [of years] belonging to his wife is the same as that of his own.
O Dear One, whatever the number for a Śūdra, that of his wife is double.
Elsewhere also:
"Whatever caste a Śūdra relies upon, he should follow its prescribed rule;
for a Śūdra who relies on no [caste], the number of directions is declared."

For a Śūdra who serves a Brāhmaṇa, the recitation (japa) is equal to that [of his master]; for the wife of such a [Śūdra], it is the same. For a Brāhmaṇa who performs no fire-sacrifices (homa), whatever his japa may be, that is the amount for his wife. For all other castes, however, it is three times and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "beginning with three-fold": the number of oblations (*homa*) is three times the number of recitations (*japa*) to be performed by a Kṣatriya;

it should be understood that for a Vaiśya it is fourfold, and for a Śūdra it is fivefold. In cases where there is capacity, it should be known that for a Śūdra it is twofold. This applies to the four castes among the Vaiṣṇavas.

It should be understood as having four, six, and eighteen qualities; otherwise, there would arise a contradiction, such as [the qualities] being double and so forth in one place and fourfold and so forth in another.
Thus it has been stated in the Gautamīya:

"In the absence of fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa) must be performed; it is prescribed as four times the number of the homas for Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, six times for Vaiśyas, and eight times for these women. Thus it is said.
In the *Yāmala*: "If one is unable to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*), or the worship (*pūjā*), or even the libation (*tarpaṇa*),
all success (*sarvasiddhi*) arises simply through a recitation (*japa*) of that same number."

In the *Yāmala*: "If, in any instance, there should be a deficiency in the ten-fold ritual of the limbs (*aṅgakarman*), one must perform those very same ten; one should not cause [the rite] to be performed with fewer than ten."
In the *Yāmala*:
"The wise man, always pure and subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
thereafter, O Dear One, he should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with sacrificial food using one-tenth of that number."
O Pārvatī, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) using a tenth part of that [mantra-repetition],
and then one should consecrate oneself with waters using a tenth part of the libation.
One should devoutly feed twice-born brahmins with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) amounting to one-tenth of that [number];
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to the extent of one's wealth.
This is declared to be the Pāśava ritual procedure; hear now the Vīramata thereafter.
Regarding the *vīrakalpa*,
it is stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"One who is capable of consuming fish and meat may perform the ritual service of the mantra."
At night, facing east on his bed, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with devotion.
Then, the excellent practitioner should offer oblations of sacrificial food into the fire ten times that amount,
and satisfy [the deities] ten times that amount with substances mixed with meat.
One should sprinkle the one who embodies the universe with a tenth part of the *tarpaṇa* offering;
O Goddess, one should feed a tenth part [of that number] to the practitioner, who is dear to the deity.
One should cause honey, meat, fish, and chewed food to be offered;
then, O Dear One, one should satisfy the Guru with devotion by means of gold and other gifts.
By these two kalpas, O Goddess, the mantra is certainly accomplished.
In this context, the term "one hundred thousand" (*lakṣa*) refers to the specific number prescribed for each respective *kalpa*. Thus it is stated in the *Kumārītantra*:
"At that time, the best of practitioners should perform the recitation (*japa*) as prescribed in his own *kalpa*.
"At that time" means at the time of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*). As for what is stated in the *Kumārītantra*:
One who knows the mantra should recite it one hundred thousand times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and remaining pure during the day;
at night, with his mouth full of betel, he should recite it another hundred thousand times while lying on his bed.
Having thus recited two hundred thousand times, the knower of the mantra should perform the ten-fold subsidiary rites (daśāṃśa).

Based on this statement, some say that for a specialized *puraścaraṇa*, there should be two hundred thousand recitations (*japa*). However, that is not pleasing to the mind. For on the day one is to eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), if one were to eat fish and other such items, it would result in the violation of the sacrificial food and the occurrence of improper conduct. Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*:

"One should not practice various modes of conduct, because one should not delight in various modes of conduct"—from this statement [it follows that] the intent of the Tantric statement regarding the maiden (*kumārī*) lies in the two types of *puraścaraṇa*. These two procedures are to be performed alternately by the *divya* and the *vīra*. However, by the *divya*...

It is even possible to perform these two kalpas simultaneously; for since he is a knower of reality (tattvajñānin) while possessing mental activity, there is no contradiction between his mental activity and external activity.
The Vīra, however, being one who does not know reality, possesses both external and internal activity.

For him, there is no simultaneity of these two kalpas, because his mind is haughty and because it would lead to a confusion of conduct; thus everything is clear. And so it is said in the Tantra: "The divine [initiate] is generally like a god, while the hero is one whose mind is haughty."
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"Completely free from all violence, devoted to the welfare of all living beings,
and devoid of desire, anger, greed, delusion, attachment, and hatred."
Indeed, only he who is satisfied even with a limited measure of worship is a qualified practitioner;
he alone shall be qualified in this scripture, while any other is a fallen seeker.

The "beast" (paśu), however, possesses doubtful knowledge yet performs ritual actions. He must not accept fish, meat, or similar items; he should not even mentally recall a woman; he should not consume betel leaf, but rather eat sacrificial food (haviṣyānna); and he should not approach a woman except during her fertile period.
Worship should be performed by way of the right-hand path (*dakṣiṇamārga*). Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"O Goddess, he who worships Mahāmāyā without [observing] propriety (*dākṣiṇya*) is a sinner; fallen from all worlds, he does not otherwise [attain liberation]."
By this, whatever procedure is prescribed for the day should also be understood to apply to the domain of the divine hero (divyavīra).
Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"During the day by the right path, and likewise at night by the left."
"And if it is your very opinion that the attainment of the fruit should be swift," according to these words.
Now, in the sixteenth chapter of the *Śrībījārṇavatantra*, concerning the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for planetary influence, these are the words of Śiva addressed to the Goddess:
"Once, the Supreme Sovereign Maheśvarī was at Kāmākhyā."
Having observed an eclipse, he asks Maheśvara what must be done;
for, O God, one does not attain success by any other method than this prescribed rite.
Śrī Śiva said:
O beloved, where is the bath? Where is the twilight rite (saṃdhyā)? Where is breath control (prāṇāyāma)?
O auspicious one, where is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi)? O fair-faced one, where is the worship (pūjā)?
O Goddess, O lover of desire, having abandoned everything out of fear of the passing of time,
one should perform the recitation after forming a mental resolve, O fair-faced one.
O Goddess, by means of the five-limbed rite one attains success, and not otherwise;
whether it be a mantra, a vidyā, O Maheśānī, a kavaca, or even a hymn of praise.
O Supreme Goddess, O lotus-eyed one, whether it be meditation or ritual placement (nyāsa),
by a single utterance, O Mistress of the Gods, ten million [merits] are attained.
O Goddess, that recitation is said to be incalculable during the eclipses of the moon and sun;
how then, O Supreme Lady, is a specific number for the recitation prescribed?
Therefore, O Maheśānī, O lady of pure smiles, there is no fire-oblation (homa), nor, O Queen of the Gods, is there consecration (abhiṣeka) or the like, such as libations (tarpaṇa).
O Maheśānī, O lotus-faced one, there is indeed no food;
O Goddess, O beloved, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, the five limbs [of ritual] do not exist.
Even if one is devoid of the five limbs, one becomes accomplished; it is not otherwise.
Know, O Goddess of Gods, that *saṅkalpa* is whatever mental resolve has arisen.
One should understand that intention to be present during the eclipses of the moon and sun;
therefore, O lady of tremulous glances, one should certainly not form such an intention.
O Goddess, mental resolve (saṅkalpa) bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, it is remembered as "mental" (mānasa).

For a gross conceptualization, O Supreme Goddess, is said to be useless. O Goddess, whatever a wise person performs without conceptualization, O Mistress of the Gods, all that is indeed useless; it is not truly mental.
Regarding the time for eating during an eclipse, O auspicious lady, if a lunar eclipse occurs in the first watch of the day,
one who eats on that very day shall quickly go to hell.
And at midnight, O Great Goddess, whenever an eclipse occurs,
one should eat and drink during that very day and become filled with bliss.
During a lunar eclipse, one should perform the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) and other rites.
And when, O auspicious lady, a solar eclipse occurs during the day,
one may perform the sacrifice of recitation and so forth after having eaten and drunk at night.
"O Maheśānī, among all the Viṣṇu-mantras, as well as those of Śiva, Gaṇapati, and likewise the Śākta-mantra, one should constantly recite that which is praised;
thus it was proclaimed by Śiva himself in the Bījārṇava Tantra."
All of this must be performed by those who possess knowledge; however, regarding what must also be performed by ignorant ones— the bound souls (paśus)—
it is stated in the Gandharvatantra:
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
at the time of an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, one should first remain pure and have fasted.
Standing in a river flowing toward the ocean with water reaching up to his navel, he should,
with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra from the moment of the eclipse's onset until its release.
In the Sanatkumāra Tantra:
"Having seen [the deity] and bathed with a firm resolve, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) until liberation;
and one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the rules, consisting of a tenth part of the recitation."
For the purpose of the fire oblation, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind, either twice as many times as the oblation;
then, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of the number of oblations.
One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with a tenth part of the libation (tarpaṇa);
one should provide a meal for Brahmins with a tenth part of the consecration.
At the conclusion of that, the best of practitioners should perform a great worship;
he should give a sacrificial fee to the guru and satisfy the Brahmins with devotion.
Regarding the specific details of the Śyāmā-vidyā, the Kālītantra states:
"Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired by another method:
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, from the moment of total immersion until liberation [from the eclipse]."
Having recited the mantra for as many times as the count [prescribed], one should perform the fire oblation (homa) and other rites for that same number of times.

If the river is defiled by crocodiles and the like, or if it does not flow toward the ocean, then what should be done? Regarding this, the Rudrayāmala states: "Alternatively, having bathed in pure water, being composed in a clean place..."
One should recite the mantra with undistracted mind from the time of initiation until liberation;
by doing so, one will undoubtedly partake in the fruit of the recitation.

As for those who say that on the day preceding the lunar eclipse one may eat sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), fruit, or milk due to an inability to fast— that is not pleasing, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence and because fasting is mandatory.
As for those who say that recitation is the primary requirement—
here, one who does not perform the śrāddha sinks like a cow in the mud.
Thus, because of hearing such disparaging statements, it is the *śrāddha* that is essential, not the *japa*; therefore,
he spoke accordingly in the *Sanatkumāra-tantra*:
If a person should abandon his recitation out of regard for ancestral rites and the like,
he becomes an offender against the deity and leads seven generations of his ancestors to the netherworld.
In the Mahiṣamardinī Tantra:
"By reciting [the mantra] during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a person shall attain liberation;
however, by failing to perform the recitation of the mantra, one shall quickly go to hell."
In the *Guptadīkṣātantra*:
"He who does not properly perform the recitation (*japa*) during an eclipse of the moon or sun is fallen,
he is most sinful, and he will suddenly become a pig."
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, by my word there is no doubt that his food and water become equal to urine, blood, and feces.
Elsewhere also:
"O Goddess, he who engages in other thoughts without the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) shall remain submerged in the Raurava hell until the dissolution of all beings."
Having returned again from Raurava, he is born in sinful wombs;
O fair-limbed one, for him too there is never any atonement whatsoever.
Therefore, having renounced everything, one should perform recitation (*japa*) during a lunar eclipse.
O Goddess, O Beloved, as is the solar eclipse, so too is the lunar eclipse;
having abandoned all else, O Great Sovereign, one should perform the sacrifice of recitation.
From such various scriptural statements in the Tantras, since one hears the censure of other activities [if performed] without *japa*,
*japa* alone is mandatory. Regarding the fault in counting by means of heaps (*rāśi*) and so forth,
the *Yāmala* states:

O lady with tremulous glances, if one should perform the calculation of the lunar mansions and so forth out of ignorance, delusion, or negligence, and if, having reflected, one does not behold the eclipse,
the merit accumulated in previous births perishes at that very moment.
In the *Kāmadhenu-tantra*:
"The lunar festival (*candraparva*) and the solar festival (*sūryaparva*) are never to be questioned.
If a base man should behold the solar festival, O lady of beautiful hips..."
Let it be that the subsequent dharma exists; nevertheless, the preceding dharma perishes.
In the *Yāmala*:
"When the Moon is situated in the seventh, eighth, twelfth, or tenth house from birth, Rāhu, if aspected [by it], bestows misfortune; this occurs unless there is recitation and worship."
The *puraścaraṇa* for the armor (*kavaca*) in the *Bhairavatantra*: Now, O Maheśānī, [I shall describe] the preliminary rite (*puraskriyā*) for the armors in the context of subjugation (*vaśya*).
Having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
The ritual acts for the limbs, such as the fire-oblation (homa) and others, are performed individually according to a tenth part [of the total].
Thereafter, having perfected his armor, that meritorious soul becomes like the god of love.
If one is personally incapable, the rite should be performed through a representative. As stated in the *Jñānapradīpa*:
"One should perform the *puraścaryā* with a Guru or someone like him."

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Determination of Puraścaraṇa," in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī composed by the wandering ascetic teacher, the Paramahaṃsa-tīrtha Avadhūta, the venerable Brahmānandagiri.
The Thirteenth Chapter: The Consecration of the Yantra. Without a yantra, the deity does not become pleased by worship.
The worship of all the gods within the yantra is highly praised.
Gold, silver, and copper are considered superior, middling, and inferior respectively;
copper is said to yield a hundred thousandfold merit, while silver yields ten millionfold.
Gold, however, yields infinite fruit, and crystal likewise may be so;
[the weight] may be one tola, two tolas, three tolas, or five tolas.

Having ascertained the mantra of the practitioner, the practitioner should prepare [the substance] in measures of one *rasa* (sixteen *māṣas*), four *tolas*, seven *tolas*, or one *pala*, having placed it upon the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*).
Alternatively, having fashioned an image representing the form of one's own deity, one should worship it; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In the *Sammohanatantra*:
"Uttering the root mantra correctly, one should draw the supreme yantra.
In the *Tantra* [it is said]:
In the center of that, one should draw the yantra with gold or with *kuśa* grass.
[The mantra is: "O Lord of Life! O Lord of the World! You who are worshipped by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, according to the *Ūrdhvāmnāya-tantra*!"
Now, tell me the ritual for the consecration of the Wheel-King.
The venerable Īśvara said:
One should perform the consecration of the yantra in the same manner as that of the mantra;
for an unconsecrated yantra and mantra bestow disease, grief, and fear.
The tenfold consecration of mantras has been explained in all the tantras;
now listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess, to the consecration of the yantra by means of honey.
Regarding the ritual preparation of the yantra:
having fashioned the King of Wheels (cakrarāja), one should then perform the consecratory rites (saṃskāra).
O Goddess, there are two kinds of installation (pratiṣṭhā): the middling and the supreme.

Having bathed, the practitioner, with devotion and according to the word of the guru, should make a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), beginning with the Praṇava, followed by "Tatsat," and then specifying the month, fortnight, and lunar day.
For the pleasure of [Name], of such-and-such lineage, and of [Name] Devī, [I have performed] the installation of the vital breaths,
the life-force, and the senses of [Name] Devī within this [image].
At the conclusion of the words for the consecration rite, facing the northeast, he should say, "I shall perform [it].
Then he should choose a preceptor (guru), honoring him with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa), beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
and one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated by their respective mantras and the Śiva-mantra.
The mantra-practitioner should cast the wheel into it and gaze upon it with the *praṇava*.
Then, having lifted the wheel out, he should place it in the vessel for the wheel.
O Goddess of the gods, one should bathe the Supreme Goddess with water from a conch, as well as with water containing flowers,
and also with water mixed with sandalwood paste.
One should bathe the Supreme Goddess with coconut water, as well as with water containing all medicinal herbs, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Hot water and cold water are to be avoided; one should bathe with slightly warm water.
If it is excessively hot, there may be a stroke (vajrapāta); therefore, one should avoid that.
In the *Pañcāmṛtamāhayāmala*: "Clarified butter, curd, as well as milk, sugar, and honey combined—
this is known as the *pañcāmṛta* (five nectars), with one *pala* of each."
Regarding the measurement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the Tantra states: "One *pala* of milk is the portion, and the cow urine is likewise desired."
There should be one pala of ghee and two tolas of cow dung.
The curd should be the measure of one handful; this is remembered as the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya).
Alternatively, it is prescribed that each of the five components of the pañcagavya should be in equal parts.
One should avoid curd for bathing after six nights have passed;
clarified butter after a year has elapsed; honey at the end of six months;
and molasses, sugar, and all types of rice after one year.
The connection with the preceding [verse] is "one should avoid"; the meaning is that one should not give these.
Wherever there may be an image of the gods that is capable of being anointed with ghee,
twenty-seven palas should be offered there with faith.
One hundred and eight *pala*s should always be given for a bath;
however, for a great bath (*mahāsnāna*), the number is two thousand *pala*s.
A *pala* is known by worldly measures to be two *māṣakas* and eight *rattis*; it should be understood as three *tolakas* according to the tradition accepted by experts in astrology.

O Supreme Goddess, for daily bathing, one *pala* each of the five products of the cow is prescribed; for those who are unable, half of that amount is the rule for the *kṛcchra* penances in the rite of subjugation.
One should not give [the image] lacking the prescribed weight of gold during the ritual bath;
having completed the bath, one should place that Goddess upon a golden pedestal.
Therefore, having extracted [the breath] from there, the wise one should place it above the navel;
having worshipped the seat (pīṭha) right there, he should perform the rites for the arghya-vessel and so forth.
Having touched the yantra with the tip of a kuśa blade, he should consecrate it with the Gāyatrī mantra.
He recites the Gāyatrī:
"We know the Praṇava as the King of Yantras;
we meditate upon the Great Yantra; may that Yantra inspire us."
Having invoked [the deity], one should perform the installation of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana) by means of the five mudrās.
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The foremost of practitioners should join the two hands with palms facing upward, the pair of thumbs touching the root joints of the ring fingers."
One should lower the hands with palms joined upward; this is the *āvāhanī* (invocation) mudrā. This same mudrā, when reversed, is used for the rite of *sthāpana* (establishment).
The mudrā with the fists formed and the thumbs raised is the Sannidhāpanī;
that same mudrā, with the thumbs tucked inside, is the Sannirodhinī.
The *sammukhīkaraṇī* [mudrā] is considered to consist of two hands with palms turned upward and joined together.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the body of the deity is known as *sakalīkṛti*.
O beloved, having joined the two hands together as if they were below,
one should perform that which is called the *paramīkaraṇa* mudrā; thereafter, one should consecrate [the offering] with nectar using the seed-syllable *vaṃ* and the mudrā known as the *dhenu*.
When the little fingers and ring fingers are joined facing each other,
and likewise the index and middle fingers, it is proclaimed as the Dhenu-mudrā.
The Dhenu-mudrā is the Great Goddess; it serves for the consecration into nectar.
One should establish and worship the Goddess [with this]; otherwise, it shall be fruitless.
"Having installed" means having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the ritual installation of the vital breath) either in a yantra or in an image. Regarding the *prāṇamantra*, the *Yāmala* states:
"Then, having uttered the Goddess Bhuvaneśānī, [one should utter her] encased by the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*)."
The first [syllable] consists of seven, death (one), and eight (eight); then space (zero) conjoined with truth (one) and the moon (one).

The sky (vyoma) conjoined with the point (bindu), followed by the letter 'sa' (sarga), 'va', and 'bhṛgu'—this is the name of the Goddess; from that come the vital breaths (prāṇa) here, and from those, O beloved, [the syllables] "prāṇāḥ."
Again, having placed the mantra foremost in that same manner, the best of practitioners [should do so] by means of the name of the deity; then the life-force (jīva) remains here.
In the same way, O Goddess of the gods! having uttered all the sense organs—ending with speech, mind, and sight—one should then add the words "ear" and "nose."
Then, having caused the vital breaths (prāṇas) to come here and having spoken of happiness, one should recite for a long time;
"May they remain," ending with the word for fire's wife (svāhā)—this is declared to be the prāṇa-mantra.
"O Great Goddess, this mantra, consisting of each deity's own name, belongs to all deities.
Having thus established the vital breaths (prāṇas), one should then commence the worship.
Having displayed the mudrās according to the procedure prescribed in his own ritual manual,
the practitioner should worship the Goddess in due order with the sixteen types of offerings.
O Supreme Goddess, by the command of the Goddess, one should worship the retinue;
then, O Beloved, one should perform a thousand recitations, or one hundred and eight.
Then, having performed the offering of the bali, the excellent practitioner should prostrate to the Cakrarāja and perform one hundred and eight oblations.
O Goddess of the gods, one should perform oblations with one's own mantra for the sake of accomplishing the cakra;
at the conclusion of each oblation, one should cast the remnants of the offering into the sovereign cakra.
Having offered full oblations at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should consecrate it with those waters;
that wheel, thus consecrated by mantra, bestows accomplishment upon all.
One should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor and present a milch cow;
one should also give land that provides a livelihood, which shall follow after one's sons and grandsons.
After this, the dismissal of the Goddess should be performed with the *saṃhāramudrā*;
if one would consecrate the King of Mandalas by means of this rite.
The fruit of his *puraścaryā* shall be the attainment of all *siddhis*; and by the authority of the Guru’s command, he should place the *yantra* upon his head.
This very yantra must be kept secret and never revealed to anyone;
for if the yantra or the mantra is disclosed, Pārvatī becomes enraged.
One should not show [the mantra] even to one's guru if it has not been consecrated with its own specific mantra;
and if there should be the thundering of clouds at the time of receiving the yantra.
If, all of a sudden, there is the sound of a tumult or the blast of a conch shell,
then the practitioner of mantra has undoubtedly and instantly achieved his purpose.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and sun,
the initiation of yantras and mantras is proclaimed to be auspicious.
Now, regarding the offering of the sacrificial victim (*balidāna*),
it is stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"The human, the goat, the ram, the buffalo, and likewise the hare..."
The Śallakī, the Śūkara, and the Balaya are thus proclaimed.
The human sacrifice (narabali), however, pertains only to kings— O Supreme Goddess, a king alone may offer the human sacrifice,
and no other; by offering lions, tigers, or humans, a Brāhmaṇa would go to the Raurava hell.
One should offer a most beautiful sacrificial victim (bali) who is young, free from disease, very handsome, endowed with auspicious marks, and possessed of all perfect limbs.
Having bathed the young, beautiful, dark-complexioned [deity], who is free from defects such as wounds and the like,
one should adorn him there with offerings and flowers and sandalwood paste.
One should especially adorn [the deity] with red garlands and vermilion;
then, facing north, one should likewise offer the oblation facing east.
Having brought [the offering] to his left, he should perform the sprinkling with the root mantra;
having performed the thorough sprinkling, he should then worship the bali offering.
One should contemplate Brahmā at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the Earth on his nose,
Ākāśa on his two ears, and Sarvatomukha on his tongue.
One should worship the luminaries in the eyes and Viṣṇu in the face;
one should worship the Moon on the forehead and Śakra on the right cheek.
Likewise, one should place Vahni on the left cheek, Samavartana on the neck,
Dhṛti in the pores of the skin, and Pracetas between the eyebrows.
Having worshipped Śvasana at the base of the nose, Maheśvara on the shoulder,
and the lord of serpent-kings in the heart, one should recite this.
O illustrious one, grant me that which is accomplished by men through great austerities, knowledge, and sacrifices; may I swiftly attain prosperity.
Having worshipped with the thought that it is Śiva, one should thereafter release [the offering];
then, having intended the Goddess and one's own desire.
Having thus offered the oblation, one should thereafter worship the sword;
the practitioner of mantras should likewise worship Brahmā and Vāgīśvarī at the tip of the sword.
And in the center, O Goddess, the practitioner of mantra should worship Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
and at the base, he should worship Maheśvara together with Umā.
Having worshipped him with such rites, one should diligently offer salutation:
"O Sword, you are the form of Śiva, known by the name Krodhabhairava."
She is eternally the one who pleases Durgā, like another form of the power of Kālī;
she is intent on the task of Śakti for the sake of the sword and the sharpening stone.
"O Lord of the Sword! You must swiftly sever the sacrificial animal; salutations be unto you!
Having thus worshipped that sword, the excellent practitioner raises it aloft.
Having become one who cuts [the victim] while facing east, and [visualizing] the sacrificial offering (bali) as facing north,
he should then cut the animal with the mantra "Āṃ Huṃ Phaṭ."
Then, having carefully infused the blood of the sacrificial animals with water, rock salt, excellent fruits, honey, fragrant flowers, and perfumes;
Having sprinkled it with perfumes and flowers, one should cast it away while reciting the root mantra:
first the *praṇava*, then the *vāgbhava*, then *lakṣmī*, and thereafter the word *kauśikī*.
Thereafter, one should recite the mantra for nourishment with blood.
O Goddess! Having offered the blood to Śivā, one should present a lamp.
Then the practitioner of mantras should offer most enchanting betel-leaf.
Regarding the procedure for establishing the Blood-Headed [deity],
the Tantra states:
"One should properly join the blood from the head of a human being onto the left side of the Goddess."
One should offer a goat to the left, present a buffalo to the front, or offer a goat to the right; one should place the blood from one's own body in front.
In the *Yāmala*: "When the sound of teeth grinding is heard anywhere, one should know that death is at hand; one should predict loss in that case.
When tears are seen in the eyes, one should predict loss."
Regarding the result of the falling of the victim's head:
if the head falls in the north-eastern direction, one should know it brings all prosperity; for kings, it indicates the attainment of a kingdom.
If the head falls in the space between Īśāna and Agni,
then all accomplishments will certainly be attained in a very short time.
If its head should ever fall toward the northwest, the southwest, or even the south, one should predict misfortune for him.
Regarding the offering of lamps upon the head of the sacrificial cake (*bali*), the *Yāmala* states:
"Especially for the planets, tortoises, and lizards..."
One should not cause a lamp to be given for fish or birds at night.
For as long as the lamp burning upon the head continues to burn, for that long one shall dwell in heaven; therefore, one should cause it to be given with great effort.
In the Rudrayāmala:
"Having smelled the fragrance arising from the burning of hair, the Goddess becomes pleased;
therefore, one should offer a lamp, but one should avoid its vessel."
By offering oblations according to the prescribed rule, the fruit of the four aims of human life shall be attained.
Regarding the fault in unrighteous violence,
the *Kulārṇava* states that there is a fault in violence performed contrary to the injunctions:
"O Dear One, he who, for his own sake, kills living beings without following the prescribed rule [incurs sin]."
He shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many yugas as there are hairs on the body of a beast.
He who causes the drop of blood to fall is born in the womb of an animal;
the eight types of killers are: the one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who slays, the buyer, the seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it.
In the Rudrayāmala:
"The purchaser by means of wealth, the eater through consumption, and the slayer through the act of killing—
he who commits the killing is certainly threefold."
In the *Yāmala*: "In sacrifices to the ancestors and the gods, ritual killing (*vaidha-hiṃsā*) is prescribed.
Also elsewhere:
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; there is no happiness higher than non-violence. That violence which occurs according to the prescribed rule is proclaimed as non-violence.
One should not commit violence against living beings, and especially not violence against animals;
O Goddess, one should avoid all forms of violence everywhere, except for the offering of a sacrificial oblation.
In the *Yāmala*: "O Śivā, having consecrated the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) with this mantra, one should slay it;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), otherwise one shall go to hell."
For violence that produces evil—how can it be a means to attain heaven?
How could one commit the slaughter of a horse in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha?
He provides an illustration in the *Yāmala*:
"By that very same piece of poison by which all living beings die,
by that very same piece of poison a physician destroys the poison."
Therefore, the distilled meaning is that violence not sanctioned by scriptural injunction produces sin, whereas violence enjoined by scriptural injunction produces heaven.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Consecration of Yantras and Other Rites," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme renunciant (*paramahaṃsa*), the holy Avadhūta. 13.
The Fourteenth Chapter: The Procedure for Ritual Services.
O Pārvatī, listen with respect as I shall explain the ritual service (upacāra).
That worship which is performed without ritual services does not become pleasing.
O Dear One, the eighteen services (upacāras) are the most excellent for all;
the sixteen are considered primary, followed by those remembered as tenfold,
and subsequently those declared to be fivefold— these should be performed by one desiring prosperity.
In the Phetkāriṇītantra:
"The seat, welcome, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya),
water for sipping (ācamana), as well as bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, and ornaments in their entirety."
The practitioner of mantra should perform the worship with the eighteen services: perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, as well as food, a mirror, garlands, ointments, prostration, and dismissal.
In the Tantra: a seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, further sipping, a bath, garments, and ornaments.
One should likewise employ perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings; thus, one should perform the sixteen modes of service in the ritual worship.

The water for washing the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka) followed by another sipping, and the services beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya)— these are recorded as the ten ritual services (upacāra).
O Supreme Goddess! One should offer these five articles of worship: perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings.
The description of the water for the feet and other offerings:
Water intended for the feet is *pādya*; it should be combined with sandalwood and agallochum.
This is declared to consist of *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā*.
The water for washing the feet (pādya) should be offered in a vessel, and the respectful offering (arghya) in the arghya-vessel,
consisting of red bilva fruits, unbroken rice grains, flowers, curd, dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and water.
This arghya is prescribed as common to all the gods;
in the absence of curd, milk, and so forth, one should mentally imagine it.
One should place a three-leaved dūrvā grass that is hollow inside into the arghya water;
one should then offer the ācamanīya with jāti, lavaṅga, and kakkola.
One should cause that water—
which is fragrant and free from foam— to be offered using either a vessel made of gold or a conch shell.
That which is for the goddess is called *ācamanīyaka*;
one should offer the *ācamanīya* with auspicious, fragrant waters.
The description of the *madhuparka* offering is given in the *Bṛhat-Śrīkrama*: "One should employ coconut water in small quantity, along with sugar, curd, and ghee in equal measures;
honey should be added in greater quantity than all of these in the *madhuparka*."
The wise know that *madhuparka* consists of clarified butter mixed with curd and honey;
one should offer it especially in a beautiful vessel made of bell-metal.

According to this statement, there is no fault in offering coconut water during the *madhuparka* ceremony using a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), just as there is no fault in cooking the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) in a copper vessel. Thus it has been said:

Then, once the fire has been consecrated, one should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) with cow’s milk in a new vessel made of copper or another material, which has been cleansed with the Astra-mantra.
"Furthermore, milk from which the cream has not been removed does not become defiled when placed in a copper vessel," according to this statement.
Regarding the measurement of the vessel, he says: "A wise man should not have a vessel made that is less than eight finger-breadths in size."
Among all fragrant substances, that which originates from Malaya is preeminent for all types of perfumes;
therefore, one should always offer sandalwood with every possible effort.
O Pārvatī, the practitioner should apply pure fragrance with the tips of the middle and ring fingers pressed by the tip of the thumb, while reciting the root mantra.
The Chapter on Flowers:
O fair-faced one! Among all varieties of flowers, the red is recommended;
O wise one! it is pleasing to the Goddess and bestows the fruit of all desires.
O Queen of the Gods! likewise, a red flower made of gold and the like, a red lotus, a vajra, and the black Aparājitā.
The beautiful karavīra flower consists of five deities:
Viṣṇu, Lambodara (Gaṇeśa), Sūrya, Brahmā, and likewise Kālikā.
The five deities always reside within the five petals; it is never otherwise, O Maheśānī! [They are present] in the Javā flower, O Karavīra, and O Aparājitā.
By offering [this] to Mahādevī, one obtains the fruit of ten million worships.
Brahmā dwells in the midst of these; Janārdana dwells at their base;
Rudra dwells in front of them; and all the gods are situated upon the petals.
This refers to the flowers of the *karavīra*, *aparājitā*, and *javā*.
When the tree has blossomed at the [appropriate] time, the determination of the deities and directions is as follows:
Viṣṇu is on the western petal, and Gaṇanāyaka is in the north.
In the northeast is the god Sūrya, and in the east Brahmā is proclaimed;
in the south is the goddess Kālikā, who bestows liberation.
O Goddess, as is the karavīra flower, so indeed is the javā flower;
as it is white, so too is it red, green, and even black.
All the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others, reside within the cavity of a single drop;
in their midst is the Śiva-liṅga, conjoined with Mahākuṇḍalinī.
The abyss is the form of the Bindu, the supreme state of absolute liberation;
it is the flower consisting of Śiva and Śakti, which bestows the fruit of the four aims of human existence.
Even hundreds of millions of crores of all other flowers together are not equal to the *javā*, the lotus, and the *pārijātaka* when gathered in one place.
Where the Aparājita flower, the Karavīra, and the Javā also abide,
there indeed dwell the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
All holy fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others, truly reside at its root;
by watering its root, one has thereby worshipped the deities.
The greatness of Aparājitā cannot be fully described by me;
[it is equal to] the Mallikā, the lovely Utpala, the Śamī, and the Punnāga and Campaka.
