The aśoka, the karṇikāra, and likewise the droṇapuṣpa;
the karavīra, the javā flower, saffron, and the nāgakeśara.
He who offers [this] to Durgā shall go to the supreme state;
Brahmā dwells in the root of the flower, and Janārdana in its center.
Rudra dwells at the tip of the flower, and all the gods reside upon the petals;
all things moving and unmoving are said to be perpetually dependent upon the flower.
Since the flower consists of all the gods, one should therefore offer it to the Goddess.
With flowers grown in the forest, with leaves produced on the mountains—
fresh, without holes, sprinkled with water, and free from impurities.
Or one may worship Śivā with flowers grown from plants cultivated for one's own enjoyment;
however, if one brings flowers from trees planted by others and worships without having informed them,
that person’s worship is fruitless.
This, however, refers directly to one's own master, according to the statement:
"Theft of flowers for the sake of the gods, Manu declared to be no theft."
Regarding flowers and other offerings, there is a time limit for what has become stale;
all stale items—leaves, flowers, fruits, and water—should be avoided.
However, the water of the Ganges and the leaf of the Tulasī plant are not to be avoided.
The bilva leaf is not to be rejected, nor likewise the water-born lotus;
O Goddess, one should not worship with flowers that have been stale, even if they are made of gold.
The bilva leaf, the māghya, the leaves of the tamāla and āmalakī,
the kahlāra, the tulasī leaf, the lotus, and the munipuṣpa flower.
This [milk] would not become stale, nor would any other substance of a similar nature;
likewise, the lotus and the āmalaka fruit remain pure for three days.
O one whose wealth is austerity, for a single day, karavīra flowers are suitable,
as are white and red lotuses, kumudas, and utpalas.
For these, one should exercise caution after five days have passed;
for other flowers, as long as there is no change in their fragrance.
O Goddess of the gods! having smelled flowers, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and other ritual offerings, and having presented them [to the deity], a man shall fall into hell.
The wise should discard food that has been touched by a limb [of an impure person], smelled, stale,
defiled by hair or insects, or that which is decayed and stale.
One should discard flowers that have fallen on their own as well as those that are damaged;
however, a *śephālī* or a *bakula* flower does not become defiled even if it has withered on its own.

Everything fallen on the ground should be abandoned, with the exception of *śephālī* and *bakula*; likewise, those things eaten by worms, those that are broken, and anything fallen upon the earth must be avoided.
The Tamāla and the lotus are not defiled even when cut or broken;
nor are the Viṣṇukrāntā, Javā, Nāgakeśara, and Nāgavallabha.
The bandhūka and the mandāraka (kahlāra), along with their stalks, are praised for worship;
however, a flower that has blossomed on its own or one that has fallen to the ground should be discarded.
"Nāgavallabha" means *nāgacampaka*; "self-blossomed" means blossomed by a person.
O Goddess of Devas! In the month of Māgha, there are twelve flowers to be worshipped:
the kunda, the kuruvaka, the jhiṇṭī, the ketakī, and likewise the nicula.
One should never worship Nīla, Vikaṭaśīrṣa, Bhṛṅgarāja, Kṣudraka, Bakula, or Raṅgana on any other lunar day.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with unhusked grains, nor Vināyaka with Tulasī;
one should not worship Durgā with Dūrvā grass, nor the Sun with Bilva leaves.
As for what was stated—that *dūrvā* grass is prohibited—that refers specifically to white *dūrvā*. Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"Red *māṣa*, white *dūrvā*, blue-throated [saffron], and *kuruṣṭaka*..."
And one should not give [it] to Mahādevī if one desires one's own welfare.
In the absence of flowers, one should worship with leaves; in the absence of leaves, however, with their fruits;
or else with unbroken grains or even with water—one should never neglect the worship.
For Śiva, one should avoid the *kunda* and the *unmatta*; likewise for Hari, the *arka* and *mandāra*; for the Goddesses, the *arka* and *mandāra*; and for the Sun, the *tagara*.

"Of the goddesses" means of the primary and other goddesses; this is because the excellence of worship with *arka* flowers for the primary goddess is stated, and because of the hymn beginning with "A thousand *arkas*" which mentions camphor and so forth. *Tagara* means *kāṣṭhatagara*.
In the *Yāmala* concerning the worship of Śiva: "One who desires his own welfare should not offer the *bakula*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *kunda*, *śephālikā*, or *javā* to Mahādeva."
Mālatī, mallikā, jātī, yūthikā, and likewise mādhavī; tagara, karṇikāra, droṇa, utpala, and campaka.
The aśoka, the kumuda, the śephālikā and the kadambaka,
the ketakī, the vanamālā, as well as the kusumbha and the kiṃśuka.
Kahlāra, bakula, lavaṅga, and nāgakeśara—these too are dear [to her]; one should not worship Śivā with leaves.
And with hibiscus flowers, fragrant substances, dūrvā grass, and leaves of the bilva tree—
indeed, there is never any worship of the Goddess without dūrvā grass.
Therefore, durvā grass should be taken, for it consists of all flowers;
for the gods, one should offer that which is rich in all fragrances, or in its absence, a leaf of tulasī.
One should worship the gods with *tulasī*; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O beloved, without *tulasī*, bathing and other rites, as well as ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) and sacrifices, are not pleasing [to the deities].
They declare that everything is fruitless; this is determined to be the case everywhere.
Therefore, practitioners should accept either dūrvā grass or tulasī.
If Sundarī, Bhairavī, Kālī, Brahmā, Vighneśvara,
and Vivasvat are worshipped while devoid of Tulasī, that worship shall become fruitless.
Regarding the worship of Śakti with Tulasī leaves,
the *Yāmala* states concerning the subject of Śakti:
"One should worship Sāvitrī, Bhavānī, Durgā-devī, and Sarasvatī..."
He who worships with Tulasī leaves prospers in all his desires.
In the *Yāmala*: "During the worship performed at night, one should always avoid *tulasī*;
by the mere scent of *tulasī*, Caṇḍikā becomes enraged."
Tulasī is the embodiment of Brahman, auspicious and composed of all the gods;
yet, though she consists of all the gods, she is not dear to Gaṇeśa.
Indeed, [this is] unfavorable for both the goddess Lakṣmī and likewise for the goddess Tārā;
by joining the thumb and forefinger, one should cast the flower on the right.
Neither a flower, nor a leaf, nor a fruit should be offered with its face turned downwards.
That which causes suffering has been thus described; one should offer it exactly as it arose.
O Goddess! Without a handful of flowers, one should offer it exactly as it arose.
Regarding the time for gathering flowers and so forth, the *Yāmala* states:
"Those twice-born who, having performed their ablutions, gather flowers..."
Neither the deities nor the ancestors accept that.

This, however, pertains specifically to the midday bath. According to the traditional authorities (*sampradāyikāḥ*), the gathering of flowers and other materials should be performed after the morning bath. As stated in the *Tantra*:
"Having bathed at the time of midday, the wise man should not pluck a flower."
One who worships the Goddess with those flowers is cooked in hell.
The term "the Goddess" is illustrative; one should not worship other deities either. Having performed the morning bath and other such rites, one should gather flowers.
By worshipping the Goddess with those flowers, one is instantly liberated from sins.
The mention of "the Goddess" is an elliptical expression meaning that one should also worship other deities.
One should not pluck flowers with the left hand for the sake of the deity,
nor should one offer them to them with the left hand, or having placed them there from the left hand.
Regarding the section on incense:
this incense composed of agallochum, ushira, guggulu, sugar, honey,
and sandalwood is proclaimed as the general offering for all the gods.
Of all incenses, guggulu is dear to Durgā;
when combined with ghee, it especially and constantly increases her delight.
Having sprinkled the incense vessel with the Astra-mantra and worshipped it with the Hṛdaya-mantra,
one should burn guggulu while sounding the bell that has been consecrated with the Astra-mantra.
Having worshipped the incense burner while touching it with the left index finger, one should then utter:
"O Mother, victory! Sound! To me! Svāhā!"
Having worshipped and rung the bell, the preceptor should then fumigate [the object] with those incenses,
using his middle and ring fingers upon the middle joint.
O Goddess of gods! Holding the incense with the tip of the thumb, one should offer it;
lifting the incense up to the crown of the head while sounding the bell.
The preceptor should burn incense mixed with clarified butter before the deity;
he should not offer the incense upon the ground, nor through the nose, nor likewise into a water-pot.
Having taken that which is located below in whatever manner, one should present it;
however, one should not fumigate here with these incenses gathered into a heap.
Having acted in such a way, like [pouring] fire into chaff, one would not obtain that fruit.
Regarding the section on lamps:
one should not give lamp-oil, ghee, and so forth by mixing them together.
Having given mixed oil, one shall go to the Tamisra hell.
Having prepared wicks filled with camphor and using either clarified butter or sesame oil,
one should raise and display lamps that are fragrant and held high.
"Highly" means up to the head of the deity.
Having performed the raising [of the lamp] three times through the application of the Gāyatrī and the Mūla-mantra,
one should then perform the *nīrājana* rite ten times with lamps.
A lamp should be offered to a worthy recipient, but never upon the ground;
for that man who offers a lamp while causing distress to the earth [is guilty].
He will undoubtedly reach the terrible Tāmisra hell;
for the earth, though all-enduring, cannot bear these two things.
One should likewise avoid placing a foot on something that should not be stepped upon and similarly avoid heating a lamp;
therefore, one should perform [the rite] in such a way that one does not indeed incur the heat of the earth.
One must never extinguish a lamp prepared for the sake of the deity;
the stealer of the lamp shall become blind, and the one who extinguishes it shall become one-eyed. Such a person should not even engage in worldly transactions with the best of practitioners.
The Section on Food Offerings (Naivedya).

Regarding the food offering, he says: One should repeatedly offer to the Goddess as food offerings that which is baked in an oven, cooked in oil, or milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee—whatever is pleasing to the mind.
"Kandupakvam" means that well-cooked rice, flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), and so forth should be offered. Whatever object is desired, one should give it during the worship of the deity;
having presented the *naivedya* (food offering) dear to Bala, one should worship the Goddess.
One should not offer anything unpleasant to oneself as an oblation during the worship of the deity;
rather, one should also present whatever is pleasing to women.
By the offering of betel-leaf, the Goddess becomes well-pleased.
The procedure for circumambulation is as follows:
with the hand holding a conch, one should perform the circumambulation once or twice at every point;
then, having completed the encircling, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff.
Likewise, one should properly perform the circumambulation of the deity in three ways:
once for Caṇḍī, seven times for the Sun, and three times for Vināyaka.
One should perform four circumambulations of Keśava and half a circumambulation of Śiva;
having gone from the south to the northwest, and from there to the north.
Going further south from there, one should perform the salutation in the shape of a triangle.
This triangular salutation increases the pleasure of Tripurā.
The form of the goddess Tārā is described as having the shape of a woman’s triangle;
she displays her right hand and is right-minded even in her thoughts.

And that circumambulation should be known as one that pleases the entire host of gods. But the man who, having passed behind the deity, bows while breaking the [prescribed] path— for that evil-minded person there is no fruit in this world nor in the next.
The procedure for salutation consists of mental, vocal, and physical bowing; thus,
homage is threefold, and the physical is considered the most excellent.
The gods are always pleased by physical prostrations;
having gone to the ground on one's knees, one should touch the earth with the head.
That which is performed as the supreme physical salutation is traditionally defined as being made with the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, and the eyes.
Prostration with both speech and mind is declared to be eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga),
consisting of the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, and the head.
This five-limbed salutation is prescribed as the rule for all occasions;
it is performed by joining the palms together and placing them upon the head.
Even he who does not touch the earth with his head and knees is considered the lowest;
indeed, physical [worship] is said to be threefold, distinguished by the eight limbs and so forth.
The eight-limbed [prostration] is declared the best; the five-limbed is remembered as middling;
one should avoid the inferior salutation performed with only the hands and head.
This very act of prostration, known by the name "daṇḍavat" (like a staff), should be understood as a "praṇāma" (obeisance); it was first taught by the Pratimā [Tīrthaṅkara].
That salutation which is performed by one endowed with devotion, composed personally in both prose and verse,
is considered the highest form of vocal worship.
The salutation performed with either Puranic or Vedic mantras is always considered the middle form of salutation, which is verbal in nature.
O Pārvatī, that salutation which is always performed by means of human speech is to be known as the lowest form of verbal salutation.
Now, the section on ritual services:
one should perform the services mentioned in the Tantras, beginning with the seat.
One should offer a seat and flowers, and utter words of welcome and inquiry after one's well-being.
On the left side of the deity, one should offer a seat with the root mantra;
it may be made of flowers, wood, cloth, leather, silk, or metal.
The sixfold seat is said to bring delight to the deity;
the preceptor should offer water for the feet with the word "namas" at the end [of the mantra] applied to the feet, and [offer] the foot-water with the head-mantra.
Then one should offer the *arghya* upon the head; with the word "svadhā," one offers water for sipping (*ācamana*) into the mouth;
and the water for sipping, with "svadhā," three times into the lotus-like face.
One should offer the madhuparka into the lotus of the mouth with the mantra ending in *svadhā*;
one should offer the bath and the fragrance with the *hṛdaya* mantra, and the flowers with *vauṣaṭ*.
O Supreme Goddess! One should offer water for bathing upon all the limbs;
having performed the sprinkling with *tāya*, one should present a silk garment (*dukūla*).
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) after the bath, the clothing, and the food offering;
one should also give all ornaments, whatever may be beautiful.
One who has realized the truth should apply [unguents] to the limbs of the image and so forth as appropriate;
one should apply sandalwood paste to the entire body and place flowers upon the head.
One should offer incense and lamps ending with the word "namaḥ" in the order from right to left,
and present suitable food offerings, such as meals and the like, in front [of the deity].
One should offer the food oblation (*naivedya*) consisting of nectar and say "namas. Then,
saying "I offer this food oblation prepared with these materials," one should present everything, O Maheśvarī, while reciting "tato nivedayāmi" (then I offer).
The necessity of providing coverings for the food offerings and other items is stated in the Gāndharva [Tantra]:
"Whatever food offerings and the like there may be, as well as whatever perfumes, flowers, and so forth..."
One should provide clothing for everyone until one has invoked the Supreme Goddess.
Since the *rākṣasas* accept that which is without a covering,
the procedure for the offering of food (*naivedya*) at the conclusion of the rite for the Goddess is now described:
that which is unrefined must not be given, for it is not accepted by the deities.
Regarding the procedure for offering the food oblation (*naivedya*), the *Yāmala* describes the consecration as follows:
"Having brought [the food] before the Goddess and sprinkled it with the water of the *arghya* offering..."
Having sprinkled [the water] with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā).
Above that, the wise practitioner should recite the root mantra eight times;
having formed the wheel-mudrā, he should contemplate it as being well-protected.
One should dry up the affliction with the *raṃ* mantra, burn it away with the *raṃ* mantra,
contemplate it as nectar with the *vaṃ* mantra, and flood it with the *ṭhaṃ* mantra.
One should perform this consecration in this manner for all edible substances;
one should offer water with the mantra: "Thou art the spreading of nectar, svāhā."
One should offer this water to [Name] Devī with the mantra: "Oṃ, you are the spreading of the nectar, svāhā.
Having given the water for *āpośāna*, one should present it to Mahādevī, saying:
"May this food, along with its accompaniments, be *svadhā* for Mahādevī."
The Guru should offer oblations into the mouth of the Goddess with the aforementioned mantras beginning with the *praṇava*. The mention of "the Guru" is illustrative;
[the procedure is] as follows: having raised [the disciple] with both hands in the presence of the deity’s face, [he should address him as]:
"O Mother of the World, O Sustainer of the World, O Goddess [Name], and thereafter..."
"I offer whatever little there is; please accept this oblation of mine.
O Goddess! Having offered it with this mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), [one should proceed].

One should display the five mudrās either on the left or on the right. With the fingers curved and their tips slightly separated from one another, this is declared to be the *grāsa-mudrā*; one should employ it with the right hand.
The mudrās begin with prāṇa; the vital winds are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
Samāna is to be known as the fifth; thus the five prāṇas are proclaimed.
The *prāṇamudrā* is fully described as being used for the act of offering (*havana*) into the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
when the index finger, middle finger, and thumb are joined together as one.
In the oblation of apāna, there may be a mudrā formed by the ring finger and the middle finger joined with the little finger; this is employed in the homa of vyāna.
The mudrā formed with the little finger extended is prescribed for the offering of food;
all mudrās, when properly prepared, are equal in their function for the rite of oblation.
Having paused for a moment, one should contemplate that the Goddess has accepted it;
O Goddess, as long as she consumes the oblation, the wise practitioner should mutter the root mantra.
Then, having offered water with the root mantra, the practitioner,
for the sake of increasing that splendor, offers the oblations and subsequently gives the *apośāna* water.
One should offer this water with the mantra: "Thou art the covering of nectar, svāhā.
Then, one should give water for sipping (ācamana) and mouth-perfume. Having purified the place, the practitioner of the mantra should also present betel-leaf.
O Goddess of Gods, if any of these aforementioned substances should be difficult to obtain, it may be mentally conceived through visualization;
however, water must be offered everywhere, interspersed between each of the ritual services.
Regarding the time when substances become *nirmālya* (remnants of worship),
the *Yoginīhṛdaya* states the rule for specific substances:
"Those gems, pearls, and gold that have indeed been offered to the Deity [become *nirmālya*]."
Neither a faded flower offering nor a copper vessel should be kept for twelve years.
O beautiful one, as soon as the offering of a fine cloth, a garment, and sweetmeats along with rice-and-pulse porridge was given for six months, [the results were attained] within half a watch.
Silk cloth [is prescribed] for three months, while the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) is prescribed for a single day;
likewise, food should be served while it is still warm, as should the finest rice-milk (paramānna).
O Pārvatī, the head and blood [are attained] in a day and night;
O Śaṅkarī, curds and milk in a muhūrta, and clarified butter in a watch (yāma).
The *karavīra* flower remains as an offering for a full day and night, as does the *bilva* leaf;
however, the red *javā* flower becomes an *nirmālya* (discarded offering) after one and a half watches of the night.
O Īśānī! Within half a watch [of the day], water is offered; O beloved! as soon as it is given, there is no *nirmālya* (remnant offering), nor pomegranate, nor *bilva* fruit.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of Ritual Honors and the Like," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme renunciant (*paramahaṃsa*), the holy Avadhūta. 14.
Fifteenth Chapter:
Now, the Śākta Conduct.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, the Goddess said:
Listen, my son! To my secret concerning the conduct of the observance (samayācāra), without which one does not attain success even in hundreds of millions of births.
Abandoning impermanent actions and intent upon constant practice,
one should offer all actions to the Supreme Deity.
A wise person should not spend time in vain on gambling, games, and the like;
rather, he should pass it through activities such as the worship of deities, japa, and sacrifices.
Internally Śākta, externally Śaiva, and in the assembly considered Vaiṣṇava—
the preeminent practitioner should always maintain the state of Viṣṇu.
If the practitioner should see the family tree, he should then prostrate.
Regarding the family trees (*kulavṛkṣa*),
it is stated in the *Kulāvatāntra*:
"The *aśoka*, the *keśara*, the *bilva*, the *karṇikāra*, and likewise the *cūta*."
The *nameru*, the *priyāla*, the *sinduvāra*, the two types of *kadambaka*,
the *maruvaka*, the *campaka*, and the *bilva*— these are recorded as the twelve.

The *nameru* is the *rudrākṣa*; the *piyāla* is a specific type of tree; the *sindhuvāra* is known by the name *niśundā*; and the *maruvaka* is the *jhiṇṭikā*. These twelve should be known as the family trees (*kulavṛkṣa*).
Elsewhere also: "Śleṣmātaka, the one called Karañja, Nimba, Aśvattha, Kadambaka, Bilva, Aśoka, and Campaka— these are the eight family trees (kulapādapa)."
The *śleṣmātaka* tree is known as the *baheḍā* tree. Kulayoginīs always reside within all of these;
one should not sleep beneath a kula-tree, nor should one cause any harm to it.
In the *Yāmala*:
"If by chance one should go to a grove, a mountain, a deserted place, an empty pavilion, a crossroads, or the midst of a *kalā*..."
Having remained for a moment, having recited the mantra, and having bowed, one should depart at ease; that is to say, to the seat (*pīṭha*) of the Goddess at the crossroads.
Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*:
That place where the auspicious Tāriṇī resides should be known as a crossroads (catuṣpatha); the meaning is that she is called "Tāriṇī" because she effects crossing over.
Regarding the description of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), the Gāndharva states:
"Kāmarūpa is the great seat, and after that, Vārāṇasī."
Nepāla is a great pīṭha, as is Pauṇḍravarddhana.
O Great Goddess! Beyond this is Purasthira;
beyond that is the great seat (pīṭha) Pūrṇaśaila, and after that is Arbuda.
Likewise, Kāśmīra is a pīṭha, and then there is Kānyakubja;
O Śivā, there is also the pīṭha Āmrātakeśvara and likewise Ekāmra.
Tisrotas is designated as a pīṭha, and beyond that is Kāmakoṭi;
Kailāsa, Bhūtanagara, and Kedāra are the most excellent pīṭhas.
The Śrīpīṭha, likewise Oṅkāra, and beyond that Jālandhara;
Mālava, Kalānta, and Devamātṛka as well.
And likewise, O Goddess, Gokarṇa and Māruteśvara,
as well as Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, and beyond that, Rājagiri.
Pīṭha, Kolvagiri, and then Elāpura;
the great Pīṭha Kāleśvara, Praṇava, and Jayantikā.
The seat of Ujjayinī, the seat of Kṣīrikā,
the seat of Hastināpura, and the seat of Uḍḍīśa.
Prayāga, Ṣaṣṭhīśa, Māyāpura, Jaleśvara, Malaya— the great pīṭha— and likewise Śrīśaila, O beloved.
Merugiri, Mehendra, and Vāmana, O Maheśvarī;
likewise the Hiraṇyapura-pīṭha and Mahālakṣmīpura.
Uḍḍīyāna is a great pīṭha, and after that is Chāyāpura.
O Goddess of Gods! these pīṭhas are recommended for the practice of japa. [The fruit of japa performed at these sacred seats.]
Regarding the fruit [of this practice], it is said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"Worship performed constantly at Vārāṇasī bestows the full fruit;
that which is performed in the presence of Puruṣottama is declared to be twice as effective."
It is said that [the merit] there is double, especially in Dvārāvatī;
in all sacred fields and holy fords, worship is equal to that of Dvārāvatī.
The Vindhya is said to be a hundredfold [meritorious], and the Gaṅgā is equal to that;
so too is it in Āryāvarta, Madhyadeśa, and likewise in Brahmāvarta.
It is said that at Prayāga and likewise at Puṣkara, [a gift] yields fruit equal to that of the Vindhya;
however, on the banks of the Karatoyā river, it is said to yield four times that fruit.
Beyond that, four times as much is prescribed at the Bhairava pool in the river;
beyond that, four times as much again is prescribed in the vicinity of Vālmīkīśvara.
There, at Siddheśvarī-yoni, it is remembered as being double that [size];
and at the pool of the Lauhitya river, it is said to be four times that.
Equal to that [is the merit] everywhere in Kāmarūpa, both in water and on land;
likewise, the worship of the Goddess is highly praised in the divine abode of Kāmarūpa.
The field of the Goddess exists in Kāmarūpa; there is nothing else equal to it.
In other places the Goddess is rare, but in Kāmarūpa she is in every house.
Thereafter, it is said that at the head of the river-pool (nadīkuṇḍa), the measurement is fourfold;
from that, it is further said to be twofold in the case of a wooden Śivaliṅga.
Twice that [merit] is said to be obtained in the self-originated [yoginīs] of Śailaputrī;
and a hundred times more than that is said to be the merit of the Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala.
If one should perform worship of Mahāmāyā even once at Kāmākhyā, one attains one's desire in this world and the nature of Śiva in the next.
O Goddess of the Gods! if by chance one should find access to these places, then, having performed worship and other rites and having bowed down, one may depart at ease.
The meaning is that one should go into the midst of the *kalā*s— that is, into the midst of the collection of *prakṛti*s— perform worship and so forth, and having bowed, depart happily.
Thus it is said in the *Samayātantra*:
O Supreme Goddess! Worship and recitation performed in the presence of a woman are declared to be a hundred times more effective and imperishable than those performed at Kāmarūpa.
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"Upon seeing a single liṅga, a cremation ground, a multitude of women,
or even a woman dressed in red garments, one should salute them with devotion."
Seeing the vulture, Mahākālī; the jackal, Yamadūtī;
the black cat and the owl, Kṣemaṅkarī; and likewise the hawk.
A person should pay homage to Kurarā and recite this mantra:
"O slender-waisted one! O greatly fierce one! O you with loose hair! O you who are fond of offerings!
O you whose face is pleased by the family tradition! Salutations to you, the beloved of Śaṅkara!"

Having seen the father’s body devoid of life and circumambulating it while following it clockwise, the minister shall obtain happiness by bowing down with this mantra: *Pitṛbhūmiṃ vyasuṃ dṛṣṭvā pradakṣiṇamanuvrajan | praṇamya'nena manunā mantrī sukhamavāpnuyāt ||*
Oṃ! O you with terrible fangs! O you with a gaping mouth! O you who utter the loud sound "kiṭi"!
O you who resound with a deep and formidable roar! Homage to you, O dweller in the cremation ground!
Upon seeing red garments and flowers, a person should gaze upon Tripurāmbikā,
prostrate like a staff upon the ground, and recite this mantra:
Oṃ! To you who resemble the bandhūka flower, O Tripura, destroyer of fear, arisen from the dawning of good fortune—salutations to you, O lady of excellent complexion!
Black clothing, as well as flowers, kings, princes (or warriors),
elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, shields, and heroic men.
Having seen the family deity upon the buffalo and Mahiṣamardinī, one should bow to Jayadurgā; such a person is not tainted by obstacles.
They are known as the Phalakonaṭas. Oṃ! O Victorious Goddess! O Sustainer of the World! O Primordial One of the Three Cities! O Goddess of the Triple Deities!
O Goddess who grants boons to your devotees! O Slayer of Mahiṣa! Salutations be unto you!
[One should offer] a vessel of liquor, fish, meat, and an excellent woman.
Having seen the goddess Bhairavī, one should bow down while reciting the mantra:
"Oṃ, for the destruction of terrible obstacles and for the prosperity of the Kula practice."
I bow to you, O boon-granting Goddess, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
I bow to you whose face is drenched with streams of blood.
O Goddess who removes all obstacles! Salutations to you, O beloved of Hara!
He who, having heard the words spoken by Śivā, [worships] Śivadūtī, the bestower of auspiciousness—
The practitioner should bow with devotion; his desire is held in the hand [of the deity].
Even by the mere sight of these [deities], if one does not act in this way, [the goal is not attained].
If one prioritizes the mantra of power (śakti-mantra), its accomplishment does not arise;
for these [mantras] result only in killing, expulsion, or injury by means of snares and the like.
If that sinful soul performs [this], how could he be my devotee?
He who is intent on doing this would, for his own sake, paint with darkness.
Regarding the *Nityasaṃketastava* in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, he states the *Nityasaṃketastava*:
the Śrī Devī said:
Oṃ! Tripurā, Tripureśī, Sundarī, Purasundarī, Śrīmālinī, Siddhāmbā, and Mahātripurasundarī.
Manifest is this [state], and likewise sleep; hidden is another, and more hidden still;
belonging to the lineage of the oral tradition, it pertains to the Kaula, the secret, and the most secret.
Parāpararahasyā, the auspicious Kāmeśvarī,
Bhagamālā, Klinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnisundarī.
Mahāvidyeśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī,
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
O child! [They are] Jvālāṃśumālinī, Citrā, Vaśinī, Śubhagā, Kulā, the one named Pūrṇā, as well as Kāmeśī and Modinī.
Vimalā, Aruṇā Devī, Jayantī, Kulabhairavī,
Sarveśvarī, as well as Kaulī, Vāgīśī, and Sarvakāminī.
Siddheśvarī, as well as Ugrā, Durgā, Mahiṣamardinī,
Svapnāvatī, Śūlinī, Mātaṅgī, and Surasundarī.
Mahākālī, Mahogrā, Citrarūpā, Mahodarī,
Prāṇavidyā, as well as Ekākṣī, Ekapādā, and Mahāṅkuśā.
Vāmā, Śivā, as well as Jyeṣṭhā, Surūpā, Cāruhāsinī,
Trikhaṇḍā, Triśiras, Saurī, Gaurī, and Vindhyanivāsinī.
Kṣobhiṇī, Nādinī, Bhadrā, Lalitā, Bahurūpikā,
Sarvasampatkarī, Tārā, Bhāvānī, and Viśvavāsinī.
The great vidyā Kūṭeśvarī has been declared to you, O Bhairava!
Now listen yourself with a single-minded focus, O Mahādeva, to [the description of] her worshippers.
Manu, Candra, Kubera, and Manmatha after him;
then the sage who is the husband of Lopāmudrā, Nandin, Śatru, Skanda, and likewise Śiva.
Krodhabhaṭṭāraka is indeed proclaimed as Śakti;
and Durvāsas, Vyāsa, Sūrya, Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara.
Aurva, Vahni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa,
as well as Vāyu, Viṣṇu, Svayambhū, Bhairava, and Gaṇaka.
Aniruddha, Bharadvāja, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
the lords of the Gaṇas and the protectors of the Kulas; as well as Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, and Sarasvatī.
Dhātṛ, Śeṣa, Pramatta, Unmatta, Kulabhairava, Kṣetrapāla, Hanumān, Dakṣa, and Garuḍa.
Śukadeva, Prahlāda, Rāma, and Rāvaṇa;
Kāśyapa, Kautsa, and Kumbha, as well as Jamadagni and Bhṛgu.
Bṛhaspati was Yaduśreṣṭha, Dattātreya was Yudhiṣṭhira,
Arjuna was Bhīmasena, and Droṇācārya was Vṛṣākapi.
Duryodhana, as well as Kuntī, Sītā, Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Draupadī, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā.
Puṣpadanta, Mahābuddha, Bāla, Kāla, Mandara, Kailāsa, Kṣīrasindhu, Udadhi, and likewise Himavat.
And Nārada, O great heroes, has been described as a hero-adept (vīrasādhaka),
who, through the grace of Mahāvidyā, was fully absorbed in his respective duties.
O child! He who, having become pure and self-restrained, recites the names of these [sages] who constantly practice the eternal Vidyā at the time of dawn—
Having become pure at the time of worship, one should recite this supreme hymn;
or, even if impure, one should do so while relying on Nirālambā in the presence of the Kula.
I grant him the fruit of daily worship and his desired boon,
as well as the secret convention of the wheel (cakrasaṃketaka) and likewise the secret convention of the guru (gurusaṃketaka).
He who acts here without knowing the secret convention of mantras, the secret convention of names, and the secret convention of the conduct of the pledge (samaya) [is lost].
Recitation, worship, adoration, and fire-offerings lead only to malevolent magic;
however, by reciting this hymn, one will certainly become possessed of the secret signs.

Thus ends the Nityasaṃketastavarāja in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi. Since it is stated in the scripture regarding the declaration of fruits that "liberation occurs even at the fall of the body through the observance of the rules of conduct," this [practice] is also for the sake of specific desires.
Now, regarding the *śivābali* (offering to the goddess Śivā), the *Viśvasāra* states: "Having presented the *śivābali*, one should then satisfy the Mother of the Universe;
for he who does not offer the *bali* to Śivā cannot attain the state of Śiva."
"That most wicked person who does not worship the family deity (kuladevī) cannot be tolerated," according to the statement in the *Yāmala*;
and likewise in the *Yāmala*:
"He who does not worship the goddess Śivā in her animal form in a secluded place [is a sinner]."
By the howling of jackals, everything of his is certainly destroyed instantly.
Taking with her all the rules for recitation and worship, as well as whatever meritorious deeds there were,
Śivā took them and wept in a secluded place at nightfall.
In the Tantra— where it should have been said "Kālikā," it is stated that there Umā,
in the form of Śiva, comes assuming the form of a jackal along with her retinue;
one must certainly and invariably please Śivā by the gift of food.
Just as the daily *śrāddha* is constant— like the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vandana*) and the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛ-tarpaṇa*)—
so too is the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*bali-dāna*) and the worship of the family lineage constant.
In the *Yāmala*:
"At the root of a *bilva* tree, on a riverbank, or even in a cremation ground,
the practitioner should offer an oblation consisting primarily of meat at the time of twilight."
The mantra for offering the oblation to Śiva is stated as follows: Oṃ! O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O Śivā, you who have the form of the fire of time (Kālāgni)! [Accept this offering!]
"Having accepted your offering, tell me clearly the fruit of both the auspicious and the inauspicious."
Having spoken thus, O beloved, the bali offering should be given by the family members;
it is where [the food] is consumed by one person for the benefit of the practitioners.
At that very moment, the supreme and most rare favor of all the powers is attained,
when one raises the face toward the northeast and cries out with a beautiful voice after eating.
At that very moment, O Goddess, there is auspiciousness; it certainly does not happen otherwise.
When nothing deficient is perceived, then indeed no inauspiciousness occurs.
Knowing this, O Great Goddess! one should perform rites for peace and prosperity:
the power of the animal (paśu-śakti), the power of the bird (pakṣi-śakti), and the power of man (nara-śakti), in their proper order.
Since worship accomplishes even the most difficult task with double the efficacy and all its qualities,
one should perform this great worship with every possible effort.
Regarding the fruit of the worship of Śiva and so forth, he states the fruit of worship, recitation, and the like:
"Just as fire burns grass, so too shall one always conquer enemies."
He is himself Brahmā, he is himself Viṣṇu, and he is himself Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Before long, the practitioner becomes the stainless Brahman; it cannot be otherwise.
Any woman who recites this vidyā shall become the Supreme Goddess herself.
A woman who is barren like a crow, or one who is barren, or one who miscarries—by worshipping [him], she shall obtain a son who is truthful and long-lived; this is the truth.
That mistress shall be difficult to attain, yet she will be endowed with wealth and grain;
in the end, she will not be born as a cow—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"One who, being composed, constantly recites or even merely remembers the Great Vidyā,
in his house shall dwell Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī shall reside upon his tongue."
The Śruti declares that the deity Nārāyaṇa dwells in the heart;
Brahmā resides in the region of the throat, and I abide in front of him.
Having become one, the Goddess protects the practitioner with all of them;
by reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, the practitioner is liberated from great sin.
By two hundred thousand [recitations], one destroys the sins committed even over seven lifetimes;
by three hundred thousand, one destroys even those committed over ten thousand lifetimes.
By reciting the mantra four hundred thousand times, the practitioner of mantras becomes equal to the Lord of Speech;
by five hundred thousand recitations, even a poor man becomes like Vaiśravaṇa himself.
O Goddess, by reciting it six hundred thousand times, one becomes a great Vidyādhara;
by reciting it seven hundred thousand times, one becomes a partaker of the siddhi of Khecarī.
O Maheśvarī, by reciting this vidyā eight hundred thousand times, one becomes a master of the eight siddhis, beginning with aṇimā; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess! By reciting it one hundred thousand times, one becomes like another form of Rudra;
O Great Goddess! he is the creator, the destroyer, and an unimpeded lord in the world.
O Goddess! the fruit of ten million recitations cannot even be described.
Also in the Śrīkrama:
"O Mistress of the Gods, one should certainly bring the deity by means of the bond of mantra;
having accomplished the success of the practitioner's task, the Goddess will depart."
Then, having performed one hundred and eight circumambulations of Kālikā as a fruit of prostration to the Goddess,
and having attained all desires, one shall subsequently obtain liberation.
In this context, the words "he who" (yaḥ saḥ) should be applied respectively to the first and second halves [of the verse].
Those men who bow to Durgā, endowed with supreme faith,
attain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and go to the world of Durgā.
Even if a person performs obeisance to the Blessed Lady but once, even with deceit or without devotion, he goes to the abode of the gods.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, all fasts, and all sacred fords—
that fruit the world obtains by bowing the head to Satī.
He who, with his body fully extended, falls upon the ground like a staff before Caṇḍikā with devotion, attains the supreme goal.
In the tenth canto of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the words of Rukmiṇī are as follows:
"O Kātyāyanī! O Mahāmāyā! O Sovereign of the great Yoginīs!
O Goddess, I bow to you; make the son of Nandagopa my husband."
O Kātyāyanī! O you who have appeared for the sake of the sage Kātyāyana! O Mahāmāyā!
You are Mahāmāyā because you are both great (*mahatī*) and an illusion (*māyā*), being the cause of delusion even for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
Since Viṣṇu, I myself, and even Īśāna have been made to assume physical bodies by you,
who then would be capable of praising you?
Thus from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: O Mahāyoginī!
She in whom exists the Great Yoga—that Māyā consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) which is the cause of the creation and so forth of the universe—is Mahāyoginī.
O Adhīśvarī! She who is the sovereign (īśvara) of the Īśvaras—the Śaivas who are devoted to Śiva—is Adhīśvarī.

"According to the words of Mārkaṇḍeya, she is the Sovereign of all sovereigns. Therefore, make the son of Nanda—the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is esteemed as the Joy of the Nandas—my husband, my wedder, in that very same form as a deity; for without your grace," [it cannot be so].
Since no task whatsoever can be accomplished [without you], salutations to you!
This prostration is performed through body, speech, and mind.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Fruits of Recitation and Other Practices," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* composed by the wandering ascetic teacher, the supreme *paramahaṃsa*, the holy *avadhūta* Brahmānandagiri. 15.
The Sixteenth Chapter:
Determining the Causes for the Absence of Fruits from Recitation and Other Practices.
In the Mahiṣamardinī Tantra, the Goddess said:
By whom is the vidyā recited, and by whom is it not recited?
O Lord, how does the certain absence of fruit arise?
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
"O fair-limbed one! O Supreme Goddess! Although this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is known to you alone, nevertheless hear this secret."
O Maheśānī! In the Kali age, there is the defect of association; many people are heretics.
O Maheśānī! Due to the defect of such association, one's merit perishes at that very moment.
Therefore, O Goddess, a wise person should diligently avoid such association;
indeed, it would be better for the best of practitioners to touch a Cāṇḍāla.
Nevertheless, one should always abandon that which produces non-attainment;
for in the Kali ages, the various subjects in Bhārata have been corrupted.
Therefore, O Maheśānī! all are defiled by contact. O Devī! one should carefully avoid touching a Brāhmaṇa who acts as a mediator.
O lady worshipped by the gods, there are many defects in Bhārata during the Kali age;
O beautiful woman, in the Kali age, Brāhmaṇas [dwell] in the houses of Śūdras!
O beloved! Those Brāhmaṇas who are intent on reciting the Purāṇas while being devoted to hypocrisy and envy are most sinful; they are like Cāṇḍālas.
A twice-born man should not recite the Purāṇas in the house of a Śūdra during the Kali age;
O Maheśānī! if he should recite a Purāṇa in the house of a Śūdra, [he incurs sin].
Indeed, by mere association with this [world], all states of existence arise;
through such contact, there is a loss of accomplishment, and one never attains success at any time.
And in the Kali age, O Goddess, there will be many people in Bhārata who are revilers;
some will be intent on reviling Śiva, while others will be intent on reviling Viṣṇu.
They constantly utter insults against all the gods and goddesses alike; they would not entertain any doubt regarding this matter.
In the Kali age in Bhārata, the lowest of men, considering themselves Vaiṣṇavas, procreate sons even by union with the wives of others.
O daughter of the mountain! Having worn a garland of *tulasī* on the ear, the neck, as well as the hand and the heart, and having applied the *tilaka*, which is the abode of Hari.
While chanting the names of Hari with melodious voices from house to house,
those lowest of men, heretics, would instead amass wealth for others.
O Maheśānī! the sin of those who, being devoted to unrighteousness, should utter the name of Hari, cannot indeed be described.
At that time, if one abandons the *saṃdhyā* and the *gāyatrī* and remembers the name of Hari, all sins without exception will certainly be destroyed.
O lady of pure smiles! For as many syllables as reside in the Name alone, there are that many countless sins at every step.
O beloved! Food, water, and flowers that are offered to Viṣṇu—his food is considered equal to excrement, and his water is considered equal to urine.
O Maheśānī! In every house there are Vaiṣṇavas, and the people are devotees of Viṣṇu;
wherever there is a multitude of Vaiṣṇavas, that land is eternally fallen [at your feet].
Intoxicated by song and intoxicated by instrumental music, the Brahmins were intent on dancing;
in every house, an emotional state was aroused among the Brahmins by the songs.
O lady of beautiful limbs! There is certainly no existence in hell for one who strikes the earth with their feet while all the Brahmins are present in Bhārata.
O lovely-limbed one! Those lowest of the twice-born who shall strike [me] before Viṣṇu will cause many of their own ancestors to fall, equal in number to those kicks.
O Goddess! O lady of beautiful limbs! they cause one to fall from heaven into hell, and not otherwise, if there is no bliss of meditation at the time of worship.
At that very time, whatever singing and dancing the twice-born perform before Viṣṇu, Śiva, or the Goddess, their sin is destroyed.
If one, having become possessed by the spirit of song, performs a dance while holding ten million bamboo flutes, that twice-born man shall go to hell.
In the Kali age in Bhārata, those Brāhmaṇa women who were devoted to singing likewise become addicted to instrumental music and dance, O lowest of the twice-born.
By mere association with them, everything would go to ruin;
therefore, O Goddess, one should not associate with them with any effort.
In the Kali age, however, O lady of beautiful limbs, one does not attain success in the land of Bhārata through mere association;
even if success is attained, it occurs only after many days have passed.
O lady of tremulous glances! Since this land of Bhārata in the Kali age is filled with every kind of defect, there exists therein one single means for attaining liberation.
O Mahāmāyā! If one should recite the Great Vidyā even once, being liberated from all sins, he attains the Great Liberation.
O Dear One, a Śākta, a Śaiva, or a Vaiṣṇava should diligently avoid contact with Vaiṣṇavas born of mixed castes.
Now, regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*):
expiation is an action that destroys all manner of evil. As it is said in the *Tantra*:
"If one desires the destruction of all the evils residing within the body..."
O Goddess! O Supreme Sovereign! [I offer] Kāma, Māyā, and likewise Manmatha.
O Goddess! One should recite this vidyā for the removal of that sin;
having recited it one hundred and eight times, one is liberated from that sin.
And in the *Yāmala*:
"Just as the tarnish on gold is completely purified by fire,
so too is the impurity of improper conduct [purified] by the fire of expiation."
O Goddess! For the expiation of sins, one should recite the root mantra eight thousand times, or else chant the Gāyatrī, which destroys all sins.
"Aṣṭasahasrakam" means one thousand and eight. Regarding the *gāyatrī*:

because a Śūdra lacks the entitlement to the Vedic *gāyatrī*, he should recite the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) one thousand and eight times, or the Tantric *gāyatrī*. Since women are equal to Śūdras, this same practice applies to them as well.
Now, regarding the expiation for the loss of the armor (*kavaca*) as stated in the *Yāmala*: "O Goddess, if the armor that has been worn should ever be lost..."
I shall declare the means for that; listen, O lotus-faced one.
Having sat down and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Then, having meditated upon the six chakras, one should contemplate the Guru upon the crown of the head.
O Goddess! One should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca), which consists of the seed-syllables of the Mātṛkā enclosed by them in both direct and reverse order, twelve times in succession.
Then one should recite the Great Vidyā a thousand or a hundred times in succession;
having written down the armor-mantra (kavaca), O Goddess, one should wrap it with a red thread.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should encase that which is so difficult to obtain with gold;
having encased it with gold, O Great Goddess, that which is most difficult to obtain,
one should then wear this newly consecrated armor.
Regarding the sequence for the consecration of a lost kavaca,
he states the procedure for consecration: having bathed [the image] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) on an auspicious day...
One should establish the vital breaths therein with the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra.

Having worshipped the armor (*kavaca*), which is the form of the deity and grants all desires, one should then recite the Great Vidyā a thousand or a hundred times in succession. O Great Goddess! the practitioner should then wear it upon the appropriate parts of the body.
Thus concludes the expiation for the destruction of the armor.
Now, regarding the expiation for the destruction of the yantra,
it is stated in the *Navaratneśvara*:
O Goddess! if by fate the established machine should perish, one should reverently observe a fast for a full day and night.
Having drawn the yantra on a leaf made of gold or other materials with which the yantra was fashioned, one should worship the deity therein.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with the sixteen services as far as one's ability allows, being well-composed, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
The practitioner, having stirred that water and drunk it, should then consume [the medicine];
he shall observe celibacy for as long as it takes to prepare the yantra.
Furthermore, endowed with purity, one should procure a new and beautiful yantra;
having procured the new yantra, one should perform its consecration (pratiṣṭhā). Then, once it has been consecrated, one should perform worship as previously described.
Now, regarding the expiation for the falling of the yantra or other objects during the time of worship:
"O Goddess, if at any time during the period of worship the yantra should fall..."
Whether it be the *liṅga* or Śiva himself, hear now, O Pārvatī, what the fruit of that [offense] is:
loss of life, loss of wealth, physical exhaustion, and likewise the destruction of kinsmen.
Having thus determined that [the offense] has occurred, one should then perform an expiation;
one should observe a fast for either three nights or one night.
O Goddess! One should likewise recite the root-mantra one thousand and eight times, and one should likewise offer oblations with *japā* flowers one hundred and eight times.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and worship the yantra with a concentrated mind;
the term "yantra" here is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for Śiva and the other deities as well.
The expiation for the falling of a rosary:
if a rosary should fall from the hand or likewise be destroyed,
one should mutter [the mantra] a thousand times and thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas.
O Goddess! A meal for Brahmins destroys all that is undesirable;
or else, being composed, one should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
"One should mutter the Gāyatrī"—the meaning is that one should mutter the Gāyatrī of each respective deity. Then, having worshipped it, one should indeed take up that rosary once again.
When this has been done, O lady of excellent hips, one is not overcome by obstacles.
Now, regarding the expiation for the destruction of the garland:
if the garland should be destroyed, one should perform everything as before;
thereafter, O fair-faced one, one should prepare another garland of the same kind.
Having collected [the water] and established it, one should indeed take it up again.
In the *Yāmala*: "O Great Goddess, even one burdened with great sins, if he should recite the Gāyatrī, truly, truly, he becomes liberated at that very moment."

One who is impure shall not touch a garland, nor should one cause it to fall from the hand. If a sound occurs, disease will arise; if it falls from the hand, it causes destruction; if the thread breaks, death will occur; therefore, one should be diligent in its care.
In another tantra:
"If the rosary falls from the hand, it should not be used for recitation by the wise;
an expiation must be performed by reciting the mantra one thousand times."
"Thousandfold" means one thousand plus eight.
When the string has worn out, one should string it again with new threads and recite [the mantra] a hundred times.
"A hundred times" means that one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
If the garland should break, one should perform worship even more extensive than before;
having strung that garland again, one should perform the consecration as previously described. Then, one may recite with the garland, and one shall not incur any fault therein.
Now, the expiation for pacifying the anger of the guru:
When Śiva is angry, the guru is the protector; when the guru is angry, there is no one at all [to save].
Having observed a fast during the guru's anger, one should indeed propitiate him.
One should indeed renounce food until serenity arises;
when the Guru is pleased, one may eat, and thus no fault occurs.
Now, regarding the expiation for eating without having made an offering, the Matsyasūkta states:
"One should not eat any food, whether chewed or swallowed, without first having offered it."
Food that has not been offered to Viṣṇu is excrement; milk [that has not been offered] is urine.
The station of Viṣṇu is the supreme [abode] of one's own respective deity to be accomplished. Also elsewhere:
"One must never consume what has not been given; it is remembered as being equal to forbidden food (abhakṣya), O Dear One—whether it be a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a root, food, drink, or medicine."
One should not eat what has not been offered; one should indeed eat what has been offered.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Whether he be a great sage, a Brahmin, or anyone else,
whatever food he is capable of eating should be excellent, in whatever manner possible."
One should offer [the food] to one's chosen deities and likewise receive it oneself.
In the *Yāmala*: "In whatever manner an edible substance is consumed, one should cause it to be offered in that very same manner;
otherwise, by offering it differently, one shall not obtain its fruit."
Whatever substance is to be consumed in whatever manner, that substance must not be given in any other manner.
One who eats without first offering it to Hari becomes a denizen of hell for seven lifetimes.
The mention of "Hara" is illustrative. Thus it is stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Fruit, flowers, betel, food, drink, and whatever else—without having offered these to Mahādevī, one must never consume them."
A man should not eat without having offered [the food]; otherwise, he becomes subject to penance.
By reciting the mantra of the Goddess eight hundred times, a man becomes purified.
The phrase "of the Goddess" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for one’s own respective deity of worship. Thus it is stated in the Yāmala:
"O Maheśānī! One who eats without having made an offering becomes a sinner;
by reciting one's chosen mantra a hundred times, one is purified from that sin."

Nor should it be argued that, based on the statement, "Whoever is devoted to the worship of a particular deity should consume only the *naivedya* (food offering) of that deity," one must not consume the *naivedya* of another deity; for the injunction that "the *nirmālya* (remains of an offering) of Śiva is not to be taken" applies to the ignorant, whereas for the wise...
The consumption of *prasāda* alone is essential.
As it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "That which is given by Śiva, that which is given by Viṣṇu, and likewise that which is given by Girijā..."
One should eat only upon obtaining [the food]; otherwise, one becomes a sinner.
In the Agni Purāṇa: "Having placed in his stomach the food offering given by Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Pārvatī, a man shall attain union (sāyujya)."
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"The deluded one of confused intellect who, having abandoned the food offering (naivedya) at the Liṅga, eats it out of ignorance, is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell; of this there is no doubt."
This, moreover, is the supreme offering (naivedya) presented upon the head of Śiva. In the Skanda Purāṇa:

"By consuming the food offering of Śambhu from a Bāṇaliṅga, a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga, one made of crystal, or one fashioned from clay, one obtains merit equal to that of Indra (Śatakratu)."
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"He who wears upon his head the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of the Lord of Pārvatī obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice."
And so it is said in the Liṅgārcana-tantra:
"Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā, and other great sages attained Yoga; even Viṣṇu attained the state of Viṣṇu. By whom is Śiva not served?"
The remains of the offerings (nirmālya) certainly remove all sins of Śambhu;
one should eat the offered food (naivedya), of this there is no doubt.
For the fools who consume [the offerings] do not themselves fall into hell;
rather, one should partake of the *naivedya* after having given it to one who possesses devotion to Him.
Otherwise, there will be no success, and the worshipper shall go to hell.
Thus, by various scriptural statements from the Tantras and Purāṇas, it is established as a certainty that one should consume only what has been offered, and not what has not been offered.
Seeing one who reviles the food offering, the hosts of Yoginīs dance;
intent on drinking blood, they all become eager to chew flesh and bones.
Therefore, having seen or heard of what has been offered to the Goddess,
a human being should not revile it in thought or speech, thereby turning away from the disease of leprosy.

Thus, from the statement in the *Kālīkulasarvasva*: "In the *Kumārītantra*—one should never give the food offering (*naivedya*) of the deities to women. And in the *Tantra*: "Having offered [the food] to one's own powers (*śakti*s) and to the powers of others, one may then partake of it oneself."
In the *Yāmala*: "The Goddess becomes enraged with those practitioners who eat the food of the bound soul (*paśu*) in various ways; therefore, one should not allow contact with them."
In the Tantra: "Having killed a collection of boneless living beings, one should recite the mantra ten times;
and having killed any bird, one should recite it eleven times thrice."

In the *Yāmala*: "On a festival day (parvan), having failed to worship the Goddess of the gods, the Guru, and the Śakti according to one's ability, and having not offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) there, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times."
O Dear One! A Śākta, a Śaiva, or a Vaiṣṇava should diligently avoid association with Vaiṣṇavas who are born of mixed castes (varṇasaṅkara).
Having gazed upon their faces, one should look at the sun;
by reciting one's chosen mantra a hundred times, one is purified from that sin. Thus it is said.
One should perform only Vedic rites for the purpose of pleasing one's chosen deity. As stated in the Tantra:
"One who desires to please the deity should always perform the rite in Sadāśiva;
however, if one performs the rite while deluded by ritual rules and desiring something else," [the result is otherwise].
No fruit arises for him, and the deity becomes angry with him.
Furthermore:
"O beautiful one, those men who perform their duties properly without desire,"
To them, the Lord of All, the Blessed One, the Sovereign, grants liberation.

For those with desires, liberation consists of union (*sāyujya*) and so forth; however, such union is not the supreme liberation because of the continued association with a body. For those without desires, liberation is indeed *nirvāṇa*, as it is the supreme goal of man, according to the Vedic scripture: "He does not return again."
But surely: "One must inevitably experience the fruit of the karma one has performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
even in hundreds of millions of eons, karma does not perish without being experienced."

If it is argued that since karma alone is destroyed by experience according to this statement, liberation for the individual soul (jīva) would be impossible—given that it is impossible to exhaust through experience the infinite karma accumulated over many births—then it is replied: [The following is provided as the response: It is said: [text continues]
One who desires the favor of the deity should always perform ritual action toward Sadāśiva;
for the God, when pleased, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
If one who is free from desire, being of a sattvic nature, should offer whatever he possesses in this world,
he attains that state where, having gone, he does not grieve.
The wise declare that liberation is the absolute cessation of suffering.
In the *Yāmala*: "Dharma and adharma are declared to be the two fetters known as karma;
however, rites that please the deity lead neither to bondage nor to liberation."
The god receives with his head whatever has been done out of desire for him.
Because of such statements as these, present actions produce only the pleasure of the Lord and do not generate *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit); therefore,
all actions other than those already commenced (*prārabdha*) are destroyed by the knowledge obtained through the grace of the Lord.
And since the prārabdha [karmas] are exhausted only through experience, liberation occurs upon the destruction of the subtle body (liṅgadeha).

Regarding the subtle body (liṅgadeha), the Gāndharva [text] states: "The body consisting of seventeen— namely, the five vital breaths, the mind, the intellect, and the ten sense organs— is called this subtle liṅga."
In the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the twelfth book:
"Just as when a jar is broken, the space within the jar becomes the [universal] space as it was before,
so too, when the body has died, the individual soul (jīva) again attains Brahman."

The meaning is that when the physical body has perished and the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) has been destroyed; otherwise, birth and death would indeed occur again and again. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
At that very moment, one assumes a subtle body (ātivāhika-śarīra);
this occurs only for human beings, and never for other living creatures anywhere.
Then, when the sapindikarana rite has been performed by his kinsmen at the completion of one year, that man attains another body.

Consequently, one does not go to hell or to heaven by virtue of one's own karma at that very moment—that is, at the moment of death. And the *preta* body has the form of the previous body, yet possesses an entirely different mode of movement. As the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:
When the body has been extended by the vital air (vāyu), it then assumes another [body],
possessing the same dimensions, age, condition, and configuration as its previous existence.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Faults of Association and Other Matters," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*), the supreme renunciant (*paramahaṃsa*), and the *avadhūta*. 16.
The Seventeenth Chapter:
Now, the procedure for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the *Govindavṛndāvana*:

The preceptor, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules and having sat down upon his seat, should take possession of the ground as far as the sacrificial site extends.
Then, one should offer an oblation of black gram and cooked rice according to the prescribed rite:
"Oṃ, those deities of the site who reside in heaven, the netherworld, and the middle realm..."
May the Mothers, the Bhūtas, the Vetālas, and whoever else desires the bali-offering, accept this bali that has been given and return to their own abodes, being well-pleased.
And those who are the attendants of the Goddess, let them accept this bali offering. Regarding the construction of the pavilion for Śāradā:
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should construct an auspicious pavilion with an internal space measured by five,
seven, or nine cubits.
It should be provided with sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the center;
having erected them to a height of eight cubits, twelve [others] are placed at the perimeter.
Those who know the Tantras and the Vedas understand that a cubit (hasta) consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
In the construction of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for houses and the like, as well as for altars (vedikās) and pavilions (maṇḍapas),
these must be made according to the standard measure of finger-breadths (mānāṅgula), and never by any other means.
Regarding the definition of the measuring finger (mānāṅguli), the Tantra states:
"Of the middle finger of the right hand of the practitioner, [the middle joint...]"
The measurement-finger (mānāṅguli) is declared to be the length-measurement of the middle finger.
Regarding the measurement of the site for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The site for the pavilion is said to be twelve *aṅgulas* in height above the ground."
Then one should cover the pavilion with coconut leaves and *vaśa* grass,
provided it is equipped with four doors and adorned with plantain pillars.
It is joined with mango leaves and encircled by ropes;
in the eight directions are eight banners, according to the colors of the four guardians of the quarters.
Regarding the colors of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*), the *Śāradā-tilaka* states:
"Yellow, red, white, smoky-grey, white, smoky-grey, and both white."
These are proclaimed to be fair-complexioned and reddish in sequence according to their color.

There is no sacrificial fire-pit (kuṇḍa) without a body; there is no oblation (homa) without a pit. Therefore, the pit is highly praised. One should know that the form of the pit is the supreme body of primordial nature (prakṛti).
The head is declared to be in the east; the arms are in the south and north;
the belly is said to be the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); and the feet are in the west, which is the womb (yoni).
Regarding the characteristics of the square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): one should lay down a thread extending from east to west measuring one cubit;
likewise, one should lay down a thread extending from south to north.
Having likewise laid down four threads at the tips of those [lines],
the great quadrangular sacrificial pit (mahākuṇḍa) is proclaimed as the practice for all yogas.
A pit measuring one fist is prescribed for fifty oblations;
for a hundred oblations, it should be one aratni in measure, and for a thousand oblations, one hasta.
For ten thousand [homages], two cubits are prescribed; for a hundred thousand, four cubits are declared;
for a million, six cubits are taught; and for ten million, eight cubits are recorded.
The measurement of the excavation is said to be as wide as the pit itself;
for a *sahasraka* [homa], it should be twenty-four finger-breadths and devoid of barley-grain measurements.
Then, for a measurement of two cubits, thirty finger-breadths are prescribed;
for four cubits, the middle measurement is calculated as thirty-eight.
In the case of a lakṣahoma, it is proclaimed that there should be a space of one finger-breadth (aṅgula) for each barley-corn (yava);
likewise, the measurement for the ṛtuhasta is forty-three [finger-breadths].
A *niyuta* is said to be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) plus four barley-corns (*yava*); likewise,
in the case of eight cubits (*vasuhasta*), the measurement is declared by the wise to be forty-eight [finger-breadths] together with seven barley-corns.
One should fashion a beautiful lotus with a central aperture in the middle of the pit (kuṇḍa);
furthermore, all pits indeed have three tiers (mekhalā).
Leaving aside one finger-breadth at the edge, one should fashion the girdle for it;
and one should gradually increase the neck by the measure of half a finger-breadth.
In another Tantra:
"One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring two cubits according to the measurement of the corner-threads;
in that manner, the pit for a hundred thousand [recitations] and so forth should be understood according to the prescribed rule."

The measurement obtained by means of the diagonal cord of a one-cubit pit— that is, the cord extending from corner to corner— is itself the conventional measurement for pits of two cubits and so forth; it does not mean doubling the measurement of the original cubit and so on.
Now, the description of the girdles (mekhalā) is set forth; the measurement of the girdles and so forth is being declared.
Whatever is the form of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), such is the form of the girdles as well.
The three girdles of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) should be known, in order,
as being one, two, and half a finger-breadth in both height and length, measured by the span of a closed fist.
The measure of the yoni is two finger-breadths (yuga-aṅgula), and the tip of the yoni is one finger-breadth;
the navel-lotus is said to be two finger-breadths in fifty [spokes].
In a fire-pit measuring one *aratni*, three, two, or one finger-breadths thick, the girdles (*mekhalā*) should be made;
the womb (*yoni*) should be measured at four finger-breadths.
One should make the tip of the yoni one finger-width long and slightly downward-facing;
the beautiful navel-lotus should likewise be three finger-widths in size.
In a sacrificial pit measuring one cubit, the girdles should be made four, three, and two finger-breadths wide;
and one should likewise fashion the womb (yoni) at six finger-breadths.
The navel-lotus is known to be four finger-breadths [in diameter], and the tip of the womb [the pericarp] is remembered as one finger-breadth;
in a two-cubit sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), those [dimensions] are to be known as six and forty finger-breadths respectively.
The womb should be seven finger-breadths in length, with the tip of the womb being two finger-breadths;
one should likewise fashion the beautiful navel-lotus as five finger-breadths.

In a sacrificial pit measuring four cubits, three girdles should be made with dimensions of eight, six, and four finger-breadths respectively; the tip of the yoni should be three finger-breadths wide.
In a sacrificial pit measuring six spans (rasakara), the yoni should be eight finger-breadths wide, the navel-lotus six finger-breadths,
and these [other dimensions] should be provided with ten, eight, and six finger-breadths respectively.
The vulva should not be less than four finger-breadths; the tip of the vulva should be four finger-breadths, and one should fashion the navel-lotus as seven finger-breadths, making it very beautiful.

In a sacrificial pit measuring eight cubits, the yoni should be made with a depth of ten fingers and a width of eight fingers according to the sequence of the sun (twelve) and the eight Vasus; likewise, it should be fashioned facing downwards.
The tip of the yoni should be made five finger-breadths wide, and likewise eight finger-breadths [in depth];
the knower of the tantras should thus fashion the navel-lotus for the hundred-thousand-fold homa.
In front of the Hotṛ priest, one should fashion that womb-shaped altar situated among the girdles; its form should be like the frontal globe of an elephant, with the opening facing downwards.
One should not direct the opening toward the west in the corners of the sacrificial pits;
thus is the rule for all sacrificial pits proclaimed.
The description of the stalk:
starting from the ground, the stalk should be hollow up to the middle of the yoni;
the term "hollow" (*sarandhrakam*) is connected to both [ends]. Thus it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
One should make an opening in the middle of the *yoni*; that is known as the *ājyagrāhin* (the ghee-receiver).
Regarding the rule for the ground, the *Kriyāsāra* states:
"The area situated outside the place of the fire-offering (*homasthāna*) is designated as the 'ground' (*sthala*)."
In the *Gautamīya*:
"The stalk is desired to have a fine tip, a thick base, and to be perforated.
In the *Sammohana-tantra*:
The base, the middle, and likewise the top are six, four, and three [units] respectively;

thus, the meaning is that the stalk (*nāla*) is thirteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of placing the circumference between the stalk and the girdle (*mekhalā*).
Then the wise one should make an opening above the second girdle.
Regarding the defects of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), Viśvakarman says: "If [the pit] is deeper than prescribed, there will be illness; if it is shallower, there is loss of wealth."
There is suffering in a crooked sacrificial pit, and death when the girdle is broken.
If the girdle is missing, there is indeed grief; if it is excessive, there is loss of wealth. A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made without a yoni is said to cause the destruction of one's wife.
A pit that is devoid of a rim is declared to be a "dhvasana" which destroys one's offspring;
such a pit should not be used, or else one should resort to a leveled sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Regarding the characteristics of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), the *Yāmala* states:
"One may perform the daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) rites upon the sacrificial ground."
One should construct that very beautiful [mandala] out of sand, measuring one cubit in size,
square on all sides, and one finger-breadth in height.
"Quadrangular" means having four corners.

Thus ends the chapter titled "The Determination of the Fire-pit" (*kuṇḍanirṇaya*) in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic (*paramahaṃsa*) and Avadhūta disciple of the venerable Parivrājakācārya Paramahaṃsatīrtha.
The Seventeenth Chapter (Ullāsa) || 17 ||
The Eighteenth Chapter: Now, the Procedure for Homa.
Next, I shall describe the generation of the fire according to all the tantras.
Having smeared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) everywhere with cow dung,
the knower of mantras should then prepare the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya) and purify it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The eighteen purificatory rites for the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) are stated in the *Śāradā*:
"Eighteen purificatory rites for the sacrificial pits have been taught in the Tantra."
Beholding with the root mantra and sprinkling with the arrow-mantra are prescribed.
Striking with that same [mantra] is prescribed; sprinkling with darbha grass is performed with the armor-mantra (varma).
Dugging and lifting up are done with the weapon-mantra (astra), while filling is with the heart-mantra (hṛd).
Leveling is performed with the weapon-mantra, and sprinkling is considered to be with the armor-mantra.
Pounding, incantation with the causal mantra, purification with the armor-mantra,
anointing, and thereafter the fashioning of the artistic forms.

Thereafter, the tripling of the thread is performed; worship with the heart-mantra is prescribed, followed by the "vajrīkaraṇa" (thunderbolt-strengthening) with auspicious kusha grass using the weapon-mantra and the heart-mantra.
One should protect the crossroads and the grinding-stone with the armor-mantra;
one should consecrate the sacrificial pits during the rite with these aforementioned consecrations.
The meaning of this is as follows: *kuṭṭana* is hardening; *vilepana* is smearing with cow-dung water;
*kalārūpakalpana* is the visualization of the form consisting of the digits (*kalā*) of the Moon, Sun, and Fire;
*trisūtrīkaraṇa* is encircling it three times with a red thread; and *vajrīkaraṇa* is the visualization of it in the form of a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
The making of a square is the [preparation of] the crossroads; the "striking down of the axle" is the opening of the sense-faculties. This is the consecration by means of another method;
or else, one should consecrate those [elements] by means of the four, beginning with the gazing [mudrās].

One should draw three lines each, directed toward the east and the north, with the heart mantra; for those lines pointing eastward, the presiding deities are traditionally held to be Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara.
At the northern ends of the lines are Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu.
Alternatively, one should fashion a triangle outside of that, a hexagon outside of that, and an eight-petaled lotus;
or likewise, a square with four doors as the fire-mandala.
And on the northern side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), there should be three lines measuring one cubit.
Likewise, one should draw three auspicious lines from south to north;
having sprinkled everything with water for the *arghya* offering, one should indeed perform the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*).
The remainder [of the ritual] is that one should sprinkle all [the items] with the *tāra* [syllable].
Regarding the five purifications, the *Śāradā-tilaka* states:
"Inspection with the root mantra and sprinkling with the *śara*-mantra are prescribed."
One should perform the striking with the *hetimantra* and then smear [it] with the *kavaca*.
Having performed protection with the Astra-mantra, one should then carry out the consecration (saṃskāra).
Then, one should worship the seat of the fire-goddess upon the pericarp;
one should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya starting from the southeast.
One who knows the ritual procedure should worship the unprecedented deities beginning with Dharma in the directions starting from the east,
and in the center, he should worship the nine powers of Fire.
Yellow, white, reddish, black, smoky, intense, and emitting sparks.
Rucirā and Jvālinī are proclaimed as the nine powers in sequence;
the knower of mantras should worship their maṇḍala together with their constituent parts (kalās).
One should likewise worship the solar mandala ending with the syllable *aṃ*, the lunar mandala with *uṃ*,
and similarly the fire mandala with *maṃ*, using perfumes and flowers.
One should worship Vāgīśvarī— who resembles a blue lotus and has bathed after her menses—
together with Vāgīśvara, using the ritual offerings.
Regarding the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), the *Tantra* describes the prescribed fire as follows:
"That which is produced from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) or the like, or that which comes from the house of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*)."
Regarding the carrying forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana), he says:
"One should perform the carrying forward of the fire in an auspicious vessel such as a copper bowl covered by another vessel, or even in a similar earthenware dish."

As for that which is stated in the *Smṛtisāra*: "One should not perform the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) in a shallow dish, a broken vessel, a potsherd, or even on a firebrand; for it brings about disease, loss, and fear."
