The intent here is that, when a primary vessel is available, a shallow earthen bowl (śarāva) should not be accepted.
Having brought [the wood], one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) in the southwest (nairṛtya) using the Astra-mantra.
And with the Astra-mantra alone, O Dear One, one should cast away that wood in the southwest.
In the *Śāradā-tilaka*:
"The preceptor should purify it according to the rule by means of inspection and other rites,
while meditating on the terrestrial [element] as one with the gastric and lunar fires of the abode."
Then one should unite the consciousness with the fire-seed (raṃ) within the fire;
having consecrated it with the Tāra mantra (oṃ), one should render it nectar-like by means of the Dhenu-mudrā.

Then the preceptor, having protected it with the Astra-mantra and subsequently enveloped it with the Tanutra-mantra, should circumambulate it three times while worshipping it above the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
performing the circumambulation preceded by the recitation of the Tāra-mantra.
Facing the fire with his knees touching the ground,
he should cast this [substance] into the womb of the Goddess with the thought that it is the seed of Śiva.
In the *Samayātantra*:
"Having covered that womb with kusha grass, one should place a square cloth over it;
then one should offer water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīyaka*) to the deity and the goddess."
The Guru should meditate on Hari in the form of fire, sustained by the umbilical cord within the womb.
The mention of "Hari" is an illustration [representing] one's own respective chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*). In the *Samayātantra*:
"One should place a *darbha* bracelet on the left hand of the Goddess for the sake of protection;
one should adorn the Goddess—the Mother who is the source of the three worlds—with ornaments."

The mantras of the tongues are proclaimed as follows: joined with the letter *ra*, the wind (*ya*), and the Lord of the Half (*ha*), and adorned with the nasal sound (*nāda*) and the bindu, they consist of the letters from *sa* to *ya*; these are the mantras of the tongues.
One should place the tongue, radiant with flames, in the anus, the genitals, the navel, the heart, at the root of the throat, on the uvula, and between the eyebrows.
The tongue is said to be threefold in its functions, which are distinguished by their qualities:
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and another is considered to be Suprabhā.
Bahurūpā, Suvarṇā, and thirdly Bhadralohitā;
after Lohitā comes Śvetā, then Dhūminī and Karālikā.
The tongue of Fire in rites performed for desired objects is the Rājasyā;
it is smoke-colored, swift as thought, and possesses sparks that are the universal form.
Lohitā, Karālāsyā, and Kālī are said to belong to the Tamas quality;
these seven are employed by practitioners of mantra in cruel rites.
The presiding deities of the tongue are said to be the immortals, the ancestors, the gandharvas, the yakṣas, the nāgas, the piśācas,
and the rākṣasas; these seven are indeed declared to be the presiding deities of the tongues.
One should perform the placement of the limbs of Fire upon the body according to the method previously described,
[reciting] *Sahasrārcis*, *Svastipūrṇa*, and likewise *Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa*.
Dhumavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara—
these are declared to be the six-limbed mantras, joined with their respective seed-syllables (jātis).
Regarding the ritual placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa), the Śāradā-tantra states:
"The preceptor should place the eight forms of Agni upon his own body."
On the crown of the head, on the shoulder, on the left side, on the hip-joint, and on the side of the waist.
Likewise, one should assign them to the [five] aggregates (skandhas) in a clockwise sequence:
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and the one named Havyavāhana.
Another is known as Aśvodaraja, while another is called Vaiśvānara;
Kaumāratejas, Viśvamukha, and Devamukha are also recorded [as names].
The forms of Fire, ending with *namaḥ*, beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and *agnaye*, and starting from the feet [should be placed];
having thus performed the placement of the body (*dehanyāsa*), one should kindle [the fire] with this mantra.
"One should cause to blaze" means having displayed the *jvālinī-mudrā*. Its definition is given in the *Rāghavīya*:
"Having made the two wrists level and the hands with fingers extended, having joined the two middle fingers, one should insert the two thumbs [into the palms]."
That mudrā is called Jvālinī, employed for the rite of igniting fire. Thus it is said.

The mantra for igniting the fire is stated in the *Śāradā*: "O Citpiṅgala, slay, burn, cook; having uttered these pairs [of syllables], say 'O Omniscient One, give the command, svāhā!'—this is the proclaimed mantra."
I bow to Agni, the kindled fire, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations—
pure, golden-hued, fully ignited, and facing in every direction.
One should attend upon the fire according to the rule with this mantra from the Manu-saṃhitā.
In the Sāradā-tilaka: "Then one should sprinkle water purified over the girdle;
[the fire should be surrounded] with pure darbha grass and fuel-sticks covered at their roots, middles, and tips."
The practitioner of mantra should perform the strewing according to the rules, moving clockwise as far as possible;
he should perform this strewing while avoiding the direction of his own seat.
In the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "One should surround the fire with high-pointed *darbha* grasses facing east;
likewise, one should provide three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made from the wood of sacrificial trees."
The best of those who know the tantra should spread [the grass] within the girdle;
however, if the practitioner performs it on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), he should spread everything upon the ground.
The characteristic of the enclosing-stick (paridhi) is as follows:
produced from sacrificial wood, measuring a span (prādeśa) in length, and auspicious;
such is the paridhi described by all the preceptors who are most proficient in the Tantras.
The most excellent of gurus should place boundary-sticks (paridhis) in the directions, excluding the east;
having worshipped them in a clockwise direction, he should install the forms of Brahmā and the other deities within them.
Having honored them thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, he should meditate upon the deity of fire.
The meditation on Fire is as follows: [one should meditate on] the three-eyed one, red in luster, with his crown bound, white,
with a parrot and a red lotus, possessing many ornaments, and seated upon a lotus.
[One should meditate on] Agni, who possesses the power of his desired boons, who holds aloft the svastika and the gesture of fearlessness,
and whose limbs are adorned with a garland of bent lotuses.
In this manner, the supreme guru should meditate with the mind during rites for pacification and the like.
In the rite of killing (māraṇa), one should meditate upon the color black as the color of Kṛṣṇa’s movement.
Having worshipped the eight forms and the six limbs in the hexagon,
one should worship the tongues, radiant with flames, in the center and in all six corners.
One should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) upon the filaments according to the stated method;

one should worship the Mūrtis, who bear the Śakti and the Svastika, upon the petals; then, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions according to the described characteristics.
In the Śāradā-tilaka:
"One should worship the meditated fire in the center with perfumes and other offerings using this mantra:
'O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come here after [the invocation]!'"
Accomplish all rites at the conclusion of the *lohitākṣa* mantra;
this mantra, beloved of the Fire-god, is said to end with the wife of Vahni (the *svāhā* utterance).
In the Kulārṇava:
"Having worshipped Brahmā on the right, one should worship the vessel of ghee;
having brought the vessel of clarified butter (ājya), one should wash it with the Astra-mantra."
Having lifted up coals from the hearth, one should place them there with the Astra-mantra;
having poured clarified butter into it, one should indeed recognize that as "heating."
In the *Śāradā-tilaka*:
"Having poured clarified butter into that [fire] and consecrated it with the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth,
one should extinguish the embers of the northwest wind with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and settle [the fire] upon them."
This is designated as *tāpana* (the heating) by the teachers who are knowers of the tantras.
In the ocean [of the fire]:
having ignited a bunch of *kuśa* grass and cast it into the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should throw it into the fire;
this is called "illumination" (*abhidyotana*) in all rites everywhere.
In the *Śāradā*:
"With a pair of blazing *darbha* blades and the *varman* mantra, he should offer clarified butter into the fire;
this is declared to be the 'illumination' (*abhidyotana*) of the *darbha*."
Furthermore, having rekindled the embers, the wise practitioner should cast [the ladle] into the midst of the clarified butter;
this is declared to be the consecration of the clarified butter (ājyasaṃskāra) by means of the root mantra.
Having kindled a pair of *darbha* blades and cast them into the clarified butter, one should throw them into the fire;
this, performed by the preceptor with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, is indeed the rite of purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*).
Having consecrated it with the root mantra, one should protect it while reciting the weapon mantra;
then, having displayed the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās, that clarified butter becomes of the nature of nectar.
Regarding the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa):
having placed a pair of darbha blades, each a span in length and joined at their knots, within [the hands],
one should form two portions as wings and visualize them as white and its opposite [black].
Having meditated upon the *iḍā* channel on the left side and the *piṅgalā* on the right,
and the *suṣumnā* in the middle, one should perform the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rule.
Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles fashioned according to the prescribed rite,
the Guru should thereafter take those two ladles in his hands with their openings facing downwards.
Taking blades of darbha grass, the preceptor should heat them three times in the fire and purify their tips,
middles, and roots respectively with them.
Having taken them with the left hand, the practitioner of mantra should sprinkle them with the right;
having heated them again, he should cast the darbha grasses into the fire.
Taking the *sruva* ladle, the wise one should hold it at one-third [of its length];
leaving aside four finger-breadths (*vedāṅgula*), he should hold it with the *śaṅkha* mudrā.
In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"Taking ghee from the southern portion with the *sruva* ladle,
the Guru should offer it into the right eye of the fire, saying 'To Agni, svāhā!', while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*."
Taking that [liquid] from the left side, he should offer it into the fire in the left eye with the mantra "To Soma, Svāhā," using the heart-mantra.
Taking clarified butter from the center, the Guru should offer it into the eye on the forehead of the fire with the mantra: "To Agni and Soma, Svāhā!"
Having taken a portion of clarified butter from the southern part with the heart-mantra using the *sruva* ladle, one should offer it into the mouth of the fire with the mantra:
"Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."
Thus the Guru should perform the opening of the eyes and mouth of the fire;
he should again offer oblations with clarified butter using the Vyāhṛtis together with the stars (Savitṛ),
and the Guru should offer oblations three times with the Vaisvānara mantra.
In the *Samayātantra*:
"O Goddess of the gods! One should perform the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) in sequence, using each individual syllable of the root-mantra ending in *svāhā*."
The rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana),
as well as the birth ceremony (jātakarma), the naming (nāmakṛti), and the first outing (niṣkramaṇa).
The tonsure ceremony, the initiation into sacred study,
the ritual cutting of the beard, and marriage— these are the purificatory rites for auspicious actions.
Then, having worshipped the two parents with fire, one should lead them into the heart;
according to the rule, one should perform five oblations with the fire-mantra.
The preceptor should offer five fuel-sticks, drenched with root-juice, tips, and clarified butter,
according to the rule using the Heart-mantra, but without the word *svāhā*.
In the *Śāradā*:
"The best of those who know mantras should offer one oblation for each of the mantra, tongue, limbs, and forms of the fire, in due order and according to the rule."
Having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle and poured it four times into the *sruc* while holding it steady,
the preceptor, standing with a concentrated mind, should offer it into the fire with the Vahni-mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ" for the sake of perfection.

In the Mādhavīya-saṃhitā: "Alternatively, sacrificial twigs of the Palāśa tree should be twelve finger-breadths long, straight, naturally dried, with their bark intact, free from blemishes, and uniform."
Alternatively, they are prescribed as being ten finger-breadths long, measured by the little finger;
however, if those of the span (prādeśa) length are unavailable, all [the other sizes] may be used for the oblation.
One should offer eleven oblations with the mantra of Mahāgaṇeśa from the Gautamīya;
this is remembered as the common "mouth of the fire" for all the deities.
O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings the tongue named Bahurūpā, one should offer sixteen oblations of clarified butter according to the rule with the root mantra;
this indeed is the unification of the faces.
In the Śāradā-tantra: Then, having worshipped the pedestal,
one should worship that deity who bestows desired boons in the form of fire within the sacrificial fire.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations into its mouth twenty-five times with clarified butter using the root mantra; this is indeed the unification of the faces.
Contemplating the identity of the fire and the deity with one's own self,
one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
This connection of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) has been taught by those who know the scriptures;
one should offer a single oblation for each of the attendants, beginning with the limbs.
Having again performed the oblation with the *vyāhṛtis* according to the prescribed rule,
one should offer sesame seeds and clarified butter by the thousands and so forth, in accordance with the ritual injunctions.
When the sacrificial substance is not specified, sesame and clarified butter are said to be the oblation.
A wise person should offer only a small amount into the fire in all rites;
likewise, one should pour the remnants of the clarified butter into the various portions in their proper sequence.
Regarding the specific details, another tantra states: "In the [portion] for Agni, saying 'svāhā,' one should cast the remainder into the fire with:
*oṃ bhūr agnaye pṛthivyai mahate ca svāhā*. *Oṃ bhuvo vāyave*..."

Svāhā to the intermediate space and to the great heaven! Om, svāhā to the self-luminous moon, to the lunar mansions, to the quarters, and to the great one! Om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, svāhā to the self-luminous moon, to the lunar mansions, to the quarters, and to the great one!
Having taken up the *sruva* ladle and filled it again with clarified butter,
and having placed the oblation materials therein, it is then established at the navel.

O Dear One, having performed the naming rite for the fire, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Again, one should offer the final oblation with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam," and the best of practitioners should then unite his chosen deity within the abode of his own heart.
Regarding the description of the mouth of Agni in the *Śāradā*:
"Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, here is the nose."
Where the eye has little light, from there comes the ash, which is the head;
where the fire blazes intensely, that is the mouth of Jātavedas.
Regarding the fruit of the oblation performed upon the ears and other [senses], the Śāradā-tantra states: "By offering an oblation on the ears, one incurs deafness; on the eyes, one suffers injury."
Mental anguish occurs in the nose; indeed, an oblation into the Śiva-fire causes colic.
An oblation into the fire of vermilion and the rising sun in the mouth brings auspiciousness.
The sound of a drum, a cloud, an elephant king, or fire is auspicious.
Smoke resembling the moon, sandalwood, or the kunda flower bestows the accomplishment of all aims;
fire with a sound like that of a donkey or a crow brings about total destruction.
A black horse with black hooves would destroy the sacrificer;
likewise one resembling the color of a nāga, a campaka, a punnāga, a pāṭala, or an āyūthikā flower.
The auspicious fragrance of fire is described by those learned in the Tantras as being like that of the red lotus, the blue lotus, the white water lily, clarified butter, and guggulu resin.
If the fire emits a foul odor, it will bring about suffering;
when such defects occur, the preceptor should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra for the sake of expiation.
Thus concludes the determination of the rules for the fire-oblation (homa).
Regarding the meaning of the names such as Sarvamaṅgalā and others, he states the etymological meanings (yogārtha) of these names:
Since you are worthy of being the auspiciousness of all, you are therefore called Sarvamaṅgalā;
and since you grant boons to mortals, you are celebrated as Varadā.
Because you conquer all difficulties without exception, you are called Durgā;
because you bestow welfare upon your devotees, you are indeed sung of as Śaṅkarī.
For all living beings here who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra,
this alone is the supreme boat for the liberation of men, ever difficult to find.
For those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, Durgā alone is the supreme state;
Durgā alone is all the deities; Durgā alone is the Vedic ritual.
Durgā alone is supreme knowledge; Durgā alone is supreme strength.
There is no being, whether stationary or moving, that exists apart from you.
Durgā alone is the supreme goddess; Durgā alone is the supreme state.
Durgā alone is the supreme knowledge; Durgā alone is indeed knowledge itself.
Durgā alone is the supreme truth; Durgā alone is the ultimate refuge;
Durgā alone is the supreme deity; Durgā alone is the supreme medicine.
One alone is difficult to attain, yet it brings ultimate happiness; one alone is difficult to attain, yet it is supreme peace;
one alone is difficult to attain, yet it is the highest contentment; one alone is difficult to attain, yet it is the greatest glory.

Durgā alone is the supreme reality; this entire universe is non-different from Durgā. The two syllables of the name "Durgā" are the provisions for the journey when life departs, the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra, and the salvation from the ocean of distress.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Homa and Other Rites," in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, composed by the venerable Brahmānandagiri, the wandering ascetic (avadhūta) and supreme sage (paramahaṃsa-tīrtha).
It is concluded. || 18 ||
This work is completed.
